scenario: A 27-year-old man is stabbed in the back. The blade enters the left side of the cord at about T8. Two days later the left leg is weak, vibration and joint position are gone in the left foot, and pain and temperature are lost on the right from about T10 downward. The right leg is strong and the left trunk still feels pinprick.
question: Which pattern of tract damage explains these findings?
options: Left lateral corticospinal and left dorsal columns at T8, plus right spinothalamic fibers that crossed a level or two below entry
Right motor cortex, because weakness is always contralateral to the lesion
A complete cord transection, with spinal shock explaining the asymmetry
Left spinothalamic tract only, because pain loss is the localizing sign
Right dorsal columns, because proprioception loss is contralateral in the cord
correctAnswer: Left lateral corticospinal and left dorsal columns at T8, plus right spinothalamic fibers that crossed a level or two below entry
explanation: Hemisection hits the already-crossed lateral corticospinal tract and the uncrossed dorsal columns on the same side, so motor and vibration loss are ipsilateral. Spinothalamic fibers cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments of entry, so pain and temperature loss is contralateral and begins slightly below the lesion. Right motor cortex is the trap if you apply the brainstem crossing rule inside the cord; the corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla. A complete transection would weaken both legs and wipe sensation on both sides. Left spinothalamic damage alone would not cause ipsilateral paralysis or dorsal-column loss. Dorsal-column fibers do not cross until the medulla, so proprioceptive loss is ipsilateral, not right-sided.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden vertigo, hiccups, and a hoarse voice. The right side of his face has lost pain and temperature, the left body has lost pain and temperature, and the right palate does not rise. There is no hemiparesis. A student localizes this to the right middle cerebral artery because the face is involved.
question: Which vessel and which spared tract best fit?
options: Right vertebral or PICA territory, with the corticospinal tract spared in the medial medulla
Right MCA superior division, with the face area of the cortex infarcted
Left medial medulla, because the body findings are contralateral
Right AICA with lateral pontine hearing loss as the required feature
Anterior spinal artery, because the medulla is supplied only by that vessel
correctAnswer: Right vertebral or PICA territory, with the corticospinal tract spared in the medial medulla
explanation: Ipsilateral face pain loss, contralateral body pain loss, nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness, palate), and vestibular nuclei without hemiparesis are lateral medulla. The pyramid is medial, so vertebral or PICA infarction spares strength; that missing hemiparesis is what excludes a cortical stroke. MCA would cause contralateral face and arm weakness, not crossed pain loss or a hoarse palate. Left medial medulla would cause contralateral arm and leg weakness and ipsilateral tongue weakness, not this sensory cross. AICA is lateral pons and typically adds hearing loss from the labyrinthine artery; hearing is not the finding here. The anterior spinal artery supplies medial medulla, not the lateral tegmentum.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 70-year-old woman develops right arm and leg weakness with preserved face strength, loss of vibration in the right limbs, and a left tongue that deviates to the left. Pinprick on the body is intact.
question: Where is the lesion?
options: Left medial medulla, affecting the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve
Right motor cortex, arm and leg area, sparing the face
Left lateral medulla, because the tongue is a cranial nerve
Right medial medulla, because the weak limbs are on the right
Left internal capsule, which explains an ipsilateral tongue
correctAnswer: Left medial medulla, affecting the pyramid, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nerve
explanation: The hypoglossal nerve exits medially and is ipsilateral, so a left tongue means a left lesion. The pyramid has not yet reached the spinal cord but has already been destined to cross, so left pyramid damage weakens the right arm and leg and spares the face, whose corticobulbar fibers have left higher up. The medial lemniscus has already crossed, so vibration loss is also contralateral. Right cortex would not deviate the tongue to the left or spare pain while killing vibration in this pattern. Lateral medulla spares the pyramid and hits spinothalamic and nucleus ambiguus, not the tongue. Right medial medulla would point the tongue right and weaken the left limbs. An internal-capsule lesion does not hit the peripheral hypoglossal nerve.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 48-year-old woman has a dilated left pupil that reacts poorly to light, with the eye down and out and ptosis. She has a sudden severe headache. Glucose is normal and there is no painless chronic course. A colleague says diabetic microvascular ischemia and plans observation.
question: Which mechanism makes observation the wrong plan?
options: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the dorsomedial parasympathetic fibers before the motor fibers
Diabetic ischemia hits the superficial parasympathetic fibers first, so the pupil is the earliest sign
The trochlear nerve is the one that dilates the pupil
A cavernous sinus lesion would dilate the pupil and spare every other eye movement
Uncal herniation dilates the contralateral pupil first
correctAnswer: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the dorsomedial parasympathetic fibers before the motor fibers
explanation: Parasympathetic pupillary fibers travel on the outside of the third nerve, so extrinsic compression from a PCOM aneurysm dilates the pupil early and is a surgical emergency, especially with a thunderclap headache. Diabetic microvascular ischemia affects the central motor fibers and typically spares the pupil, so 'pupil involved, therefore diabetes, observe' reverses the rule. The trochlear nerve depresses and intorts; it does not carry pupillary parasympathetics. Cavernous sinus disease hits III, IV, V1, V2, and VI together, not an isolated down-and-out eye. Uncal herniation compresses the ipsilateral third nerve, not the opposite pupil first.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 31-year-old woman has diplopia on right gaze. The left eye does not adduct, and the right eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is preserved. She had a prior episode of unilateral vision loss that recovered.
question: Which tract is damaged, and why is convergence spared?
options: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus; convergence uses a midbrain pathway that bypasses the MLF
Left oculomotor nerve; convergence and adduction share that nerve so both must fail
Right abducens nucleus, which would paralyze ipsilateral gaze entirely
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus, on the side of the abducting eye
Optic nerve, because a prior episode of vision loss means the lesion is ocular
correctAnswer: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus; convergence uses a midbrain pathway that bypasses the MLF
explanation: The MLF links the abducens nucleus to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus for conjugate gaze. A left MLF lesion blocks left adduction on right gaze while the right eye abducts and beats; multiple sclerosis is the classic cause in a young adult, fitting her prior optic neuritis. Convergence is intact because that signal reaches medial rectus neurons without the MLF, which is how INO is separated from an oculomotor palsy. A left third-nerve palsy would also lose convergence, pupil control, and depression. A right abducens nucleus lesion would prevent both eyes from looking right. The MLF is named for the eye that fails to adduct, not the abducting eye. A prior optic neuritis does not cause a gaze disconjugate pattern.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 66-year-old man has a right homonymous hemianopia. The central few degrees of the right field are spared in both eyes. Motor strength is normal. The occipital pole is intact on the clinical story you are given; the infarct is in the left occipital lobe but not at the pole.
question: Why is the macula spared?
options: The occipital pole, which sees the macula, has collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery
The optic chiasm has been cut, which always spares central vision
A left temporal lobe lesion hits Meyer loop and spares the macula by definition
Macular fibers never reach the occipital cortex
The right eye's blindness is monocular, so the left eye compensates at the macula
correctAnswer: The occipital pole, which sees the macula, has collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery
explanation: PCA infarction of the visual cortex causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. The macula is mapped at the occipital pole, which often stays alive through MCA collateral, so central vision is spared. A chiasm lesion causes a bitemporal field cut, not a homonymous one. Meyer loop in the temporal lobe causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia without this macular story. Macular fibers do reach the occipital pole. The defect is the same in both eyes, so it is not monocular blindness with the other eye filling in.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 44-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has fever, a swollen left eye, and double vision. The left eye cannot abduct. Forehead and cheek sensation are reduced. The pupil is involved and the eyelid droops. A nasal furuncle was squeezed two days ago.
question: Which combination is in the cavernous sinus, and which nerve is typically affected first by stretch?
options: III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, with VI affected early because it is free in the sinus
II only, because orbital swelling is an optic nerve problem
VII and VIII, because facial pain and eye movement share the facial canal
V3 and XII, because jaw and tongue sensation travel through the sinus
The abducens nerve outside the sinus and a spared trigeminal nerve
correctAnswer: III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, with VI affected early because it is free in the sinus
explanation: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis from a facial danger-zone infection inflames the structures in the sinus: III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, plus the carotid sympathetics. VI lies free in the lumen and is often the first ocular motor nerve to fail, which matches the abducting palsy plus forehead and cheek numbness. The optic nerve is in the orbit, not the sinus, and would cut acuity rather than this combination. VII and VIII are in the temporal bone. V3 exits the foramen ovale and does not traverse the cavernous sinus. A pure abducens palsy without V1 or V2 loss is not this picture.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 19-year-old man is unconscious after a motorcycle crash. The right pupil becomes dilated and fixed while the left pupil is still small. CT shows a right epidural hematoma and early right uncal herniation. Blood pressure later rises as the pulse slows.
question: What is being compressed, and what does the later vital-sign change mean?
options: The right oculomotor nerve against the tentorium; Cushing triad means rising intracranial pressure and brainstem compression
The left oculomotor nerve, because herniation always dilates the opposite pupil
The right abducens nerve, which carries the parasympathetic pupil fibers
Isolated cortical blindness, which dilates one pupil and slows the pulse
A Horner syndrome, which dilates the ipsilateral pupil
correctAnswer: The right oculomotor nerve against the tentorium; Cushing triad means rising intracranial pressure and brainstem compression
explanation: The uncus of the temporal lobe herniates through the tentorial notch and compresses the ipsilateral third nerve, so the pupil on the side of the mass dilates first. Hypertension and bradycardia are the Cushing response to brainstem ischemia from high intracranial pressure, a late and dangerous sign. The contralateral pupil is the trap; the first dilated pupil is ipsilateral. The abducens nerve does not carry pupillary parasympathetics. Cortical blindness does not fix one pupil or cause Cushing physiology. Horner syndrome constricts the pupil and adds ptosis and anhidrosis; it does not dilate it.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 22-year-old man is hit in the temple, loses consciousness, wakes and talks, then deteriorates over two hours. The pupil on the side of the blow dilates. A second patient, an older adult with a fall a week ago, has a fluctuating headache and a crescentic collection that crosses suture lines but not the falx.
question: Which vessels and which spaces fit these two patients?
options: Middle meningeal artery in the potential epidural space; bridging veins in the subdural space
Bridging veins for the lucid-interval hematoma; middle meningeal artery for the week-old crescent
Both are subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm
Both are intraparenchymal hypertensive bleeds in the putamen
The lucid interval is a subdural hygroma from a torn arachnoid granulation
correctAnswer: Middle meningeal artery in the potential epidural space; bridging veins in the subdural space
explanation: A temporal blow, lucid interval, and rapid decline are arterial epidural bleeding from the middle meningeal artery under the pterion. A slower, fluctuating bleed in an older patient is venous, from bridging veins torn in the subdural space; the collection is crescentic and can cross sutures. Swapping the vessels is the usual miss. Aneurysmal subarachnoid blood sits in cisterns and presents with thunderclap pain, not these two time courses. Hypertensive putamen bleeds are inside the brain. A hygroma is not the arterial lucid-interval hematoma.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 74-year-old man has a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, and forgetfulness. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is normal and ventricles are large out of proportion to the sulci. A second patient, an infant, has a huge head, a sunset gaze, and imaging that stops the aqueduct.
question: Which mechanisms match?
options: Impaired arachnoid granulation resorption with a normal pressure; aqueduct obstruction with trapped lateral and third ventricles
Both are noncommunicating hydrocephalus from choroid plexus overproduction
The adult has Alzheimer disease, which enlarges ventricles by sulcal atrophy in the same pattern
The infant has a Dandy-Walker malformation as the only cause of aqueduct stenosis
Both need a third ventriculostomy because granulation failure is treated by bypassing the aqueduct
correctAnswer: Impaired arachnoid granulation resorption with a normal pressure; aqueduct obstruction with trapped lateral and third ventricles
explanation: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is communicating: CSF gets out of the ventricles but is not resorbed at the arachnoid granulations, so pressure is normal or only briefly high and the clinical triad is gait, incontinence, and dementia. Aqueduct stenosis blocks flow out of the third ventricle, so the lateral and third ventricles enlarge and the fourth does not; that is noncommunicating. Choroid plexus papilloma can overproduce CSF but is not the mechanism of either classic case. Alzheimer atrophy enlarges sulci as well as ventricles, which is the imaging contrast with NPH. Dandy-Walker is a different posterior-fossa malformation, not the definition of aqueduct stenosis. Third ventriculostomy bypasses an aqueduct block; it is not the logic for granulation failure.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 58-year-old man who smokes has trouble rising from a chair that gets a little easier as he keeps trying. His mouth is dry, and reflexes are reduced. Strength improves after he exercises the limb for a few seconds. A second patient, a young woman, has ptosis that is worse at the end of the day and gets worse, not better, with repeated use. Chest imaging in the man shows a hilar mass.
question: Which receptors and which tumor association fit the man rather than the woman?
options: Presynaptic P/Q voltage-gated calcium channels, associated with small-cell lung cancer
Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, associated with a thymoma
Muscle ryanodine receptors, associated with malignant hyperthermia
Sodium channels on peripheral nerve, associated with multiple sclerosis
Nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglia only, with no skeletal-muscle effect
correctAnswer: Presynaptic P/Q voltage-gated calcium channels, associated with small-cell lung cancer
explanation: Lambert-Eaton is a presynaptic attack on voltage-gated calcium channels, so less acetylcholine is released. Repeated use can temporarily improve strength, reflexes are down, and autonomic dryness is common. Small-cell lung cancer is the classic paraneoplastic source. The young woman has myasthenia gravis: postsynaptic acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, fatigable weakness that worsens with use, and a thymoma association, not a smoker’s hilar mass. Ryanodine receptors are the malignant-hyperthermia muscle channel, not this pattern. Multiple sclerosis is central demyelination, not a neuromuscular junction that improves with repetition. Autonomic ganglia alone would not explain the skeletal-muscle facilitation.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 34-year-old woman has descending weakness, double vision, and dilated pupils that react poorly. Sensation is normal. She canned vegetables last week and a friend who ate the same food is ill. There is no fatiguing ptosis that worsens only late in the day and no thymic mass.
question: Where does the toxin act, and which finding separates this from myasthenia?
options: It prevents acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal; pupils are involved, unlike myasthenia
It blocks postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; pupils are spared, as in myasthenia
It destroys anterior horn cells, so sensation is lost in a stocking pattern
It demyelinates peripheral nerves, so a spinal tap shows high protein and no cells
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so pupils constrict and secretions pour out
correctAnswer: It prevents acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal; pupils are involved, unlike myasthenia
explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release. The illness is descending, and because autonomic synapses are also cholinergic, pupils dilate. That pupillary involvement is the board separator from myasthenia gravis, which spares the pupil. A postsynaptic receptor block is myasthenia, and that option also gets the pupil wrong. Anterior horn-cell loss is polio or ALS and does not start with poorly reactive pupils after home canning. Albuminocytologic dissociation is Guillain-Barré, usually ascending after an infection. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is organophosphate poisoning, which constricts pupils.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 40-year-old farm worker is wet with insecticide. He has pinpoint pupils, diarrhea, vomiting, bradycardia, wheezing, and fasciculations with weakness. He is given a large dose of atropine. The secretions dry and the heart rate rises, but he remains weak and still fasciculates.
question: Why did atropine not fix the weakness, and what should be added?
options: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only; pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase at nicotinic sites if given before aging
Atropine blocks nicotinic receptors, so weakness means the dose was too small
Pralidoxime is a muscarinic agonist and would worsen secretions
The weakness is a benzodiazepine-deficiency state and is treated with flumazenil
Succinylcholine will outcompete the toxin at the neuromuscular junction
correctAnswer: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only; pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase at nicotinic sites if given before aging
explanation: Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase. Atropine competes at muscarinic receptors, so it dries secretions and raises heart rate, but skeletal muscle and ganglia use nicotinic receptors, which atropine does not block. Pralidoxime pulls the phosphate off the enzyme if aging has not locked it. Saying atropine is nicotinic reverses the pharmacology and would make you keep giving atropine for paralysis it cannot fix. Pralidoxime is not a muscarinic agonist. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and is irrelevant and unsafe here. Succinylcholine is a depolarizing blocker and would add paralysis, not restore acetylcholine breakdown.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A dentist injects lidocaine around an acidic dental abscess. The patient still feels the incision. The same dose works well on healthy tissue nearby. The student proposes a larger dose of a permanently charged anesthetic because 'infected tissue needs a drug that is already ionized.'
question: Why did the anesthetic fail, and why is a permanently charged drug worse?
options: In acid the drug is protonated and cannot cross the membrane to reach the inner sodium-channel site; a permanently charged drug cannot enter from outside
Infection induces CYP3A4 in the gum and clears lidocaine in seconds
Sodium channels in infected tissue open only from the outside, so the charged form works better
Lidocaine blocks potassium channels, which are closed by acid
The abscess is ischemic, so a charged drug is required to bind the outside of the channel
correctAnswer: In acid the drug is protonated and cannot cross the membrane to reach the inner sodium-channel site; a permanently charged drug cannot enter from outside
explanation: Local anesthetics are weak bases. They must be uncharged to cross the membrane, then become charged inside to block the sodium channel from the axoplasm. Pus is acidic, so the drug stays charged outside and never reaches the site. A permanently charged analog cannot cross either, which is why that suggestion fails. Gingival CYP induction is not the mechanism of a failed block. The binding site is on the inside, not the outside. Lidocaine’s local-anesthetic action is sodium-channel block, not potassium-channel block. Ischemia does not create a requirement for an extracellular charged drug.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 67-year-old man has a resting tremor, rigidity, and slow steps. Substantia nigra compacta neurons are lost. A teaching slide asks what that loss does to the two striatal pathways and why a D2 blocker would make him worse.
question: Which statement is right?
options: Less nigral dopamine removes facilitation of the direct (D1) pathway and removes inhibition of the indirect (D2) pathway, so the thalamus is over-inhibited; a D2 blocker worsens that
Dopamine loss turns the direct pathway up, so movements become large and dancing
The subthalamic nucleus dies first, which is why tremor starts
D2 receptors excite the direct pathway, so a blocker increases movement
The striatum releases more acetylcholine because dopamine loss destroys cholinergic interneurons
correctAnswer: Less nigral dopamine removes facilitation of the direct (D1) pathway and removes inhibition of the indirect (D2) pathway, so the thalamus is over-inhibited; a D2 blocker worsens that
explanation: Nigral dopamine normally turns up the direct pathway through D1 and turns down the indirect pathway through D2. Losing it does both, and both changes increase inhibition of the thalamus, so movement shrinks. A D2 blocker imitates that indirect-pathway problem and worsens parkinsonism. The direct pathway is underactive, not overactive; overactivity of movement is the Huntington or hemiballismus direction. The subthalamic nucleus is the lesion of hemiballismus, not the first loss in Parkinson disease. D2 receptors are on the indirect pathway and are inhibitory there. Cholinergic interneurons are relatively overactive, not destroyed; that is why antimuscarinic drugs can help tremor.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 38-year-old man has choreiform movements and a father who died with the same illness in his fifties. Caudate atrophy is marked. A different patient has wild flinging of one arm that began the day after a small deep stroke.
question: Which nuclei fit, and what does anticipation imply for the first patient?
options: Caudate loss from a CAG repeat that expands in successive generations; contralateral subthalamic nucleus for the flinging arm
Subthalamic nucleus for the hereditary chorea; caudate for the acute one-limb fling
Substantia nigra for both, because both are hypokinetic
Cerebellar hemisphere for the chorea, because CAG diseases are all spinocerebellar
Bilateral subthalamic nuclei for a disease that gets worse in the children
correctAnswer: Caudate loss from a CAG repeat that expands in successive generations; contralateral subthalamic nucleus for the flinging arm
explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG expansion in huntingtin. Anticipation, earlier and worse disease in the next generation, follows further expansion, often in spermatogenesis, which fits a father-to-child story. The caudate is lost and movements are extra, not missing. Hemiballismus is an acute contralateral subthalamic lesion, classically a lacunar stroke, and it is one limb, not a family disease. Swapping the nuclei is the usual miss. Both are hyperkinetic, so substantia nigra loss, which is hypokinetic, does not fit. Not every CAG disease is cerebellar. Bilateral subthalamic damage is not the Huntington mechanism.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 19-year-old man has a new tremor, depressed mood, and mild liver-enzyme elevation. Slit lamp shows a brown-green ring at the corneal rim. Serum ceruloplasmin is low. A sibling was treated with a drug that chelates copper and another relative was kept on oral zinc after the liver recovered.
question: Which protein failed, and why is zinc not the initial chelator?
options: ATP7B cannot excrete copper into bile or attach it to ceruloplasmin; zinc blocks gut absorption and is maintenance, not the drug that removes a large copper load
ATP7A failed, the same protein as Menkes disease, so hair is kinky and the liver is spared
Ferroportin failed, so the ring is iron and the treatment is deferoxamine
Ceruloplasmin itself is the mutated enzyme, so chelation cannot help
Alpha-1 antitrypsin failed, which deposits copper in the basal ganglia
correctAnswer: ATP7B cannot excrete copper into bile or attach it to ceruloplasmin; zinc blocks gut absorption and is maintenance, not the drug that removes a large copper load
explanation: Wilson disease is hepatic ATP7B failure. Copper is not excreted in bile and is not loaded onto ceruloplasmin, so serum ceruloplasmin is low, a Kayser-Fleischer ring forms, and the basal ganglia and liver fill with copper. A chelator such as trientine or penicillamine removes stored copper. Zinc induces metallothionein in the gut and reduces absorption; it maintains a treated patient and does not empty a large existing load. ATP7A is Menkes disease, an uptake problem with kinky hair and deficiency, not hepatic overload. Ferroportin and deferoxamine are iron. The ceruloplasmin level is low because copper is not incorporated; the gene is ATP7B, not the ceruloplasmin gene. Alpha-1 antitrypsin lung and liver disease does not make a copper ring.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 71-year-old woman has a macrocytic anemia and numbness in both feet. Vibration is gone at the toes and the gait is unsteady with eyes closed. Methylmalonic acid is high and homocysteine is high. She has been taking folic acid, and the anemia improved for a month while the numbness worsened.
question: Why did folate help the blood count and hurt the neurologic choice?
options: Folate bypasses the megaloblastic block in marrow but does not repair the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase pathway in myelin
Folate replaces B12 as the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
High methylmalonic acid means folate deficiency, so more folate is the specific fix
The dorsal columns are spared in B12 deficiency, so the numbness is diabetic and unrelated
Folate deficiency raises methylmalonic acid and B12 deficiency raises only homocysteine
correctAnswer: Folate bypasses the megaloblastic block in marrow but does not repair the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase pathway in myelin
explanation: B12 is required for methionine synthase and for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Folate can feed the marrow methylation cycle enough to improve the anemia, which hides the diagnosis, but it does nothing for the mutase reaction. Myelin injury continues, which is the subacute combined degeneration of dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts. Folate is not a mutase cofactor. High methylmalonic acid points to B12, not folate. Dorsal columns are exactly what B12 deficiency hits. The lab split is the opposite of the last option: both deficiencies raise homocysteine, and only B12 raises methylmalonic acid.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 55-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in confused, with nystagmus and a wide gait. A nurse is about to infuse a liter of dextrose because the fingerstick is borderline. He has not received vitamins.
question: What can glucose administration do before thiamine, and which structures are at risk?
options: Glucose drives thiamine-dependent pyruvate dehydrogenase and can precipitate Wernicke injury in the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray
Glucose binds GABA and causes immediate respiratory arrest unrelated to vitamins
Thiamine is required only for heme synthesis, so the risk is acute porphyria
The mammillary bodies are injured by folate deficiency, not thiamine
Dextrose is safe because Wernicke disease is a glucose-excess state already
correctAnswer: Glucose drives thiamine-dependent pyruvate dehydrogenase and can precipitate Wernicke injury in the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray
explanation: Thiamine is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase. A glucose load increases flux through those enzymes and can exhaust the last thiamine, worsening Wernicke encephalopathy. The vulnerable zones are the mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, which matches confusion, eye-movement change, and ataxia. Glucose does not bind GABA. Acute porphyria is an ALA synthase problem, not this triad. Folate deficiency does not target the mammillary bodies. He is thiamine-poor, not glucose-toxic; the danger is giving sugar first.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 49-year-old woman with chronic hyponatremia from a thiazide has sodium corrected from 112 to 138 mmol/L over 12 hours because she seized once. Two days later she is quadriparetic and cannot speak clearly, but she seems aware. MRI shows a central pontine lesion. The seizure has stopped.
question: What happened, and what pace would have avoided it?
options: Rapid rise in serum osmolality stripped myelin from the basis pontis; chronic hyponatremia should be corrected slowly, often near 8 mmol/L in 24 hours or less in high-risk patients
The pontine lesion is an infarct from the seizure, and any sodium goal is safe
Too-slow correction caused the demyelination
The lesion is central pontine myelinolysis from low sodium itself, independent of the correction rate
This is Wernicke encephalopathy, and the MRI lesion is the mammillary body
correctAnswer: Rapid rise in serum osmolality stripped myelin from the basis pontis; chronic hyponatremia should be corrected slowly, often near 8 mmol/L in 24 hours or less in high-risk patients
explanation: Oligodendrocytes in a chronically hyponatremic brain have adjusted. A fast osmotic rise pulls water out and demyelinates the central pons, so the patient is locked in or quadriparetic while awareness remains. The correction here, 26 mmol/L in half a day, is far above a cautious limit. A seizure does not infarct the center of the pons in this pattern. Slow correction does not cause osmotic demyelination; the risk of slow correction is ongoing severe hyponatremia, which is a different problem. The low sodium alone did not make this delayed lesion; the jump did. Mammillary bodies are Wernicke disease, not a central pontine T2 lesion after a sodium spike.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: After pituitary surgery, patient A has high urine output, low urine osmolality, rising serum sodium, and thirst. Patient B, with a small-cell lung cancer, has low serum sodium, high urine sodium, concentrated urine, and a normal volume status without edema.
question: Which ADH states fit?
options: A lacks ADH effect, so water is lost and sodium rises; B has too much ADH, so water is retained and sodium falls while urine stays concentrated
Both have too much ADH; the only difference is oral intake
A has SIADH because urine output is high; B has diabetes insipidus because sodium is low
B should be given normal saline as the primary treatment because he is volume depleted
Desmopressin would worsen patient A and fix patient B
correctAnswer: A lacks ADH effect, so water is lost and sodium rises; B has too much ADH, so water is retained and sodium falls while urine stays concentrated
explanation: Central diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery is absent ADH. The kidney cannot concentrate, urine is dilute, water leaves, and serum sodium rises. SIADH from small-cell cancer is the opposite: ADH is high, urine is inappropriately concentrated, and water retention drops the serum sodium in a clinically euvolemic patient. Calling both 'too much ADH' misses the sodium direction. High urine output is diabetes insipidus, not SIADH, and a low sodium with concentrated urine is SIADH, not diabetes insipidus. SIADH is treated with fluid restriction, not a saline bolus as if the patient were dry; saline can worsen the sodium if the urine is very concentrated. Desmopressin replaces ADH and helps central diabetes insipidus; it would worsen SIADH.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 9-year-old girl stops talking for a few seconds many times an hour, then resumes as if nothing happened. There is no fall and no postictal confusion. EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave. A relative with focal seizures was helped by carbamazepine, and the family asks for the same drug.
question: Which channel is the right target, and why is carbamazepine a poor choice?
options: Thalamic T-type calcium channels, blocked by ethosuximide; carbamazepine can worsen absence
Voltage-gated sodium channels only, so carbamazepine is first-line for 3 Hz spike-and-wave
GABA-B receptors, blocked by baclofen, which stops absence
NMDA receptors, blocked by ketamine as outpatient therapy
The same sodium channel as phenytoin, because all childhood seizures share one mechanism
correctAnswer: Thalamic T-type calcium channels, blocked by ethosuximide; carbamazepine can worsen absence
explanation: Childhood absence is a thalamocortical oscillation that depends on T-type calcium current. Ethosuximide blocks that current and is the narrow drug for pure absence. Carbamazepine and phenytoin, which are sodium-channel drugs useful for focal seizures, can aggravate absence, so the family history is a trap. Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist and can promote spike-and-wave, not treat it. Ketamine is not outpatient absence therapy. Not every childhood seizure uses the phenytoin mechanism; the EEG and the brief, nonconvulsive pauses are the clue to switch mechanisms.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man in convulsive status epilepticus receives lorazepam and the seizures stop. A student asks how a benzodiazepine increases GABA effect compared with a barbiturate, and whether the benzodiazepine opens the channel by itself.
question: Which pairing is correct?
options: Benzodiazepines increase how often the GABA-A channel opens when GABA is present; barbiturates lengthen each opening and can open the channel at high doses without GABA
Benzodiazepines lengthen channel opening and work without GABA; barbiturates only increase frequency
Both drugs block GABA-A, which is why they stop seizures
Lorazepam acts on GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord, like baclofen
Status epilepticus is treated first with a neuromuscular blocker because the brain activity has already stopped
correctAnswer: Benzodiazepines increase how often the GABA-A channel opens when GABA is present; barbiturates lengthen each opening and can open the channel at high doses without GABA
explanation: Both drug classes facilitate GABA-A chloride channels, but the kinetics differ. Benzodiazepines need GABA and increase opening frequency. Barbiturates increase open duration and, at higher concentration, have direct agonist activity, which is one reason overdose is more depressant. Reversing frequency and duration is a standard miss. They do not block GABA; blocking GABA would cause seizures. Lorazepam is not a GABA-B drug; baclofen is. A paralytic stops the visible jerk but not the cortical seizure, so it is not the first treatment of status.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 24-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry is started on carbamazepine for focal seizures. Two weeks later he has a painful rash, fever, and a sodium of 124 mmol/L. He also takes a drug whose level has fallen because of a new enzyme inducer. HLA typing was not done.
question: Which mechanisms sit in this one drug?
options: HLA-B*1502 raises Stevens-Johnson risk, the drug stimulates ADH-like water retention, and it induces CYP3A4
HLA-B*5701 is the carbamazepine allele, and the drug inhibits CYP so other levels rise
The rash is a dose-related histamine effect with no HLA link
Hyponatremia means renal salt wasting from aldosterone blockade
Carbamazepine closes T-type calcium channels and is first-line for absence
correctAnswer: HLA-B*1502 raises Stevens-Johnson risk, the drug stimulates ADH-like water retention, and it induces CYP3A4
explanation: Carbamazepine is a sodium-channel antiseizure drug with three traps in this vignette. HLA-B*1502, enriched in some Asian ancestries, marks a high risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so the allele is checked before starting. The drug can cause SIADH and hyponatremia. It induces CYP3A4, so other drug levels fall, not rise. HLA-B*5701 is the abacavir allele, and carbamazepine induces rather than inhibits CYP. The severe rash is immune and HLA-linked, not simple histamine. The low sodium is water retention, not aldosterone blockade. T-type calcium block is ethosuximide; carbamazepine can worsen absence.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 28-year-old woman of childbearing potential is put on valproate for a mixed seizure disorder and a mood label. She is not using contraception. A month later a toddler in the family, also given valproate, develops vomiting and high ammonia with a sick liver.
question: Which two toxicities are the point of this drug, and which population is the liver risk?
options: Neural-tube defects if used in early pregnancy, and idiosyncratic hepatic failure that is most feared in very young children
Gingival hyperplasia and fetal hydantoin face, the phenytoin pair
Agranulocytosis and HLA-related rash, the carbamazepine pair
Cartilage damage and permanent teeth staining in the toddler
Pulmonary fibrosis, which is the reason it is avoided in pregnancy
correctAnswer: Neural-tube defects if used in early pregnancy, and idiosyncratic hepatic failure that is most feared in very young children
explanation: Valproate is teratogenic and specifically raises neural-tube defect risk, so it is a poor default in a woman who may conceive. It also causes idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, historically concentrated in young children on several antiseizure drugs. Gingival hyperplasia and the hydantoin face are phenytoin. Agranulocytosis and HLA rash point to carbamazepine or other drugs, not this pair. Tooth and cartilage toxicity is tetracycline. Pulmonary fibrosis is not the valproate pregnancy problem.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A patient on phenytoin has a level of 12 mcg/mL and is still seizing, so the dose is doubled. A week later he is ataxic with nystagmus and a level of 28. He also has tender gums. His warfarin dose, started years ago while he was on phenytoin, had to be increased.
question: Why did a doubled dose overshoot, and why did warfarin need a higher dose?
options: Phenytoin is zero-order near the therapeutic range, so small dose increases saturate metabolism; it also induces CYP enzymes that clear warfarin
Phenytoin is purely first-order, so the level must exactly double
Gum overgrowth means the level is subtherapeutic and the dose should rise again
Phenytoin inhibits warfarin metabolism, so the INR would have been too high on a usual warfarin dose
Nystagmus at a level of 28 means the assay is falsely high and the drug is not the cause
correctAnswer: Phenytoin is zero-order near the therapeutic range, so small dose increases saturate metabolism; it also induces CYP enzymes that clear warfarin
explanation: Phenytoin hydroxylation saturates, so kinetics become zero-order in the usual range. Doubling the dose does not double the level; it can jump into toxicity, with nystagmus and ataxia. Chronic phenytoin induces CYP enzymes, so warfarin is cleared faster and needs a higher dose to keep the INR in range. First-order doubling is the calculation trap. Gingival hyperplasia is a chronic effect and is not a sign to push the level higher. The warfarin interaction of phenytoin is induction, not inhibition. A level of 28 with ataxia is real toxicity, not a false assay.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man who injected a long-acting opioid is apneic with pinpoint pupils. Naloxone wakes him and his breathing returns. Ninety minutes later, after the team has relaxed, he is apneic again. The pupils had started to pinpoint once more.
question: Why did he relapse, and what does that imply for monitoring?
options: Naloxone’s half-life is shorter than many opioids, so the antagonist wears off while agonist remains; he needs repeat dosing and observation
Naloxone is an opioid agonist at high dose, so the second apnea is a new overdose of naloxone
Pinpoint pupils mean a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is now required
The relapse proves naloxone does not bind the mu receptor
Opioid apnea is treated with succinylcholine so the chest can be ventilated chemically
correctAnswer: Naloxone’s half-life is shorter than many opioids, so the antagonist wears off while agonist remains; he needs repeat dosing and observation
explanation: Naloxone competitively blocks mu receptors and reverses apnea and miosis, but it is cleared faster than heroin, methadone, or many sustained-release opioids. Recurrence of apnea is expected if you give one dose and walk away. Naloxone is not an agonist; a second apnea is return of the opioid, not naloxone toxicity. Pinpoint pupils and apnea are opioid, not benzodiazepine; flumazenil is the wrong reversal and can seize. Relapse shows that the block was temporary, not that the drug misses the receptor. A paralytic does not treat the brainstem respiratory depression.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

blueprintTopic: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
scenario: Patient A started linezolid while still taking an SSRI and now has fever, clonus, hyperreflexia, and diarrhea over hours. Patient B has taken haloperidol for years, was given more after agitation, and over two days became rigid, mute, and hot, with a high creatine kinase and slow reflexes.
question: Which mechanisms match?
options: A is excess serotonin-receptor activity with neuromuscular excitation; B is dopamine D2 blockade with lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia
Both are dopamine blockade; clonus is required for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
A is malignant hyperthermia from succinylcholine; B is serotonin syndrome because it evolved over days
B should be treated with cyproheptadine and A with dantrolene as the syndrome-specific first facts
Linezolid has no serotonergic activity, so A cannot be serotonin syndrome
correctAnswer: A is excess serotonin-receptor activity with neuromuscular excitation; B is dopamine D2 blockade with lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia
explanation: Serotonin syndrome is fast, with clonus, hyperreflexia, and often gastrointestinal hyperactivity, after combining serotonergic drugs. Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor and is a classic partner to an SSRI. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is slower, after dopamine blockade, with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and high creatine kinase. Clonus points away from NMS, not toward it. Malignant hyperthermia is a ryanodine-receptor crisis during anesthetics, not a linezolid interaction, and the time course of B is days, which fits NMS rather than serotonin syndrome. Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist used in serotonin syndrome; dantrolene or a dopamine agonist is the NMS discussion. Swapping them ignores the reflex exam. Linezolid does have MAO inhibition.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 30-year-old woman is unconscious after taking her amitriptyline. The QRS is 160 ms, she just had a seizure, and the blood pressure is low. pH is 7.25. Charcoal is being considered, but the immediate cardiac problem is the wide QRS.
question: What should be given for the QRS, and why?
options: Sodium bicarbonate; it raises extracellular sodium and pH, which reduces tricyclic binding to the cardiac fast sodium channel
Physostigmine, because anticholinergic toxicity is reversed and the QRS narrows
A class I antiarrhythmic such as procainamide, to stabilize the sodium channel further
Flumazenil, because wide-complex tachycardia after a sedating drug is a benzodiazepine effect
Calcium gluconate, the antidote for sodium-channel blocker QRS widening
correctAnswer: Sodium bicarbonate; it raises extracellular sodium and pH, which reduces tricyclic binding to the cardiac fast sodium channel
explanation: Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels, widen the QRS, and cause seizures and hypotension. Bicarbonate narrows the QRS by increasing the sodium gradient and by alkalinization, which decreases drug binding to the channel. Physostigmine can reverse delirium but can worsen conduction and seizures; it is not the QRS drug. Procainamide is another sodium-channel blocker and would widen the QRS further. Flumazenil does not bind cardiac sodium channels and can precipitate seizures. Calcium is the membrane stabilizer discussed for calcium-channel blocker or hyperkalemia physiology, not the specific fix for tricyclic sodium-channel block.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 33-year-old woman on lithium for bipolar disorder has a new tremor, is thirsty, and passes large amounts of dilute urine. She also takes ibuprofen for a sprain and started a thiazide last week. She asks whether lithium is a problem if she becomes pregnant. Creatinine has risen slightly.
question: Which effects belong to lithium, and which drug change raised the level?
options: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Ebstein anomaly; thiazides and NSAIDs reduce clearance and raise the level
Central diabetes insipidus and neural-tube defects; ibuprofen lowers the lithium level
Agranulocytosis and a flat facial philtrum, the valproate pattern
Gingival hyperplasia and fetal hydantoin syndrome
Serotonin syndrome as the chronic tremor, treated by raising the lithium dose
correctAnswer: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Ebstein anomaly; thiazides and NSAIDs reduce clearance and raise the level
explanation: Lithium enters principal cells through sodium channels and commonly causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so urine is dilute and the patient is thirsty. In early pregnancy it is linked to Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve. Thiazides cause volume contraction and more proximal lithium reabsorption, and NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance, so both raise the level. Central diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem, and the teratogen usually named with neural-tube defects is valproate, not lithium. Agranulocytosis is clozapine. Gum overgrowth is phenytoin. A coarse tremor with rising creatinine is toxicity, not a reason to increase the dose, and it is not serotonin syndrome.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man on haloperidol develops painful sustained twisting of the neck hours after a dose, and his prolactin is high. A second patient on the same drug class has a shuffling gait after months. Neither has fever or lead-pipe rigidity.
question: Which pathways explain the neck, the prolactin, and the gait?
options: Nigrostriatal D2 block causes acute dystonia and later parkinsonism; tuberoinfundibular D2 block raises prolactin
Mesolimbic D2 block causes dystonia; nigrostriatal block raises prolactin
Tuberoinfundibular block causes the shuffling gait
Muscarinic agonism causes acute dystonia, so benztropine would worsen it
The neck spasm is neuroleptic malignant syndrome because it happened within hours
correctAnswer: Nigrostriatal D2 block causes acute dystonia and later parkinsonism; tuberoinfundibular D2 block raises prolactin
explanation: Dopamine in the nigrostriatal tract suppresses unwanted muscle activity. Blocking D2 there causes acute dystonia and, later, drug-induced parkinsonism. Dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular tract inhibits prolactin, so blocking it raises prolactin. The mesolimbic tract is the one whose blockade is tied to antipsychotic effect, not to dystonia or galactorrhea. The shuffling gait is nigrostriatal, not tuberoinfundibular. Acute dystonia is treated with an antimuscarinic such as benztropine; calling the drug a muscarinic agonist reverses the fix. Hours-long neck twisting without fever and rigidity is dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 60-year-old man has been on a first-generation antipsychotic for eight years. He has constant chewing movements and a tongue that darts. The team increases the antipsychotic because the movements look like agitation. For a day the chewing lessens, then it returns worse.
question: Why did a higher dose briefly help, and what is the durable mechanism?
options: The movements are from upregulated nigrostriatal dopamine receptors; more blockade masks them briefly and then deepens the upregulation
The movements are acute dystonia, so more dopamine blockade is the cure
This is Parkinson disease, and the antipsychotic is replacing lost dopamine
Chewing movements mean serotonin syndrome, treated by raising the antipsychotic
The tongue movement is a seizure, and the drug level is subtherapeutic
correctAnswer: The movements are from upregulated nigrostriatal dopamine receptors; more blockade masks them briefly and then deepens the upregulation
explanation: Long dopamine blockade causes the postsynaptic receptors in the striatum to increase in number and sensitivity. That excess dopamine signaling produces tardive chewing and tongue movements. Pushing the blocker covers the receptors for a short time, which is why the movements dipped, but it drives still more upregulation, so the problem returns worse. Acute dystonia is early, not an eight-year chewing syndrome, and more drug is not its cure. Antipsychotics block dopamine; they do not replace it, and they worsen true Parkinson disease. Serotonin syndrome has clonus and hyperreflexia, not isolated orofacial dyskinesia. This is not a seizure aura that needs a higher antipsychotic level.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 52-year-old man stops drinking two days ago. He is tremulous, sweaty, tachycardic, and then has a seizure. He is oriented enough to refuse 'another sedative' and asks for haloperidol only, because he is seeing shadows. Blood pressure is high.
question: What is upregulated, and why is an antipsychotic alone the wrong plan?
options: Chronic alcohol facilitated GABA and suppressed NMDA; stopping it leaves NMDA excess. A benzodiazepine replaces GABA tone; an antipsychotic alone does not and can lower the seizure threshold
Withdrawal is a dopamine-deficiency state treated first with haloperidol
The seizure means he needs phenytoin loading and no GABA drug
Sweating and tremor are serotonin syndrome from alcohol itself
Benzodiazepines worsen withdrawal seizures because they block GABA
correctAnswer: Chronic alcohol facilitated GABA and suppressed NMDA; stopping it leaves NMDA excess. A benzodiazepine replaces GABA tone; an antipsychotic alone does not and can lower the seizure threshold
explanation: Long alcohol use downregulates GABA-A signaling and upregulates NMDA glutamate receptors. When alcohol stops, the balance is excitation: tremor, autonomic surge, seizures, and later delirium. A benzodiazepine restores GABA-A activity and is the treatment that prevents the seizure from recurring. Haloperidol may quiet hallucinations but does not replace GABA and can make seizures more likely, so it is not the sole plan. This is not dopamine deficiency. Phenytoin does not fix alcohol-withdrawal seizures. The autonomic picture is withdrawal, not serotonin syndrome. Benzodiazepines facilitate GABA; they do not block it.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man with alcohol use disorder is confused, cannot abduct either eye fully, and walks with a wide base. He receives thiamine and the eye movements improve. Weeks later he invents detailed stories for events that never happened and cannot lay down new memories. Old childhood memories are relatively spared.
question: Which lesion explains the lasting memory problem, and why did thiamine not erase it?
options: Mammillary bodies and the medial dorsal thalamus are damaged; the confabulatory amnesia of Korsakoff syndrome is largely irreversible even after thiamine repletes the acute Wernicke signs
The hippocampus is filled with amyloid, so this is Alzheimer disease and thiamine was irrelevant
Confabulation means he is malingering, so no structure is injured
The frontal eye fields caused the abduction failure, and memory will return with glucose alone
Both the eye and the memory findings are cerebellar, so they should have recovered together
correctAnswer: Mammillary bodies and the medial dorsal thalamus are damaged; the confabulatory amnesia of Korsakoff syndrome is largely irreversible even after thiamine repletes the acute Wernicke signs
explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia from thiamine deficiency in the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray. Treating it can improve the eye findings. If the medial thalamic and mammillary injury is established, Korsakoff syndrome remains: anterograde amnesia with confabulation that thiamine does not reverse. Amyloid hippocampus disease is a different, slower dementia without this eye-movement story. Confabulation here is a memory failure, not a choice to lie. Abduction failure is a sixth-nerve or gaze-center problem in the brainstem, not the frontal eye field, and glucose without thiamine is the precipitant, not the cure. The cerebellum may add ataxia, but the memory circuit is diencephalic, which is why the two did not recover together.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Three patients have a small pupil and mild ptosis. Patient A, with a Pancoast tumor, does not sweat on the whole ipsilateral face and neck. Patient B, with a carotid dissection, does not sweat only on a patch of the medial forehead, and the body sweating is intact. Patient C has a lateral medullary stroke and anhidrosis of the body more than a tiny forehead patch.
question: Which neuron is out in the Pancoast patient, and why is sweating different after the carotid lesion?
options: A first-order or second-order lesion is proximal to the superior cervical ganglion, so the face loses sweating; a postganglionic carotid lesion spares most facial sweating because those fibers traveled along the external carotid
All three are third-order lesions, so sweating loss is identical
Pancoast tumor hits the third-order neuron at the iris, so the whole body sweats too much
A small pupil means parasympathetic loss, so pilocarpine will dilate it
Ptosis in Horner syndrome is loss of levator palpebrae, the oculomotor muscle
correctAnswer: A first-order or second-order lesion is proximal to the superior cervical ganglion, so the face loses sweating; a postganglionic carotid lesion spares most facial sweating because those fibers traveled along the external carotid
explanation: Sympathetic supply to the pupil and lid synapses in the superior cervical ganglion. Sudomotor fibers to most of the face peel off along the external carotid, while the internal carotid carries the ocular sympathetics. A Pancoast tumor hits the second-order preganglionic chain, so the whole half of the face is dry. A carotid dissection is third-order and often spares facial sweating except a small medial forehead area. Lateral medullary lesions are first-order and can include body anhidrosis. Calling all three third-order erases the sweating map. The miotic pupil is lost sympathetic dilation, not lost parasympathetic constriction. Horner ptosis is Müller muscle, a small smooth muscle; the skeletal levator is the third nerve and causes a much larger droop.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 30-year-old man has a cerumen plug in the right ear. Weber lateralizes to the right. Rinne on the right shows bone conduction louder than air. The left ear has air louder than bone, and Weber does not go left.
question: Which type of loss is on the right, and what would a left sensorineural loss have done to Weber?
options: Right conductive loss; a left sensorineural loss would also push Weber to the right, away from the bad cochlea
Right sensorineural loss, because Weber goes toward the symptomatic ear
Left conductive loss, because Rinne was normal on the left
Right sensorineural loss, because bone louder than air is the sensorineural Rinne
A central lesion, because conductive loss makes Weber go to the good ear
correctAnswer: Right conductive loss; a left sensorineural loss would also push Weber to the right, away from the bad cochlea
explanation: In conductive loss, bone conduction bypasses the blocked canal or ossicles, so Rinne is bone greater than air, and Weber goes to the bad ear. That is the plugged right ear. Sensorineural loss does the opposite on Weber: sound lateralizes away from the dead cochlea, so a left cochlear lesion also sends Weber to the right. You cannot read Weber without knowing which ear is bad. A normal Rinne on the left does not make the left the conductive ear. Bone greater than air is conductive, not sensorineural. Conductive loss sends Weber to the affected ear, not the good one.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 60-year-old woman has spinning that lasts under a minute when she rolls over in bed or looks up. There is no hearing loss. Dix-Hallpike reproduces upbeat torsional nystagmus after a few seconds, and it fatigues. She has been taking meclizine every day for a month.
question: What is moving, and why is daily meclizine not the treatment?
options: Otoconia in a semicircular canal bend the cupula with position change; a canalith repositioning maneuver clears them, and a suppressant only sedates
Endolymphatic hydrops, so low-salt diet and diuretics are the repositioning equivalent
The vestibular nerve is inflamed, so steroids and a long suppressant are specific
A cerebellar stroke, because fatigable nystagmus with latency is central
Perilymph fistula, which is fixed by the Epley maneuver
correctAnswer: Otoconia in a semicircular canal bend the cupula with position change; a canalith repositioning maneuver clears them, and a suppressant only sedates
explanation: Short, positional, latent, fatigable vertigo with torsional nystagmus is canalithiasis, usually the posterior canal. The particles are displaced otoliths. The Epley or similar maneuver moves them back to the utricle. Meclizine can dull the sensation and cause falls in older adults; it does not remove the stone. Endolymphatic hydrops is Ménière disease, with hearing loss and longer attacks. Vestibular neuritis is continuous, not a few-second roll-in-bed spell. Central nystagmus is often immediate and nonfatigable, the opposite of this latency and fatigue. A fistula is pressure- or strain-triggered and is not cured by repositioning.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 70-year-old woman is given a dilating drop for a fundus exam. An hour later the eye is rock hard, the pupil is mid-dilated, she sees halos, and she is vomiting. A student reaches for another mydriatic because the first dose 'was not enough,' and for atropine.
question: What happened to the angle, and which drug direction is right?
options: Dilation bunched the iris into a narrow angle and blocked aqueous outflow; a miotic such as pilocarpine and a pressure-lowering agent are used, not another dilator
Dilation opened the angle, so more mydriatic will vent the aqueous
Atropine constricts the pupil and is the specific antidote
This is open-angle glaucoma, which presents as an acute hard eye after one drop
Timolol is unsafe only in asthma and is the cause of the hard eye here
correctAnswer: Dilation bunched the iris into a narrow angle and blocked aqueous outflow; a miotic such as pilocarpine and a pressure-lowering agent are used, not another dilator
explanation: In a susceptible narrow angle, mydriasis thickens the iris at the periphery and blocks the trabecular meshwork. Pressure rises within the hour, the cornea swells, and the patient vomits. The pupil needs to be constricted with pilocarpine once the ischemia allows it, and pressure is lowered with an aqueous suppressant such as acetazolamide or a beta blocker; a second dilator or atropine makes the block worse. Atropine is a mydriatic and anticholinergic; it does not constrict. Open-angle glaucoma is chronic and silent, not a one-hour crisis after a drop. Timolol can treat the pressure; it did not cause this attack, though it is avoided in asthma for a different reason.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 66-year-old man with asthma is prescribed an eye drop for open-angle glaucoma. After a week he is wheezing and his resting heart rate is 52. He never swallowed the drop; he only put it in both eyes.
question: How did an eye drop cause wheeze, and which drop is the likely one?
options: Timolol drains through the nasolacrimal duct and is absorbed, blocking bronchial and cardiac beta receptors
Latanoprost is a systemic beta blocker when it reaches the nose
Pilocarpine dries the airway by muscarinic blockade
The wheeze is an ocular-cardiac reflex from a prostaglandin and is not pharmacologic
Beta blockers in the eye cannot reach the blood, so this is coincidental new asthma
correctAnswer: Timolol drains through the nasolacrimal duct and is absorbed, blocking bronchial and cardiac beta receptors
explanation: Topical timolol is a nonselective beta blocker. It bypasses first-pass metabolism through nasal mucosa and can bronchospasm a patient with asthma and slow the heart. Punctal occlusion reduces that. Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog and darkens the iris or grows lashes; it is not a beta blocker. Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist and would increase secretions, not block them. This systemic effect is pharmacology, not a reflex from a prostaglandin. Eye drops are absorbed; 'it stayed in the eye' is the mistake that misses the wheeze.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: Patient A has sudden painless monocular blindness. The retina is pale with a red spot at the fovea. Patient B has subacute blurred vision, dilated tortuous veins, and hemorrhages in all four quadrants, and the disk is swollen. Neither has a curtain of flashes and floaters.
question: Which obstructions fit, and what does the red spot mean?
options: A is central retinal artery occlusion; the macula looks red because the underlying choroid shows through pale retina. B is central retinal vein occlusion
A is vein occlusion because a cherry-red spot is venous blood; B is artery occlusion
Both are retinal detachment, which whitens the retina and fills it with blood
A is optic neuritis, which is painless and shows a cherry-red spot
B is a vitreous hemorrhage, which leaves the retinal vessels easy to see and tortuous
correctAnswer: A is central retinal artery occlusion; the macula looks red because the underlying choroid shows through pale retina. B is central retinal vein occlusion
explanation: Arterial occlusion kills the inner retina, which turns white, while the fovea stays relatively red because it is thin and the choroidal circulation shows through. Venous occlusion backs up blood: dilated veins, disk edema, and hemorrhages all around, the 'blood and thunder' fundus. Swapping artery and vein swaps the cherry-red spot onto the wrong disease. Detachment gives flashes, floaters, and a curtain, not these two fundi. Optic neuritis hurts with eye movement and affects the nerve head or the field, not a pale retina with a red fovea. Vitreous blood obscures the fundus; you would not see tortuous veins clearly.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 16-year-old has a progressive clumsy gait, absent ankle reflexes, and upgoing toes. Position sense is poor. He has high arches and a scoliosis. A murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is new. A sibling is less affected. The repeat is GAA, and the gene product is mitochondrial.
question: Which tract pair and which protein fit?
options: Dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, from loss of frataxin
Spinocerebellar tracts only, from loss of dystrophin
Anterior horn cells only, from a CAG repeat in huntingtin
A demyelinating neuropathy from a PMP22 duplication, with a normal heart
Cerebellar Purkinje cells from a CTG repeat, with cataracts as the required finding
correctAnswer: Dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, from loss of frataxin
explanation: Friedreich ataxia is a GAA expansion that silences frataxin, an iron-sulfur protein in mitochondria. The cord loses dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, so reflexes drop from the sensory loss while toes go up from the motor tract. Kyphoscoliosis, pes cavus, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy complete the picture. Dystrophin is Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy. Huntingtin is a CAG disease of the caudate, not this areflexic cardiomyopathy. PMP22 duplication is Charcot-Marie-Tooth 1A, a peripheral myelin disease without this heart lesion as its signature. A CTG repeat with cataracts is myotonic dystrophy.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 5-year-old boy cannot get off the floor without walking his hands up his legs. Calves are large but weak. Creatine kinase is very high. A maternal uncle used a wheelchair by age 12. A cousin with a related mutation in the same gene is still walking at 20 and has a milder course.
question: What is the genetic difference between the boy and the walking cousin?
options: The boy has a frameshift that abolishes dystrophin; the cousin has a mutation that preserves the reading frame and leaves partial dystrophin
Both have the same frameshift; severity is only how much they exercise
The boy has a CTG repeat and the cousin has a GAA repeat
Dystrophin is autosomal, so an uncle on the mother's side is unrelated
The large calves mean the muscle protein is overproduced, so the gene is duplicated and working
correctAnswer: The boy has a frameshift that abolishes dystrophin; the cousin has a mutation that preserves the reading frame and leaves partial dystrophin
explanation: Dystrophin links actin to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. A frameshifting deletion removes the protein and causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with early loss of walking. An in-frame deletion shortens the protein but leaves some function, which is Becker muscular dystrophy and a later wheelchair. Exercise does not choose the reading frame. CTG is myotonic dystrophy and GAA is Friedreich ataxia. The gene is on X, so a maternal uncle fits. Pseudohypertrophy is fat and fibrosis replacing muscle, not extra working dystrophin.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 42-year-old man cannot release a handshake. He has early cataracts, a long face, and a bald forehead. His mother had the same illness late in life; his child is much more affected in infancy. The repeat is CTG in a noncoding region.
question: Which phenomenon explains the child, and what is the muscle problem?
options: Anticipation from expansion of a CTG repeat; chloride-channel related myotonia from DMPK dysfunction, with cataracts and an autosomal dominant parent
A frameshift in dystrophin, which causes myotonia and cataracts
Anticipation only occurs in GAA repeats, so this child was adopted
The handshake delay is Lambert-Eaton facilitation and should improve with repetition of a different kind
This is autosomal recessive, so a mother and child pair is impossible
correctAnswer: Anticipation from expansion of a CTG repeat; chloride-channel related myotonia from DMPK dysfunction, with cataracts and an autosomal dominant parent
explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is a CTG expansion in the DMPK gene. The repeat grows in successive generations, especially through the mother for congenital disease, which is anticipation. The muscle cannot relax, a myotonia, and cataracts, frontal balding, and a distal weakness pattern come with it. Dystrophin frameshifts cause Duchenne weakness, not delayed relaxation and cataracts. Anticipation is not exclusive to Friedreich GAA repeats. Lambert-Eaton gets stronger with use; myotonia is delayed relaxation after a grip. The inheritance is autosomal dominant, so parent and child is expected.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A teenager has many café-au-lait spots, freckles in the armpit, and a glioma of the optic nerve. His father has the same skin findings. A different family has a young adult with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and fewer skin spots. No one has a renal angiomyolipoma.
question: Which chromosomes and which tumors did you use to separate them?
options: NF1 is chromosome 17, neurofibromin, with optic glioma and axillary freckles; NF2 is chromosome 22, merlin, with bilateral vestibular schwannomas
NF1 is chromosome 22 and NF2 is chromosome 17; the tumors are otherwise identical
Both are tuberous sclerosis on chromosome 9 and 16, and the optic glioma is a renal angiomyolipoma
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF1
Axillary freckles are ash-leaf spots and mean tuberous sclerosis
correctAnswer: NF1 is chromosome 17, neurofibromin, with optic glioma and axillary freckles; NF2 is chromosome 22, merlin, with bilateral vestibular schwannomas
explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is the common skin disease: many café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas, and optic pathway glioma, from neurofibromin on chromosome 17. Type 2 is merlin on chromosome 22 and is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, with a quieter skin exam. Swapping the chromosomes is a pure memory trap with a clinical cost if you counsel the wrong tumor risk. Angiomyolipomas and ash-leaf spots are tuberous sclerosis, chromosomes 9 and 16. Vestibular schwannomas are NF2, not NF1. Axillary freckles are NF1, not ash-leaf macules.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An infant has pale leaf-shaped patches that show up under a Wood lamp, a seizure, and a cardiac mass that was seen before birth and is now smaller. The mother has facial angiofibromas and a history of a kidney tumor made of fat, vessels, and muscle. Intelligence is variable in the family.
question: Which two proteins and which tumor fit?
options: Hamartin and tuberin, tumor suppressors; the heart mass is a rhabdomyoma and the kidney mass is an angiomyolipoma
Neurofibromin only; the heart mass is an atrial myxoma
Merlin; the facial lesions are bilateral acoustic neuromas
A single collagen gene; the leaf-shaped spots are café-au-lait macules
Huntingtin; the seizure is anticipation of a CAG repeat
correctAnswer: Hamartin and tuberin, tumor suppressors; the heart mass is a rhabdomyoma and the kidney mass is an angiomyolipoma
explanation: Tuberous sclerosis is TSC1 or TSC2, hamartin or tuberin, which inhibit mTOR. Ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas, seizures from cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyoma that often regresses, and renal angiomyolipoma are the cluster. Neurofibromin is NF1 and does not make a rhabdomyoma. Merlin is NF2 and the facial story there is vestibular tumors, not angiofibromas. Café-au-lait macules are NF1, not ash-leaf hypopigmentation. Huntingtin does not cause congenital heart tumors or hypopigmented macules.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A boy has a long face, large ears, and large testes after puberty. He has intellectual disability and avoids eye contact. His mother is a carrier with a premutation and premature ovarian failure. The repeat is CGG in the FMR1 promoter.
question: What does the expansion do to the gene, and why can the mother be less affected?
options: A full CGG expansion methylates FMR1 and silences it; a premutation is smaller, so she may have a late phenotype without the full childhood syndrome
The repeat is CAG in huntingtin, and methylation is irrelevant
FMR1 is overexpressed, so the testes enlarge from excess fragile-X protein
This is trisomy 21, and the repeat story is a distractor
The gene is mitochondrial, so only mothers transmit a full syndrome to every child
correctAnswer: A full CGG expansion methylates FMR1 and silences it; a premutation is smaller, so she may have a late phenotype without the full childhood syndrome
explanation: Fragile X is a CGG expansion in the FMR1 5' region. Past a threshold the repeat is methylated and the gene turns off, so the RNA-binding protein is missing. That causes intellectual disability, long face, large ears, and macroorchidism. A premutation does not fully silence the gene; women can have premature ovarian failure and older carriers can have a tremor-ataxia syndrome, which is why the mother is not a copy of the boy. CAG huntingtin is Huntington disease. The syndrome is loss of FMR1, not overexpression. Trisomy 21 has a different face and no CGG repeat. Inheritance is X-linked, not mitochondrial.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A toddler boy bites his own lips and fingers and has orange sand in the diaper. Uric acid is high. An enzyme in the purine salvage pathway is missing. He is developmentally delayed. A drug that inhibits xanthine oxidase is discussed for the gout, not for the behavior.
question: Which enzyme is gone, and why does allopurinol not stop the self-injury?
options: HGPRT is absent, so PRPP accumulates and purines are overproduced; allopurinol lowers uric acid but does not restore the salvage pathway in the brain
Adenosine deaminase is absent, so this is SCID with gout
Xanthine oxidase is absent, so uric acid is high
HGPRT is overactive, and allopurinol replaces it
The orange sand is homogentisic acid, so this is alkaptonuria
correctAnswer: HGPRT is absent, so PRPP accumulates and purines are overproduced; allopurinol lowers uric acid but does not restore the salvage pathway in the brain
explanation: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is X-linked loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase. Salvage fails, PRPP drives new purine synthesis, and uric acid rises, which stones the diaper and causes gout. The neurologic self-injury is part of the enzyme loss in brain and is not fixed by lowering uric acid with allopurinol or febuxostat. Adenosine deaminase deficiency is a form of SCID, not self-mutilation and sand. If xanthine oxidase were absent, uric acid would be low. The enzyme is missing, not overactive. Homogentisic acid darkens urine in alkaptonuria and does not cause this behavior.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024
