scenario: A 17-year-old falls asleep in class, has episodes of buckling knees when he laughs, and sometimes wakes unable to move while hallucinating a figure in the room. Night sleep is fragmented. Stimulants help the sleep attacks partially. A spinal-fluid peptide from the hypothalamus is low.
question: Which peptide, and what is the knee-buckling episode?
options: Hypocretin (orexin) is low; laughter-triggered loss of tone is cataplexy from REM atonia intruding into wakefulness
Melatonin is low; the knee buckling is a seizure from absence epilepsy
Dopamine is low in the substantia nigra; the paralysis on waking is Parkinson rigidity
Hypocretin is high, which forces sleep, and cataplexy is a dystonic reaction
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause the sleep attacks
correctAnswer: Hypocretin (orexin) is low; laughter-triggered loss of tone is cataplexy from REM atonia intruding into wakefulness
explanation: Narcolepsy with cataplexy is loss of hypothalamic hypocretin neurons. REM physiology intrudes into the day: sleep attacks, cataplexy (tone loss with emotion), sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. Low CSF hypocretin supports it. Melatonin is not the missing peptide, and absence seizures do not drop tone when the patient laughs. Waking paralysis here is REM atonia, not parkinsonian rigidity. The peptide is deficient, not high. Acetylcholine-receptor antibodies are myasthenia gravis.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 6-year-old sits up screaming 90 minutes after falling asleep, is sweaty, does not recognize his parents, and cannot be consoled. He goes back to sleep and remembers nothing in the morning. A teenager wakes from a frightening dream near morning, is immediately oriented, and can recount the plot.
question: Which sleep stages fit?
options: The child is in stage N3 non-REM sleep; the teenager woke from REM sleep and can recall the dream
Both are REM, because fear only occurs in REM
The child is in stage N1, the lightest sleep, which is why he is confused
Night terrors are seizures, and dream recall proves epilepsy
The teenager has cataplexy because he remembers the dream
correctAnswer: The child is in stage N3 non-REM sleep; the teenager woke from REM sleep and can recall the dream
explanation: Night terrors come out of slow-wave N3 sleep in the first part of the night. The child is autonomic and amnestic and should not be forced awake; he is not in a recallable dream. Nightmares are REM events, cluster toward morning, and the person wakes oriented and remembers the story. Fear is not restricted to REM. N3 is deep sleep, not N1. Amnesia and autonomic surge are not required to diagnose epilepsy, and a remembered dream is not a seizure. Cataplexy is loss of tone while awake and laughing or startled, not a recalled dream.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man had diarrhea from undercooked chicken two weeks ago. His legs are weak and the weakness is moving upward. Reflexes are gone. A spinal tap shows protein of 90 mg/dL and only two white cells. Sensation is mildly reduced. He is watching his own breathing.
question: What is the immune mechanism, and which bedside threat matters more than the cell count?
options: Antibodies to peripheral myelin after Campylobacter molecular mimicry; respiratory muscle failure can come before the protein finding and is the emergency
Anterior horn cells are invaded by polio virus, so protein is high and cells are absent
A central demyelinating plaque in the cervical cord, so reflexes should be brisk
The high protein with no cells means bacterial meningitis, and weakness is incidental
Botulinum toxin is causing an ascending sensory neuropathy
correctAnswer: Antibodies to peripheral myelin after Campylobacter molecular mimicry; respiratory muscle failure can come before the protein finding and is the emergency
explanation: Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide resembles peripheral-nerve gangliosides. Antibodies strip myelin, conduction fails, and weakness ascends with lost reflexes. The spinal fluid shows high protein from root inflammation and almost no cells. The dangerous part is diaphragmatic failure, which you follow with vital capacity, not the lab. Polio kills anterior horn cells and the fluid is inflammatory, not albumino-cytologic. A cord plaque would raise reflexes below the lesion. Bacterial meningitis is a high cell count with low glucose. Botulism is descending, pupillary, and has no sensory loss and a normal spinal fluid.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A patient loses strength in both legs and loses pain and temperature below the chest after aortic surgery. Vibration and position sense are intact. The dorsal columns were outside the infarct territory.
question: Which vessel was lost, and why is vibration spared?
options: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord, including spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts; dorsal columns are on the posterior spinal arterial supply
The posterior spinal arteries supply the corticospinal tracts, so vibration should have been lost
A single posterior spinal artery infarct causes bilateral pain loss and spares motor function
The artery of Adamkiewicz is a carotid branch, so the cord is not its territory
Intact vibration means the lesion is a peripheral neuropathy
correctAnswer: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord, including spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts; dorsal columns are on the posterior spinal arterial supply
explanation: The anterior spinal artery feeds the ventral horns, corticospinal tracts, and spinothalamic tracts. Infarction, often in the watershed of the artery of Adamkiewicz during aortic surgery, gives bilateral weakness and pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal-column sensation. Posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns, which is why vibration survives. A posterior infarct would do the opposite. Adamkiewicz is a radicular reinforcement of the anterior spinal artery from the aorta, not the carotid. A neuropathy would not cut a sharp sensory level for pain while sparing vibration in this cord pattern.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man falls forward and hyperextends his neck. His hands are weak and the arms are weaker than the legs. A second patient has a cape of lost pain and temperature across the shoulders, with preserved light touch, and wasting of the small hand muscles. MRI of the second patient shows a fluid cavity in the center of the cervical cord.
question: Why are the hands hit hardest in both, and why is light touch spared in the cape?
options: Cervical fibers of the spinothalamic tract cross near the central canal, and the cervical corticospinal fibers lie more medially; dorsal columns, which carry vibration and much discriminative touch, sit outside the cavity
The syrinx destroys the dorsal columns first, so pain is spared and touch is lost
Hyperextension injures the lumbar cord preferentially because those fibers are medial
A cape distribution is a brainstem lesion at the trigeminal nucleus
Light touch and pain share one tract, so they cannot separate
correctAnswer: Cervical fibers of the spinothalamic tract cross near the central canal, and the cervical corticospinal fibers lie more medially; dorsal columns, which carry vibration and much discriminative touch, sit outside the cavity
explanation: Crossing spinothalamic fibers decussate in front of the central canal. A syrinx interrupts them at the level of the cavity and spares the already-crossed lateral tracts and the dorsal columns, so pain and temperature drop in a cape while vibration and discriminative touch remain. In the corticospinal tract the arm fibers are more medial than the leg fibers, so a central or hyperextension injury weakens the hands more than the legs. A syrinx does not start in the dorsal columns. Lumbar fibers are lateral, so they are relatively spared, not hit first. The trigeminal nucleus would numb the face, not a shoulder cape. Pain and discriminative touch do not share one tract, which is the whole point of the dissociated sensory loss.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A speaks in short, effortful phrases, understands questions, and is frustrated. Patient B speaks fluently with invented words and does not follow commands. Patient C speaks fluently, understands, but cannot repeat a sentence. Patient D cannot repeat and also cannot read, yet he writes normally; a stroke is in the left occipital lobe and the splenium.
question: Which localizations fit A, B, and the reading-writing split?
options: A is Broca in the dominant frontal lobe; B is Wernicke in the superior temporal gyrus; D is alexia without agraphia from a splenium lesion disconnecting the right visual cortex from the left language areas
A is Wernicke and B is Broca, because effort means poor comprehension
C is global aphasia because repetition failed
D must have a blind eye, because writing can be preserved only if reading is preserved
All four are conduction aphasia in the arcuate fasciculus
correctAnswer: A is Broca in the dominant frontal lobe; B is Wernicke in the superior temporal gyrus; D is alexia without agraphia from a splenium lesion disconnecting the right visual cortex from the left language areas
explanation: Broca aphasia is nonfluent with spared comprehension, frontal. Wernicke aphasia is fluent and empty with poor comprehension, temporal. Conduction aphasia, patient C, is the arcuate fasciculus: fluent, understands, cannot repeat. Alexia without agraphia happens when a left PCA stroke takes the left visual cortex and the splenium, so words seen by the right hemisphere cannot reach the left language network, while writing, which does not need that incoming visual path, survives. Swapping Broca and Wernicke ignores fluency. Failed repetition alone is not global aphasia; global aphasia loses fluency and comprehension too. Writing can outlast reading in that disconnection. One fasciculus does not explain all four patterns.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 72-year-old man has sudden weakness of the right face and right arm, with almost normal leg strength, and he cannot name a pen. A second man has weak right leg more than arm, and a grasp reflex, after a stroke on the left cortical surface near the midline.
question: Which arteries, and why is the leg relatively spared in the first man?
options: The first is left MCA, which serves the lateral cortex including face and arm language areas; the leg homunculus is on the medial hemisphere in the ACA territory
The first is left ACA because the face is lateral; the second is MCA because the leg is medial
Both are vertebral arteries, which supply the homunculus directly
The naming problem is a right parietal lobe sign
A grasp reflex localizes to the occipital pole
correctAnswer: The first is left MCA, which serves the lateral cortex including face and arm language areas; the leg homunculus is on the medial hemisphere in the ACA territory
explanation: The motor homunculus puts the leg in the medial interhemispheric fissure, ACA, and the face and arm on the lateral surface, MCA. The left MCA also covers language, so anomia with face and arm weakness is MCA. Leg-predominant weakness plus a grasp reflex is ACA and frontal medial cortex. Reversing the arteries is the trap the homunculus was drawn to prevent. The vertebral arteries do not supply the cortical homunculus. Naming is a dominant, usually left, hemisphere function. A grasp reflex is frontal, not occipital.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man with long hypertension has sudden right face, arm, and leg weakness equally, with no sensory loss, no aphasia, and no visual field cut. CT is too early to show the lesion. The suspected site is a small penetrating artery.
question: Which vessel and why is the cortex unlikely?
options: A lenticulostriate branch to the posterior limb of the internal capsule; the cortex would have added cortical signs such as aphasia or a field cut if a large MCA trunk were out
The left MCA stem, which causes pure motor loss and always spares the face
The anterior cerebral artery, which weakens face, arm, and leg equally
A PICA infarct, because pure motor stroke is a lateral medullary sign
The ophthalmic artery, because equal face and leg weakness is ocular
correctAnswer: A lenticulostriate branch to the posterior limb of the internal capsule; the cortex would have added cortical signs such as aphasia or a field cut if a large MCA trunk were out
explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm, and leg together, without sensory or cortical signs, is the lacunar syndrome of the contralateral internal capsule or basis pontis. Lipohyalinosis of a small penetrator such as a lenticulostriate artery is the usual cause in chronic hypertension. An MCA stem stroke is a large cortical and deep infarct and brings aphasia, neglect, or a gaze preference. ACA spares the face relative to the leg. PICA is lateral medulla and is not a pure motor hemiparesis. The ophthalmic artery does not supply the capsule.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 45-year-old woman has a sudden worst headache while lifting. CT of the head an hour later is read as normal. She still has neck stiffness. A colleague wants to send her home because the CT is negative. You are asked what test still matters today and what congenital association raises her risk if imaging later shows an aneurysm.
question: What do you do next, and which condition is linked to berry aneurysms?
options: Lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia or blood that CT missed; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with saccular aneurysms
Discharge, because CT is perfectly sensitive at one hour for every subarachnoid bleed
Start heparin, because thunderclap headache is ischemic stroke until proven otherwise
Order temporal artery biopsy before any spinal fluid test
Berry aneurysms are associated with tuberous sclerosis, not kidney cysts
correctAnswer: Lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia or blood that CT missed; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with saccular aneurysms
explanation: CT is very sensitive early but not perfect, and a negative scan with a true thunderclap headache and neck stiffness still needs a lumbar puncture to look for blood or xanthochromia. Missing that send-home is how a sentinel bleed is discharged. Heparin for an unexcluded hemorrhage is dangerous. Temporal artery biopsy is for older patients with jaw claudication and a high ESR, not a sudden headache at 45. Saccular aneurysms of the circle of Willis track with ADPKD, not with tuberous sclerosis.

references.label: Hoh BL et al. 2023 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Stroke 2023

scenario: A young woman with anorexia nervosa and a body mass index of 14 starts a large caloric prescription on the first hospital night. The next day she is weak, has a hemolytic look to the blood film discussion, and cannot get out of bed. Phosphate, which was normal on arrival, is now very low. Potassium and magnesium are drifting down.
question: Why did phosphate fall after feeding, and what should have been done?
options: Insulin from the carbohydrate load drives phosphate into cells to make ATP; phosphate should be replaced before and during refeeding, and calories advanced slowly
Phosphate falls because the kidney wastes it in starvation, and feeding stops that waste immediately so the level rises
The weakness is benzodiazepine withdrawal and phosphate is unrelated
Refeeding alkalosis raises total calcium and the phosphate drop is a lab error
A high-calorie start is safe if albumin is normal, because phosphate follows albumin
correctAnswer: Insulin from the carbohydrate load drives phosphate into cells to make ATP; phosphate should be replaced before and during refeeding, and calories advanced slowly
explanation: Starved cells are phosphate-poor. When insulin rises with feeding, phosphate, potassium, and magnesium rush intracellularly to rebuild ATP and glycogen. Serum phosphate can crash and cause weakness, hemolysis, and respiratory failure. The arrival phosphate can look normal and then fall, so you replete and advance calories slowly rather than celebrate a big first meal. Feeding does not instantly stop a renal waste in a way that raises phosphate; the level falls. This is not benzodiazepine withdrawal. It is not a calcium lab artifact. Phosphate is not albumin-bound the way a fraction of calcium is, and a normal albumin does not make aggressive refeeding safe.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 29-year-old man starts sertraline for a major depressive episode. On day 3 he feels no better and has nausea and jitteriness. He wants to stop and switch to alprazolam as the antidepressant. A friend told him the drug should work overnight if it really raises serotonin.
question: Why is there a delay, and why is a benzodiazepine not the antidepressant?
options: Autoreceptor and downstream receptor changes take weeks even though reuptake blockade is immediate; a benzodiazepine may sedate anxiety but does not treat the depressive episode
Sertraline blocks dopamine reuptake, so nausea on day 3 means the dose is already therapeutic for mood
Mood must improve within 72 hours or the diagnosis is wrong
Alprazolam increases serotonin reuptake and is first-line for melancholic depression
Jitteriness is serotonin syndrome and the SSRI should be doubled
correctAnswer: Autoreceptor and downstream receptor changes take weeks even though reuptake blockade is immediate; a benzodiazepine may sedate anxiety but does not treat the depressive episode
explanation: SSRIs block the serotonin transporter within hours, but mood response tracks slower changes in autoreceptors and postsynaptic signaling, classically several weeks. Early nausea and activation are common and are not proof of failure or of serotonin syndrome. A benzodiazepine can take the edge off anxiety and insomnia and can be habit-forming; it is not an antidepressant and is a poor substitute. Sertraline is not a dopamine-reuptake blocker as its main action. A three-day trial does not falsify the diagnosis. Alprazolam does not treat melancholia by increasing serotonin reuptake. Doubling the dose for mild early jitteriness risks real toxicity and is not the move.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 64-year-old man with pneumonia understands that he may die without antibiotics, can repeat the risks of the drug, states that he prefers to leave because he does not want this hospitalization, and gives a reason that follows from his values. He is not suicidal. A resident says he lacks capacity because the choice is unwise and because only a judge can decide capacity.
question: Which element is being confused?
options: Capacity is a clinical judgment about this decision: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a stable choice. It is not the same as agreeing with the physician, and legal competence is the court finding
Any refusal of a beneficial drug proves incapacity
Capacity can be declared only by a judge at the bedside
Understanding the facts is enough, so appreciation and reasoning are optional and he fails them here
He lacks capacity because pneumonia itself always removes decision-making ability
correctAnswer: Capacity is a clinical judgment about this decision: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and a stable choice. It is not the same as agreeing with the physician, and legal competence is the court finding
explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and clinical. This man understands, appreciates the consequence, reasons from his own values, and chooses consistently, so he has capacity to refuse even a choice the team dislikes. Competence is the legal status a court determines. Disagreeing with the doctor is not incapacity. A judge is not required to decide ordinary bedside capacity. He has shown more than bare fact-recall; the vignette includes appreciation and a reason. Pneumonia does not automatically erase capacity when the conversation shows intact elements.

scenario: A student who cheated on an exam loudly accuses classmates of cheating and tells the dean the class is dishonest. He does not mention his own paper. He is not having hallucinations, and he can describe his actions when asked directly later in private.
question: Which defense is this, and which nearby defense is it not?
options: Projection: he attributes his own unacceptable impulse to others. It is not displacement, which would move the feeling onto a safer target, and not dissociation
Displacement onto the dean, because the dean is a symbol of the exam
Reaction formation, because he is doing the opposite of cheating by reporting others
Sublimation, because accusing others is a socially useful act
Altruism, because he is protecting the class
correctAnswer: Projection: he attributes his own unacceptable impulse to others. It is not displacement, which would move the feeling onto a safer target, and not dissociation
explanation: Projection puts one's own unacceptable wish or act onto other people. The student deals with his cheating by experiencing other people as the cheaters. Displacement would shift the anger at himself onto a safer person while still owning the feeling's source more honestly; that is not this accusation. Reaction formation would have him behaving with exaggerated honesty, not accusing the room. Sublimation turns an impulse into a valued activity such as art or work, not a false accusation. Altruism serves someone else's welfare; this serves his own guilt.

scenario: A man washes his hands for hours because of a thought that they are contaminated. He knows the thought is excessive and it distresses him. He does not hear voices. A low-dose benzodiazepine was tried and did not touch the rituals. A drug that raises serotonin is being considered at a dose often higher than the depression dose, and a therapy that exposes him to the sink without washing.
question: Which loop is overactive, and why is a benzodiazepine a weak plan?
options: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops; benzodiazepines do not treat the obsession-compulsion cycle the way serotonin reuptake inhibition and exposure do
The mesolimbic dopamine tract only, so an antipsychotic is the sole first-line drug
The cerebellum, because rituals are a coordination problem
A seizure focus, so ethosuximide is first-line
Handwashing proves psychosis, so insight is impossible and serotonin drugs are contraindicated
correctAnswer: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops; benzodiazepines do not treat the obsession-compulsion cycle the way serotonin reuptake inhibition and exposure do
explanation: OCD is tied to overactive cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits. Patients usually have insight, which separates the illness from a delusion. High-dose SSRIs and exposure with response prevention are the treatments with a real effect. A benzodiazepine may relax him and does not stop the ritual loop, which is why it failed. Dopamine blockade is not the first-line monotherapy implied by calling it purely mesolimbic. The cerebellum does not generate obsessions. Ethosuximide is for absence seizures. Insight is present here, so this is not psychosis and an SSRI is not contraindicated.

scenario: A 9-year-old boy cannot stay in his seat, blurts answers, and loses homework. The pattern has been present since age 5 at home and at school. Sleep is normal and there is no seizure. Methylphenidate is started and attention improves. A relative worries the drug is a sedative because he is calmer.
question: What is the drug doing, and why is he calmer rather than sedated?
options: It blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in prefrontal circuits that support attention; better executive control looks calmer and is not GABA sedation
It facilitates GABA-A receptors, like lorazepam, which is why sleepiness is the therapeutic effect
It blocks dopamine, like haloperidol, and the calm is parkinsonism
Improvement proves the diagnosis was absence epilepsy
Stimulants worsen prefrontal signal by depleting norepinephrine, which is the intended effect
correctAnswer: It blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in prefrontal circuits that support attention; better executive control looks calmer and is not GABA sedation
explanation: Methylphenidate inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine transporters. In the prefrontal cortex that increases the signal used for sustained attention and impulse control, so the child stays with the task and looks calmer. It is not a GABA sedative, and therapeutic calm is not drowsiness. It is not a D2 blocker, and parkinsonism is not the goal or the usual effect. A normal sleep history and a long behavioral pattern are not absence seizures. The drug does not work by depleting norepinephrine.

scenario: A woman speaks in halting three-word phrases and points correctly to the door when asked. She cannot repeat 'no ifs, ands, or buts' any better than she can produce her own sentences. A second patient speaks in full sentences, names objects, follows commands, and still cannot repeat that same phrase.
question: What additional deficit separates conduction aphasia from Broca aphasia?
options: Nothing in repetition: both fail it. Conduction aphasia is separated by fluent speech and intact comprehension, localizing to the arcuate fasciculus rather than Broca area
Only Broca aphasia fails repetition; conduction aphasia repeats normally
Conduction aphasia cannot comprehend, which is why repetition fails
Broca aphasia is a right-hemisphere lesion in a right-handed person
The second patient has Wernicke aphasia because repetition is the comprehension test
correctAnswer: Nothing in repetition: both fail it. Conduction aphasia is separated by fluent speech and intact comprehension, localizing to the arcuate fasciculus rather than Broca area
explanation: Repetition fails in Broca, Wernicke, conduction, and global aphasia, so it does not by itself name the syndrome. The second patient is fluent and understands, which is conduction aphasia, a disconnection in the arcuate fasciculus between comprehension and production. The first patient is nonfluent with good comprehension, which is Broca. Saying conduction aphasia repeats normally is false. Conduction aphasia keeps comprehension. Broca area is dominant frontal, usually left. The second patient understands commands, so this is not Wernicke aphasia; repetition is not a comprehension test.

scenario: A 74-year-old man is admitted with a foot abscess and osteomyelitis, and surgery recommends a below-knee amputation. Yesterday he was febrile and disoriented. This morning he is afebrile, oriented to person, place, and time, and he scores 28 out of 30 on a bedside cognitive screen. He describes the infection in his own words, states that without amputation he may die of sepsis, and explains that he rejects amputation because he watched his brother die after a similar operation. He would rather die with his leg than live without it, and he repeats that choice after the risks are restated. His adult children say he is not competent and ask you to let them sign the consent. He has no advance directive and has not named a surrogate.
options: Accept his informed refusal and do not proceed with amputation
Petition the court today to declare incompetence and authorize surgery
Let his adult children provide substituted consent because they are next of kin
Transfer him for an emergency psychiatry admission so the surgery can proceed
Ask a second surgeon to operate under a two-physician emergency waiver
correctAnswer: Accept his informed refusal and do not proceed with amputation
explanation: He currently has decision-making capacity for this choice. He understands the infection, appreciates that refusing amputation may be fatal, offers a stable reason, and expresses a consistent choice. Capacity is a clinical judgment about this decision at this time. Legal incompetence is a status a court declares, and a capacitated refusal is not a reason to seek that status. The polite path of letting worried children take over, and the legalistic path of an emergency waiver, are both ruled out by the fact that he understands the decision. Petition the court today to declare incompetence and authorize surgery would treat a value choice as a legal defect. Let his adult children provide substituted consent because they are next of kin gives relatives authority they do not have while he retains capacity. Transfer him for an emergency psychiatry admission so the surgery can proceed mislabels a reasoned refusal as a psychiatric crisis; he is not psychotic or unable to care for himself because of mental illness. Ask a second surgeon to operate under a two-physician emergency waiver misuses an exception meant for a patient who cannot consent when delay threatens life and no surrogate is available.

scenario: A 69-year-old woman with mild dementia is in the hospital for elective repair of a reducible, painless inguinal hernia. At 2 a.m. she was disoriented and pulled at her intravenous catheter. At 10 a.m. she is oriented, recalls the surgeon explanation of infection, recurrence, and nerve injury, and says she wants to decide after talking with her sister, who arrives this evening. The hernia is not incarcerated and there is no plan to operate before tomorrow. The night nurse says nighttime confusion permanently removed her authority. Her son is willing to sign immediately and says he does not want to bother her with details. She asks to speak for herself while she is clear.
options: Obtain her own consent during this lucid interval rather than accepting her son signature now
Accept the son signature now because nighttime confusion permanently removes her authority
Delay every discussion until a court declares her competent to sign
Proceed tonight under an emergency waiver because she was confused overnight
Cancel the repair permanently because any dementia eliminates consent
correctAnswer: Obtain her own consent during this lucid interval rather than accepting her son signature now
explanation: Capacity can fluctuate. She is lucid now, the repair is elective, and the decision can wait until she has spoken with her sister. The appropriate step is to use this lucid interval and let her decide, not to transfer authority because of one confused night. Accept the son signature now because nighttime confusion permanently removes her authority treats a temporary delirium as a lasting loss of her voice. Delay every discussion until a court declares her competent to sign confuses a clinical capacity assessment with a judicial competence proceeding she does not need while she can decide. Proceed tonight under an emergency waiver because she was confused overnight invents an emergency: the hernia is reducible and painless, so delay until evening does not threaten her life. Cancel the repair permanently because any dementia eliminates consent is false; mild dementia does not erase capacity when she understands this operation and states a plan to decide.

scenario: A 46-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted with wet gangrene of the left foot. At baseline he takes his antipsychotic, lives alone, and has no current hallucinations or delusions. He names the diagnosis, states that refusal of amputation may lead to sepsis and death, and says he prefers death to amputation for a religious reason he has held for years. His reasoning stays the same when the risks are repeated. Psychiatry finds no current psychosis and confirms that he appreciates the consequences. He is not asking to die by any other means. His brother says schizophrenia means he cannot refuse and demands a court order for surgery.
options: Honor his refusal of amputation after documenting the capacity assessment
Obtain a court order for involuntary amputation because schizophrenia negates capacity
Proceed with surgery under an emergency psychiatry hold
Ask the brother to sign as surrogate because a psychiatric diagnosis transfers authority
Give extra antipsychotic medication and operate only after he agrees
correctAnswer: Honor his refusal of amputation after documenting the capacity assessment
explanation: A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove decision-making capacity. He understands the gangrene, appreciates that death may follow refusal, and gives a long-held religious reason. That assessment should be documented and his refusal honored. The legalistic demand for a court order is ruled out by a capacity exam that he passes. Obtain a court order for involuntary amputation because schizophrenia negates capacity treats the diagnosis as if it automatically voided capacity, which it does not. Proceed with surgery under an emergency psychiatry hold is not supported: he is not dangerous, gravely disabled, or acutely psychotic, and a hold is not a device to force an operation. Ask the brother to sign as surrogate because a psychiatric diagnosis transfers authority skips the patient who still has authority. Give extra antipsychotic medication and operate only after he agrees uses drugs to manufacture agreement rather than to treat a psychosis he does not currently have.

scenario: A 58-year-old man is in septic shock from perforated diverticulitis. Blood pressure is 78/46 mm Hg after fluids, lactate is rising, and the surgeon says laparotomy cannot wait an hour. He is confused, pulls at lines, and says the surgeons are impostors and that nothing is wrong with his belly. He cannot repeat any risk and does not give a stable choice. No surrogate can be reached. A colleague suggests waiting for a court hearing so no one can accuse the team of operating without a signature.
options: Proceed with life-saving laparotomy under the emergency exception to consent
Honor his statement that nothing is wrong because every refusal must be obeyed
Wait for a court hearing before making an incision
Ask the hospital attorney to serve as his surrogate decision maker
Give haloperidol and delay the operation until he can sign the form
correctAnswer: Proceed with life-saving laparotomy under the emergency exception to consent
explanation: He cannot understand, appreciate, or state a choice, no surrogate is available, and delay for a signature would likely be fatal. In that narrow emergency, treatment proceeds under implied consent. His words are the product of delirium, not an informed refusal. Honor his statement that nothing is wrong because every refusal must be obeyed would let a patient who cannot appreciate a perforation decline a life-saving operation. Wait for a court hearing before making an incision mistakes a judicial competence process for the emergency exception and would cost him the hour he does not have. Ask the hospital attorney to serve as his surrogate decision maker invents a surrogate; an attorney for the hospital is not his decision maker. Give haloperidol and delay the operation until he can sign the form treats the paperwork as more urgent than source control of septic shock.

scenario: A 16-year-old girl asks to be seen alone. For two months she has had low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, and falling grades. She denies suicidal ideation, a plan, self-harm, and abuse. She agrees to psychotherapy and to call if she develops thoughts of suicide. She says that if you tell her parents she will never come back. Her mother is in the waiting room and says that because she pays the insurance she has a right to every word of the interview. The girl is willing for you to say only that she was seen and is safe.
options: Keep the interview confidential, encourage her to involve a parent later, and arrange care
Disclose the full interview to the mother because minors cannot hold confidentiality
Refuse treatment until a parent signs a release of every psychotherapy note
Tell the mother the depression diagnosis so she can monitor moods at home
Report the girl to child protective services for being withdrawn at school
correctAnswer: Keep the interview confidential, encourage her to involve a parent later, and arrange care
explanation: An adolescent may expect confidentiality for ordinary mental health care when there is no imminent danger and no abuse. She has no suicidal plan and no safety exception applies, so the interview stays private, she is encouraged to involve a parent when she is ready, and treatment is arranged. Paying for insurance does not give a parent the content of this visit. Disclose the full interview to the mother because minors cannot hold confidentiality overstates the law and would predictably drive her away from care. Refuse treatment until a parent signs a release of every psychotherapy note conditions care on a waiver she has already rejected and is not required here. Tell the mother the depression diagnosis so she can monitor moods at home is still a breach; monitoring can be offered through the adolescent, not by disclosing over her objection. Report the girl to child protective services for being withdrawn at school invents neglect from a voluntary disclosure of depression.

scenario: A 15-year-old boy is seen alone at his request. He has written a farewell note and describes a plan to die tonight by taking a bottle of acetaminophen that is in his backpack. He can show you the bottle. He begs you to keep the promise, made at a prior visit, that everything he says stays in the room, and he says he will never trust a doctor again if you tell his father. He is medically stable at this moment and is not intoxicated. His father is in the waiting room. He refuses to stay if you involve any adult.
options: Break confidentiality, stay with him, and inform his father so emergency care can proceed
Keep the promise of absolute confidentiality and send him home with a crisis hotline
Ask him to return tomorrow with a parent if he still feels suicidal
Leave a voicemail for the school principal and take no further protective step
Document his request for secrecy and discharge him because he is not yet poisoned
correctAnswer: Break confidentiality, stay with him, and inform his father so emergency care can proceed
explanation: A specific suicidal plan with means is an exception to adolescent confidentiality. The promise of privacy yields to the duty to protect him. He should not be left alone, his father should be told, and emergency psychiatric care should proceed even though he objects. Keep the promise of absolute confidentiality and send him home with a crisis hotline preserves trust on paper and leaves a planned overdose in his backpack. Ask him to return tomorrow with a parent if he still feels suicidal delays protection past the night he has identified. Leave a voicemail for the school principal and take no further protective step notifies the wrong person and does not secure him now. Document his request for secrecy and discharge him because he is not yet poisoned waits for medical injury instead of preventing a stated plan that is ready to happen tonight.

scenario: A 14-year-old girl is seen alone for abdominal pain. She discloses that her stepfather has been sexually abusing her for six months. She has no life-threatening injury today, and a pregnancy test is negative. She says that if you tell anyone she will claim she made it up, and she asks you not to call her mother because her mother does not believe her. The stepfather is not in the clinic. A senior resident suggests waiting for a forensic examination to confirm physical findings before deciding whether a report is justified.
options: Report the suspected abuse to child protective services without waiting for her consent
Honor her request for confidentiality because she is an adolescent
Confront the stepfather at the next visit and report only if he confesses
Tell the mother and leave the decision to report entirely to her
Delay any report until a forensic examination confirms physical findings
correctAnswer: Report the suspected abuse to child protective services without waiting for her consent
explanation: Suspected child sexual abuse is a mandatory report. Adolescent confidentiality does not cover abuse, and the reporter does not need the child consent, a parent permission, the alleged abuser confession, or proof on examination. A reasonable suspicion is enough, and she has given a clear disclosure. Honor her request for confidentiality because she is an adolescent applies the ordinary privacy rule to a fact pattern that is an explicit exception. Confront the stepfather at the next visit and report only if he confesses warns the alleged abuser and withholds a report that does not depend on his admission. Tell the mother and leave the decision to report entirely to her shifts a legal duty onto a parent the patient already believes will not act. Delay any report until a forensic examination confirms physical findings confuses investigation with the threshold for reporting; many abused adolescents have no confirmatory physical finding.

scenario: A 15-year-old girl has purulent cervical discharge. Nucleic acid amplification testing confirms Chlamydia trachomatis. She is not pregnant. She says her only partner is a 16-year-old classmate and that the encounters were consensual, with no force, payment, or adult involved. She asks to be treated without her parents being told because they would punish her for being sexually active. She can describe how the antibiotic is taken and why partners need treatment. The portal would automatically release the diagnosis to the parent account unless you block it.
options: Treat the infection and do not notify her parents of the diagnosis
Refuse antibiotics until a parent signs a consent form
Call her mother before writing any prescription because she is under 16
Treat her but release the visit diagnosis to her parents through the portal
Report the sexual activity to child protective services solely because she is 15
correctAnswer: Treat the infection and do not notify her parents of the diagnosis
explanation: Minors can consent to diagnosis and treatment of a sexually transmitted infection, and that care is kept confidential. She should be treated, partner treatment discussed, and her parents not notified. The consensual same-age relationship she describes is not, by itself, a child-abuse report. Refuse antibiotics until a parent signs a consent form withholds indicated treatment to satisfy a signature the minor-consent rule does not require. Call her mother before writing any prescription because she is under 16 uses age as a blanket bar and will predictably stop her from accepting care. Treat her but release the visit diagnosis to her parents through the portal defeats confidentiality after the fact. Report the sexual activity to child protective services solely because she is 15 treats consensual peer contact, with no adult, force, or exploitation described, as if it were the abuse exception.

scenario: A 16-year-old girl comes alone asking for prenatal care. Office testing confirms pregnancy at about 8 weeks. She wants to continue the pregnancy. She is hemodynamically stable, has no vaginal bleeding, and denies suicidal ideation. She says her parents have told her they would expel her from the home if she were pregnant, and she asks that they not be told. She can explain that prenatal visits, laboratories, and ultrasound are meant to protect her health and the pregnancy. A clerk says no prenatal laboratory test can be drawn without a parent signature.
options: Provide prenatal care under her own consent and do not disclose the pregnancy to her parents
Require a parent signature before any prenatal laboratory test
Notify her parents because pregnancy care is excluded from minor consent
Contact the father of the baby to obtain consent for her obstetric care
Refuse to see her until she agrees to a family meeting
correctAnswer: Provide prenatal care under her own consent and do not disclose the pregnancy to her parents
explanation: A minor may consent to pregnancy-related care, and that information is not automatically shared with her parents. She wants to continue the pregnancy and understands the purpose of prenatal care, so care starts under her consent and the pregnancy is not disclosed. Require a parent signature before any prenatal laboratory test blocks routine care with a formality the minor-consent rule removes. Notify her parents because pregnancy care is excluded from minor consent has the exclusion backward: pregnancy care is a core category minors may consent to. Contact the father of the baby to obtain consent for her obstetric care gives authority to someone who is not her decision maker and may breach her privacy. Refuse to see her until she agrees to a family meeting conditions indicated prenatal care on a disclosure she has reason to fear.

scenario: A 17-year-old boy asks to start treatment for opioid use disorder. He has daily fentanyl use, clear withdrawal symptoms, and wants buprenorphine. He is not suicidal, not intoxicated today, and can describe the risks and benefits of medication and the need for follow-up. He says that if his parents are called he will leave and keep using. A colleague says federal controlled-substance rules require a parent signature before any minor may receive buprenorphine, and that without that signature the only legal step is to discharge him with a pamphlet or to notify police of illegal drug use.
options: Arrange substance use treatment under his consent without requiring parental notification
Refuse medication until a parent signs because he is not yet 18
Notify his parents over his objection before any treatment discussion
Discharge him with a pamphlet because confidentiality and controlled substances cannot be reconciled
Report him to the police for illegal drug use as a condition of starting care
correctAnswer: Arrange substance use treatment under his consent without requiring parental notification
explanation: Minors may consent to substance use treatment, and parental notification is not a condition of that care. He has capacity for this decision, he is asking for evidence-based treatment, and calling his parents would, on these facts, drive him away. The legalistic claim that a controlled substance cannot be started without a parent signature is the trap. Refuse medication until a parent signs because he is not yet 18 withholds treatment the minor-consent rule was written to allow. Notify his parents over his objection before any treatment discussion breaches confidentiality and is likely to end the visit. Discharge him with a pamphlet because confidentiality and controlled substances cannot be reconciled is a false conflict; confidentiality and buprenorphine treatment can proceed together. Report him to the police for illegal drug use as a condition of starting care punishes the disclosure that treatment depends on and is not a therapeutic or legal prerequisite.

scenario: An 81-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease is admitted with aspiration pneumonia. Three years ago, while she still had capacity, she completed a written directive and told her daughter, who is her designated health care agent, that if she could not recognize her family and could not eat, she did not want a feeding tube. She now recognizes no one and has no safe swallow. The daughter says she cannot watch her mother starve, asks you to place a gastrostomy tube, and states that as agent she has the legal right to override the old paper. There is no new statement from the patient.
options: Decline the feeding tube and follow the patient prior written directive
Place the gastrostomy tube because an agent current wish overrides a prior directive
Place the tube under a best-interest standard because nutrition is always beneficial
Seek a court order authorizing the tube over her written refusal
Start a 30-day tube trial because withholding food differs legally from withdrawing it
correctAnswer: Decline the feeding tube and follow the patient prior written directive
explanation: The agent role is to apply substituted judgment: what the patient wanted, not what the agent now finds bearable. This patient left a written directive and a specific oral statement refusing a tube in exactly this circumstance. Artificial nutrition is a medical treatment she refused. The daughter grief does not create new authority to reverse that refusal. Place the gastrostomy tube because an agent current wish overrides a prior directive reverses the hierarchy; the directive constrains the agent. Place the tube under a best-interest standard because nutrition is always beneficial uses the wrong standard, because known wishes take priority over a best-interest guess, and nutrition is not automatically beneficial near the end of life. Seek a court order authorizing the tube over her written refusal asks a court to defeat a clear directive rather than to enforce it. Start a 30-day tube trial because withholding food differs legally from withdrawing it relies on a distinction ethics does not draw; withholding and withdrawing unwanted life-sustaining treatment are equivalent, and a trial she already refused is not required.

scenario: A 70-year-old man remains unresponsive after a witnessed cardiac arrest. Neurologic prognosis for meaningful recovery is poor. He never named a surrogate, never stated wishes about life support, and has no advance directive. Two siblings disagree: one wants every machine continued, the other wants extubation today. Both say they have no idea what he would have wanted. No spouse, children, or other relatives exist. The older sibling says birth order should settle the question in favor of indefinite ventilation.
options: Use the best-interest standard and an ethics consultation to resolve the sibling conflict
Apply substituted judgment by assuming the older sibling knew him better
Continue mechanical ventilation indefinitely because disagreement must favor life support
Let the older sibling decide because birth order creates priority when wishes are unknown
Withdraw support immediately without discussing burdens and benefits
correctAnswer: Use the best-interest standard and an ethics consultation to resolve the sibling conflict
explanation: Substituted judgment asks what this patient would have chosen. Nobody knows, so that standard cannot be honestly applied. The decision then rests on best interest: the benefits and burdens of continued support for him, not the siblings distress alone. When equal surrogates conflict, an ethics consultation is the appropriate process rather than an invented hierarchy. Apply substituted judgment by assuming the older sibling knew him better pretends to know wishes both siblings deny having heard. Continue mechanical ventilation indefinitely because disagreement must favor life support treats conflict as a reason never to weigh burdens. Let the older sibling decide because birth order creates priority when wishes are unknown invents a legal rank the facts do not provide. Withdraw support immediately without discussing burdens and benefits skips the best-interest analysis and the conflict-resolution step the disagreement requires.

scenario: A 66-year-old man cannot communicate after a large intracranial hemorrhage. Five years ago he executed a durable power of attorney for health care naming a close friend as his agent. The document is in the chart. He had told the friend he would not want prolonged ventilation if he could not recover meaningful interaction. The clinicians believe that outcome is not realistic. His wife, from whom he is not divorced, demands a tracheostomy and says a spouse outranks a friend no matter what the paper says. The friend asks that ventilation not be prolonged.
options: Follow the designated agent decision, which applies the patient stated wishes
Follow the wife because marriage automatically cancels a durable power of attorney
Poll the extended family and adopt the majority view
Ask a court to appoint the wife before any decision because the agent is not a relative
Continue ventilation by default until the wife and the friend sign a joint form
correctAnswer: Follow the designated agent decision, which applies the patient stated wishes
explanation: A valid designation selects the decision maker. The friend is the agent and is applying the patient own statement against prolonged ventilation if meaningful interaction cannot be recovered. Marriage does not silently cancel that document. Follow the wife because marriage automatically cancels a durable power of attorney is the legalistic trap; the paper exists so that a spouse does not automatically outrank a chosen agent. Poll the extended family and adopt the majority view replaces a designated decision maker with a vote. Ask a court to appoint the wife before any decision because the agent is not a relative seeks a guardian the patient already made unnecessary by naming an agent. Continue ventilation by default until the wife and the friend sign a joint form gives the wife a veto the designation does not give her and delays a decision the agent is authorized to make.

scenario: A 54-year-old man received another patient morning dose of metoprolol because of a labeling error. His heart rate fell to 48 beats per minute, he felt briefly lightheaded, the dose was held, and he was monitored. By afternoon his heart rate and blood pressure are back to his baseline and he is comfortable. The charge nurse says no lasting harm was done, telling him will only make him angry and could cause a lawsuit, and the note should describe a vasovagal episode. He is awake and asks why he felt faint after the morning medicines.
options: Tell him a medication error occurred, what was done, and how he is being monitored
Document a vasovagal episode so the record matches a harmless story
Disclose the error only if he later develops heart block
Ask the nurse to apologize alone and keep the physician out of the conversation
Offer a settlement payment before explaining what happened
correctAnswer: Tell him a medication error occurred, what was done, and how he is being monitored
explanation: The wrong drug reached the patient and caused transient bradycardia. An error that reaches a patient is disclosed even when the outcome is now back to baseline. He should hear what happened, what was done, and how he is being watched. Hiding it to avoid anger or a lawsuit is the trap these facts rule out. Document a vasovagal episode so the record matches a harmless story falsifies the chart and deceives him. Disclose the error only if he later develops heart block makes disclosure depend on a later complication instead of on the error that already occurred. Ask the nurse to apologize alone and keep the physician out of the conversation abandons the physician duty to disclose and singles out one colleague. Offer a settlement payment before explaining what happened substitutes money for the explanation he is already requesting and can look like an attempt to buy silence.

scenario: A resident discovers that a patient received 10 times the intended dose of an antibiotic because of an order-entry error. The patient is stable, the team has not yet spoken with him, and the original note correctly describes the dose given. Risk management advises deleting that note and replacing it with a note that the intended dose was given, and also changing the medication administration record, before the family requests the chart. The resident asks whether a late addendum admitting the error would only create liability.
options: Preserve the original note, add a timed addendum, disclose the error, and file a safety report
Delete the original note so the chart shows only the intended dose
Leave the inaccurate possibility uncorrected and avoid any addendum that admits an error
Alter the medication administration record to match the order that should have been written
Ask the patient to sign a waiver releasing the team from any duty to explain
correctAnswer: Preserve the original note, add a timed addendum, disclose the error, and file a safety report
explanation: The original entry is an accurate record of what happened and must stay. New facts or a correction belong in a timed addendum. The patient is told the truth, and a safety report addresses the system. Cleaning the chart to reduce liability is the trap. Delete the original note so the chart shows only the intended dose destroys the record and hides an error that reached the patient. Leave the inaccurate possibility uncorrected and avoid any addendum that admits an error confuses honesty with silence; an addendum does not rewrite history, it completes it, and disclosure is still required. Alter the medication administration record to match the order that should have been written falsifies the dose that was actually given. Ask the patient to sign a waiver releasing the team from any duty to explain tries to contract out of a duty that cannot be waived before he even knows what happened.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: You are the resident in the operating room for an elective colectomy. The attending surgeon arrives with slurred speech, the smell of alcohol on his breath, and an unsteady gait while he reviews the consent. The patient is already anesthetized. A colleague says the attending does this sometimes, that starting the case will avoid humiliating him, and that a second surgeon can assist closely enough to make it safe. The attending says he is fine and asks everyone to keep this among the team so the schedule is not delayed.
options: Stop him from operating and notify the chief of service or physician health program now
Allow him to operate with a second surgeon watching so the schedule is not delayed
Wait until after the case and then suggest he cut back on drinking
Accept his promise to drink only on weekends and tell leadership nothing
Transfer the anesthetized patient to another hospital without explaining why
correctAnswer: Stop him from operating and notify the chief of service or physician health program now
explanation: An impaired physician must not care for patients. Alcohol intoxication with slurred speech and an unsteady gait is present-tense impairment, the patient is anesthetized, and the case has not started in his hands. He is removed from the operation now, a qualified surgeon takes over or the case is delayed, and the chief of service or physician health program is notified. Collegial silence is the trap. Allow him to operate with a second surgeon watching so the schedule is not delayed leaves an impaired operator in control for the sake of the board. Wait until after the case and then suggest he cut back on drinking exposes this patient to harm and replaces a report with private advice. Accept his promise to drink only on weekends and tell leadership nothing relies on a promise that does not make him safe today. Transfer the anesthetized patient to another hospital without explaining why moves the patient recklessly and still fails to report the impaired surgeon.

scenario: A fellow resident tells you she has been drinking a pint of vodka every night. Two days ago she drove to the hospital still feeling buzzed and covered a ward shift. This morning she is sober, steady, and about to start another inpatient shift. She asks you to keep the story a secret between friends and says she will quit on her own. She does not want the program director or the physician health service involved. No patient has yet been identified as harmed. She plans to drive home after tonight shift.
options: Remove her from duty until evaluated and inform the program director or physician health service
Keep her confidence because she is sober at this moment
Watch her patients quietly while she works the shift
Report her to the state police before speaking with any clinical supervisor
Wait to act until a patient is harmed
correctAnswer: Remove her from duty until evaluated and inform the program director or physician health service
explanation: She has already come to work impaired and intends to keep working and driving. A private promise to quit is not a safeguard. She should be relieved of clinical duty until she is evaluated, and the program director or physician health service must be informed so patients are protected and she can get help. Keep her confidence because she is sober at this moment uses this morning sobriety to erase a pattern of working while buzzed. Watch her patients quietly while she works the shift is informal supervision that hides the impairment instead of removing it. Report her to the state police before speaking with any clinical supervisor jumps to a criminal report and skips the clinical safety step that has to happen before tonight shift. Wait to act until a patient is harmed uses injury as the threshold; the duty to act begins when impairment threatens care, not after a bad outcome.

scenario: A 42-year-old woman who is a Jehovah Witness is bleeding from a peptic ulcer. Hemoglobin is 4.8 g/dL. She is alert and oriented. She repeats back that she may die without blood and refuses red cells, platelets, and plasma for a religious reason she has held for 20 years. She accepts crystalloid, iron, and endoscopy. Her husband urges you to transfuse her once she is sedated for endoscopy, saying she will forgive you. He offers to sign a transfusion consent. She hears him and says again that she refuses blood even if she loses consciousness during the procedure.
options: Do not transfuse blood products and proceed with the other measures she has accepted
Transfuse once she is sedated because consent for endoscopy covers blood
Seek an emergency court order to override a capacitated adult religious refusal
Ask her husband to sign a transfusion consent that supersedes her decision
Promise to respect her refusal and transfuse if she loses consciousness during endoscopy
correctAnswer: Do not transfuse blood products and proceed with the other measures she has accepted
explanation: A capacitated adult may refuse blood even when refusal may be fatal. She understands the risk, states a long-held religious reason, and extends the refusal to a later loss of consciousness. The team uses the treatments she accepts and does not transfuse. Transfuse once she is sedated because consent for endoscopy covers blood smuggles in a product she specifically excluded; sedation is not permission. Seek an emergency court order to override a capacitated adult religious refusal asks a court to do what a capacity assessment already forbids. Ask her husband to sign a transfusion consent that supersedes her decision gives a spouse no power to overrule a capacitated patient. Promise to respect her refusal and transfuse if she loses consciousness during endoscopy is a deception: she has already refused transfusion for that exact moment, and loss of consciousness does not cancel a refusal she made while capacitated.

scenario: A 6-year-old boy, whose parents are Jehovah Witnesses, is in hemorrhagic shock after trauma. Hemoglobin is 5.1 g/dL and he is tachycardic despite crystalloid. The parents refuse all blood products and ask for saline only. They are devoted and are not abusive in any other way. There is not time for a completed trial before he needs transfusion, although the hospital attorney can be notified while care proceeds. The child is too young to understand the decision and is asked by a relative to sign a refusal form.
options: Transfuse the child while notifying the legal authorities as required
Honor the parents refusal exactly as you would for a capacitated adult
Delay transfusion until a full trial is completed even if he arrests
Ask the child to sign a refusal form
Discharge the family so they can seek care that matches their beliefs
correctAnswer: Transfuse the child while notifying the legal authorities as required
explanation: Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a child. Blood is indicated now, so he is transfused, and the legal process is started in parallel rather than used as a reason to wait through an arrest. This is the opposite of the capacitated adult who refuses blood. Honor the parents refusal exactly as you would for a capacitated adult imports an adult rule into a decision the child cannot make and the parents cannot impose. Delay transfusion until a full trial is completed even if he arrests prefers a finished hearing to survival when an emergency authorization path exists. Ask the child to sign a refusal form treats a 6-year-old in shock as if he had capacity. Discharge the family so they can seek care that matches their beliefs abandons a child who needs blood in this emergency department.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 38-year-old woman has chronic abdominal pain. Examination, laboratories, and imaging have shown no dangerous cause. She has decision-making capacity and asks for a real strong medicine, even an injection. A resident proposes injecting saline and telling her it is a potent new analgesic, arguing that a placebo response could help and that saline has almost no medical risk. She has not been told that a placebo is being considered and has not agreed to one. The resident also suggests documenting that a new analgesic was given so her expectations stay high, or asking her husband for permission to deceive her.
options: Do not give a deceptive placebo; explain the findings and offer honest symptom treatment
Inject saline and call it a potent new analgesic because the intention is beneficent
Inject saline and call it a potent new analgesic because the risk is negligible
Write in the chart that a new analgesic was given so her expectations are reinforced
Ask her husband for permission to deceive her so a surrogate preserves her autonomy
correctAnswer: Do not give a deceptive placebo; explain the findings and offer honest symptom treatment
explanation: A placebo in clinical care requires the patient knowledge and agreement. Calling saline a potent new analgesic is a lie, even if the motive is relief and the fluid is physiologically harmless. She should hear the evaluation results and be offered honest treatment of the symptom. Inject saline and call it a potent new analgesic because the intention is beneficent uses a good motive to justify deception. Inject saline and call it a potent new analgesic because the risk is negligible ignores that the harm is the lie and the corrupted consent, not the saline. Write in the chart that a new analgesic was given so her expectations are reinforced falsifies the record to prop up the same deception. Ask her husband for permission to deceive her so a surrogate preserves her autonomy is incoherent: she has capacity, so a husband cannot consent to a deception, and deceiving her does not preserve autonomy.

scenario: A 47-year-old woman who speaks only Spanish is about to learn that her breast biopsy shows invasive carcinoma. Her 11-year-old daughter is bilingual, is in the room, and says she always translates for her mother and has already looked up the word for cancer. A professional interpreter can be on the telephone within a few minutes. The daughter asks you to speak quickly so she can get back to school. The mother has not yet been told the diagnosis. There is no airway emergency or other instability that requires speech in the next minute.
options: Use a professional interpreter and do not have the child interpret the diagnosis
Let the daughter interpret because she is bilingual and the mother trusts her
Let the daughter interpret to avoid a short delay
Ask the daughter to interpret only the word cancer and then continue in English
Write the diagnosis in English and ask the child to read it aloud at home
correctAnswer: Use a professional interpreter and do not have the child interpret the diagnosis
explanation: A child should not interpret a new cancer diagnosis when a professional interpreter is minutes away. Using the daughter burdens her with grave news, risks an inaccurate translation, and may keep the mother from asking questions. The short wait is appropriate because the patient is stable. Let the daughter interpret because she is bilingual and the mother trusts her prefers familiarity over a qualified interpreter. Let the daughter interpret to avoid a short delay treats a few minutes as if they were an emergency that justified a child interpreter. Ask the daughter to interpret only the word cancer and then continue in English still uses the child for the central disclosure and then excludes the mother from the rest of the conversation. Write the diagnosis in English and ask the child to read it aloud at home moves the same inappropriate role out of the clinic and leaves the mother without a chance to ask questions of the physician.

scenario: A capacitated patient is scheduled for carotid endarterectomy this afternoon. The attending surgeon who will perform the operation tells a third-year medical student to have her sign the consent form because the risks are on the sticker and the attending is in the laboratory. The student has never seen an endarterectomy and cannot answer questions about stroke risk. The patient asks whether she will be awake and what happens if she has a stroke during the operation. She signed a general hospital consent on admission. The circulating nurse offers to read the sticker aloud.
options: The attending surgeon returns and conducts the informed consent discussion before any signature
The student obtains the signature because a signed form is the consent
The circulating nurse reads the sticker so the attending can remain in the laboratory
No further consent is needed because she signed a general hospital consent on admission
The student answers the stroke question from a textbook and then has her sign
correctAnswer: The attending surgeon returns and conducts the informed consent discussion before any signature
explanation: Informed consent is a discussion by someone who understands the procedure and will perform it, covering the nature, benefits, risks, and alternatives, and answering this patient questions. A sticker and a signature are not that discussion. The attending surgeon returns and conducts the informed consent discussion before any signature. The student obtains the signature because a signed form is the consent confuses the form, which is evidence, with the consent, which is the understanding. The circulating nurse reads the sticker so the attending can remain in the laboratory delegates a discussion the nurse is not offering as the operating surgeon and leaves the stroke question unanswered by the person who should answer it. No further consent is needed because she signed a general hospital consent on admission treats an admission form as permission for a specific operation and its particular risks. The student answers the stroke question from a textbook and then has her sign still has an unqualified person obtain consent for a procedure the student does not perform.

scenario: A 29-year-old man in the emergency psychiatry area says he will shoot his supervisor, whom he names, tomorrow morning in the office parking lot. He describes the gun in his car and the time the supervisor arrives. He refuses voluntary hospitalization. He says you cannot tell anyone because this is therapy. He is calm enough to give these details and does not appear intoxicated. A no-harm contract is offered by a colleague as a way to discharge him without calling anyone. He will not identify a family member who could remove the gun.
options: Warn law enforcement or the identified supervisor and pursue an involuntary hold
Keep absolute confidentiality because the threat was made during a psychiatric interview
Schedule outpatient therapy next week without warning anyone
Ask him to sign a no-harm contract and then discharge him
Notify his employer only of a generic stress leave without mentioning the threat
correctAnswer: Warn law enforcement or the identified supervisor and pursue an involuntary hold
explanation: A credible threat aimed at an identified person, with a plan, a weapon, and a time, creates a duty to protect. Confidentiality yields. Protective steps include warning law enforcement or the named supervisor and pursuing hospitalization over his objection. Keep absolute confidentiality because the threat was made during a psychiatric interview treats therapy privacy as absolute when this is the classic exception. Schedule outpatient therapy next week without warning anyone leaves the named person exposed tomorrow morning. Ask him to sign a no-harm contract and then discharge him substitutes a piece of paper for protection; a contract does not remove a gun or a stated plan. Notify his employer only of a generic stress leave without mentioning the threat withholds the information that would let the intended victim take the warning seriously.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 34-year-old man in weekly therapy says that people at work annoy him so much he could scream and that the world is unfair. He denies any plan, weapon, named target, or intent to harm a particular person. He has no history of violence. He agrees to keep coming and to call if he develops a plan. A colleague says every mention of anger triggers a duty to warn the police and to warn every coworker whose name appears in the notes, and that the safe clinic response is involuntary hospitalization or termination of therapy.
options: Continue assessment and treatment without a duty-to-warn notification
Notify the police that he is a danger to the public
Warn every coworker whose name appears in the therapy notes
Hospitalize him involuntarily for mentioning anger
Terminate therapy so the clinic is not liable
correctAnswer: Continue assessment and treatment without a duty-to-warn notification
explanation: A duty to warn requires a serious threat to an identifiable victim, not irritation expressed without a plan, a weapon, or a target. He should stay in treatment, and the clinician keeps assessing for a plan. The legalistic impulse to notify everyone is ruled out by the absence of those elements. Notify the police that he is a danger to the public overcalls a vague complaint into a public warning he does not meet. Warn every coworker whose name appears in the therapy notes broadcasts confidential material about people he has not threatened. Hospitalize him involuntarily for mentioning anger uses anger, without danger to self or others or grave disability, as if it met the standard for a hold. Terminate therapy so the clinic is not liable abandons a patient who is engaged in care and has no plan.

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 36-year-old man has a new diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus infection and a detectable viral load. He understands transmission. He refuses to tell his wife, with whom he continues to have unprotected sex, and he asks you to tell her that his visits are for kidney stones if she calls. She is not your patient. He has decision-making capacity and is medically ready to start antiretroviral therapy. He says he will stop coming if you involve anyone. A partner-services nurse is available through the health department.
options: Decline to lie, urge him to inform his wife, and notify public health if he will not
Agree to tell the wife he has kidney stones so he will keep coming to clinic
Promise permanent secrecy and take no further step
Call the wife yourself before giving him any chance to disclose
Withhold antiretroviral therapy until he brings his wife to an appointment
correctAnswer: Decline to lie, urge him to inform his wife, and notify public health if he will not
explanation: You do not deceive the wife. He is urged to tell her promptly. If he refuses, the public health department can carry out partner notification. His own treatment is not held hostage to that conversation. Agree to tell the wife he has kidney stones so he will keep coming to clinic is a lie told to preserve the relationship, and the facts rule it out. Promise permanent secrecy and take no further step leaves a sexual partner at ongoing risk after he has refused to warn her. Call the wife yourself before giving him any chance to disclose skips the step in which he is asked to disclose and makes the physician the first caller. Withhold antiretroviral therapy until he brings his wife to an appointment uses needed medicine as leverage and can worsen both his health and the risk of transmission.

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 33-year-old woman, capacitated and financially independent, discloses that her boyfriend hit her last night. She has a bruise on her arm, is not elderly, and is not dependent on him for basic care. No children live in the home. She says she is not ready to involve the police and that she has a safe place to stay tonight with her sister. She asks you not to file a police report. She accepts a written hotline number and a safety plan. Her boyfriend is in the waiting room and does not know what she has said.
options: Provide safety planning and resources without filing a police report against her wishes
File a police report because intimate-partner violence is reported like child abuse
Report her to child protective services even though no child lives in the home
Refuse further medical care until she leaves the relationship
Invite the boyfriend in from the waiting room to discuss the bruise together
correctAnswer: Provide safety planning and resources without filing a police report against her wishes
explanation: A capacitated, nondependent adult who discloses intimate-partner violence is offered safety planning, resources, and follow-up. She is not a child and not a vulnerable elder, no child lives in the home, and she has a safe place tonight. Filing a police report against her stated wishes is the legalistic trap that confuses this situation with mandatory child-abuse reporting. File a police report because intimate-partner violence is reported like child abuse applies the child-protection statute to an adult who can decide. Report her to child protective services even though no child lives in the home invents a child victim. Refuse further medical care until she leaves the relationship punishes her for not leaving and abandons ongoing care. Invite the boyfriend in from the waiting room to discuss the bruise together exposes her disclosure to the person who hit her and can increase the danger.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA
