scenario: An 86-year-old woman depends on her son for bathing, finances, and medications. She is brought in with stage 3 pressure ulcers, an empty donepezil bottle that should have been refilled weeks ago, and visible fear when the son speaks. She whispers that you must not report him because he will put her in a home and she would rather stay. She can state the year and can name you. The son will not leave the room until you ask him to step out. Adult protective services accepts reports of suspected abuse or neglect of dependent older adults.
options: Report suspected elder abuse or neglect to adult protective services
Keep her disclosure secret because she has decision-making capacity
Honor her request exactly as you would for a nondependent adult who declines a police report
Confront the son and close the case if he promises to reposition her
Document the ulcers as unavoidable and take no protective action
correctAnswer: Report suspected elder abuse or neglect to adult protective services
explanation: She is a dependent older adult with findings that suggest neglect or abuse: advanced pressure ulcers, a medication that was not supplied, and fear of the caregiver. Suspected elder abuse is reported to adult protective services. Her wish to avoid a residential move does not cancel that duty, even if she can state the year. Keep her disclosure secret because she has decision-making capacity confuses capacity for ordinary choices with the mandatory-report duty owed to a vulnerable elder. Honor her request exactly as you would for a nondependent adult who declines a police report imports the intimate-partner rule for an independent adult into elder neglect. Confront the son and close the case if he promises to reposition her warns the caregiver and replaces an investigation with a promise. Document the ulcers as unavoidable and take no protective action ignores the empty medication bottle and her fear and leaves her in the same care.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 7-year-old boy has newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia with a high expected cure rate if chemotherapy is started. He now has fever and neutropenia. His parents refuse chemotherapy and request only prayer. They are devoted, the home is otherwise safe, and they say parental authority is absolute, the same as an adult refusal of care. He is too young to understand chemotherapy. They ask to take him home tonight. Child protective services and the hospital attorney are available, and antibiotics for febrile neutropenia are ready.
options: Begin emergency treatment as needed and seek legal authority to provide chemotherapy
Accept the parents refusal because parental autonomy equals an adult refusal of care
Discharge him to prayer without notifying child protective services or a court
Wait for the parents to change their minds while neutropenia goes untreated
Ask the 7-year-old to sign consent for chemotherapy
correctAnswer: Begin emergency treatment as needed and seek legal authority to provide chemotherapy
explanation: Parents may not refuse life-saving treatment of a child when the expected benefit is high. Febrile neutropenia is treated now, and legal authority is sought so chemotherapy can proceed. Parental devotion does not extend adult refusal rules to a child. Accept the parents refusal because parental autonomy equals an adult refusal of care is the legalistic trap; an adult may refuse for himself, and these parents may not refuse a high-cure therapy for him. Discharge him to prayer without notifying child protective services or a court abandons a child with a treatable cancer and skips the report that medical neglect requires. Wait for the parents to change their minds while neutropenia goes untreated risks death from infection during a delay that is not medically acceptable. Ask the 7-year-old to sign consent for chemotherapy assigns the decision to a child who cannot understand it; the remedy is emergency care and a legal process, not his signature.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

references.label: American Medical Association. Code of Medical Ethics. AMA

scenario: A 22-month-old girl had a normal prenatal course. She sat at 6 months, walked at 12 months, and used several single words by 15 months. Over the past three months she has stopped using those words, lost purposeful hand use, and wrings her hands together in the midline for long periods. Head circumference was at the 50th percentile at 9 months and is now at the 10th percentile, crossing downward. Hearing testing last month was normal. There is no history of abuse and no new sibling. Motor skills she had already mastered are slipping rather than merely slow to appear.
options: Loss of skills she had already attained, indicating regression rather than simple delay
Isolated speech delay in a child who has not yet had a chance to develop language
Autism spectrum disorder as a static social delay without loss of purposeful hand use
Normal separation anxiety after a developmental plateau and a new sibling
Global developmental delay in a child who never attained motor or language milestones
correctAnswer: Loss of skills she had already attained, indicating regression rather than simple delay
explanation: Delay means a skill has not been acquired on time. Regression means a skill that was present is lost. She walked, used words, and used her hands, and those abilities are now gone, with decelerating head growth and hand wringing. That pattern is regression, classically concerning for Rett syndrome in a girl, not a child who is merely late. Hearing is normal, so the language loss is not deafness. Isolated speech delay in a child who has not yet had a chance to develop language ignores words she already had and the loss of hand use. Autism spectrum disorder as a static social delay without loss of purposeful hand use does not fit acquired microcephaly, hand wringing, and loss of skills that were already attained. Normal separation anxiety after a developmental plateau and a new sibling requires a stressor and a temporary behavioral change, not loss of walking-era skills and head-growth failure; there is no new sibling. Global developmental delay in a child who never attained motor or language milestones describes a child who was always behind, which this history contradicts.
question: Which of the following best interprets this developmental course?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 4-year-old boy was fully toilet trained by day and by night for eight months. Two weeks after his sister was born he began wetting the bed four nights a week. He has no dysuria, no daytime polyuria, and no polydipsia. Daytime continence is preserved. Growth is tracking at the same percentiles. Gait, lower-extremity reflexes, and sacral skin are normal. His parents worry that bedwetting means a global developmental delay and ask for a medication tonight. He is otherwise playing, talking in sentences, and attending preschool.
options: Transient regression of a previously mastered skill during a psychosocial stress
Primary nocturnal enuresis because he never achieved nighttime continence
Global developmental delay requiring a cognitive diagnosis before any reassurance
Diabetes mellitus as the leading explanation despite no polyuria or polydipsia
Spinal cord tethering as the leading explanation despite a normal gait and exam
correctAnswer: Transient regression of a previously mastered skill during a psychosocial stress
explanation: He had already been dry for eight months, so the skill was mastered. Losing it for a short time after a sibling birth, with a normal exam and no urinary or endocrine red flags, is regression under stress, not failure ever to develop. Reassurance and watchful follow-up fit the facts better than a new disease label. Primary nocturnal enuresis because he never achieved nighttime continence is the wrong category: primary enuresis means he was never dry for a sustained period, and he was. Global developmental delay requiring a cognitive diagnosis before any reassurance overreads one lost skill in a child who speaks in sentences, plays, and attends preschool. Diabetes mellitus as the leading explanation despite no polyuria or polydipsia would be suggested by excessive thirst and urine, which are absent, and would not spare daytime continence in this story. Spinal cord tethering as the leading explanation despite a normal gait and exam would be suggested by gait change, reflex changes, or a sacral finding, none of which are present.
question: Which of the following best interprets the new bedwetting?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 12-year-old girl has had breast development for 18 months and is now Tanner breast stage 3. Pubic hair has been present for 6 months and is Tanner stage 2. She has not had menses. Height velocity was rapid over the past year and is now slowing. Her mother is worried that pubic hair is supposed to come first and that periods should have started before breasts. There is no virilization and no galactorrhea. Bone age is 12 years, in keeping with her pubertal stage. Thelarche began after age 8.
options: Normal female puberty in which thelarche precedes pubarche and menarche follows the growth spurt
Disordered puberty because pubarche must precede thelarche
Primary amenorrhea workup now because menses should precede breast development
Central precocious puberty because breast development began before age 13
Peripheral androgen excess because any pubic hair means an adrenal tumor
correctAnswer: Normal female puberty in which thelarche precedes pubarche and menarche follows the growth spurt
explanation: In girls, gonadarche starts with thelarche. Pubarche follows, the growth spurt occurs around mid-puberty, and menarche usually comes about two to two and a half years after breast budding, often near Tanner stage 4. Breast budding at about age 10 and a half, pubic hair later, a growth spurt, bone age matching chronologic age, and no menses yet at 18 months after thelarche is an ordinary sequence. Disordered puberty because pubarche must precede thelarche reverses the order: breast development, not pubic hair, is the first sign of ovarian puberty. Primary amenorrhea workup now because menses should precede breast development uses an impossible order; primary amenorrhea is considered at about age 15 or three years after thelarche, not before breasts. Central precocious puberty because breast development began before age 13 misstates the threshold: precocious puberty in girls is secondary sexual development before age 8, and age 10 and a half is within the normal window. Peripheral androgen excess because any pubic hair means an adrenal tumor overreads normal pubarche; a tumor would virilize and advance growth and bone age out of proportion, which is not described.
question: Which of the following best interprets this sequence?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 7-year-old boy has adult-type axillary odor and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair. Testicular volume is 2 mL on each side, and the penis is prepubertal. Height velocity is normal for age. Bone age is 7 years 6 months. He has no headache, no cafe-au-lait spots, and no exposure to testosterone gel. A parent believes puberty has started in the normal male order and that pubic hair is the first sign, with testicular growth expected later. Serum studies are still pending.
options: Adrenal androgens without activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
Central precocious puberty driven by gonadotropins, which would enlarge the testes
Normal male gonadarche in which pubic hair comes first and the testes enlarge later
Klinefelter syndrome, which presents with tall stature and small firm testes after puberty
Constitutional delay, which presents with absent pubic hair and a delayed bone age
correctAnswer: Adrenal androgens without activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
explanation: True male puberty, gonadarche, begins with testicular enlargement to about 4 mL or more, because luteinizing hormone drives the Leydig cells and follicle-stimulating hormone enlarges the tubules. Pubic hair and apocrine odor with testes still at 2 mL mean the androgens are coming from the adrenal zona reticularis, as in premature adrenarche, not from a pubertal pituitary. Bone age and height velocity are essentially normal, which argues against a rapidly progressive adrenal tumor. Central precocious puberty driven by gonadotropins, which would enlarge the testes, is ruled out by prepubertal testicular volume. Normal male gonadarche in which pubic hair comes first and the testes enlarge later reverses the sequence: testicular growth is first, and pubic hair is not. Klinefelter syndrome, which presents with tall stature and small firm testes after puberty, is a later hypergonadotropic picture, not isolated pubic hair at age 7 with a normal bone age. Constitutional delay, which presents with absent pubic hair and a delayed bone age, is a late-bloomer pattern, the opposite of early pubic hair.
question: Which of the following best interprets the source of these changes?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 3-year-old boy who was born at 28 weeks walks on his toes, scissors his legs when he tries to run, and has brisk deep-tendon reflexes with a few beats of clonus at the ankles. Stroking the sole makes the great toe extend. When his head is turned to one side, the arm and leg on that side extend and the opposite limbs flex, and this fencing posture is obligatory rather than brief. A relative says babies do those things and that he will outgrow the reflexes if the family waits until school age. He is not hypotonic.
options: Persistent primitive reflexes indicating an upper motor neuron lesion
A normal residual of infancy that should be observed until school age
A lower motor neuron lesion, which would abolish reflexes and produce flaccid weakness
Isolated delay of walking with an intact corticospinal tract
A cerebellar sign, which would present with hypotonia and hyporeflexia rather than clonus
correctAnswer: Persistent primitive reflexes indicating an upper motor neuron lesion
explanation: The asymmetric tonic neck reflex and the extensor plantar response are normal early in infancy and should be gone well before age 3. An obligatory fencing response, an upgoing toe, toe walking, scissoring, brisk reflexes, and clonus together mean the corticospinal tract is not inhibiting the primitive pattern. That is an upper motor neuron picture, often cerebral palsy after prematurity, not a reflex he will simply outgrow. A normal residual of infancy that should be observed until school age ignores how late and how obligatory these responses are. A lower motor neuron lesion, which would abolish reflexes and produce flaccid weakness, is the opposite of clonus and hyperreflexia. Isolated delay of walking with an intact corticospinal tract would not add an obligatory primitive reflex, a Babinski sign, and spasticity. A cerebellar sign, which would present with hypotonia and hyporeflexia rather than clonus, does not fit a child who is spastic and hyperreflexic rather than floppy.
question: Which of the following best interprets the persistent reflexes?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An 8-year-old child agrees that two identical cups hold the same amount of water. After one cup is poured into a tall thin glass, she says the amount is unchanged because it could be poured back. She lines sticks up from shortest to longest without help. Asked what makes a pendulum swing faster, she changes the weight, the string length, and the push all at once and cannot say which variable matters. She will not reason about a world in which gravity is absent. She is past the age of simple pretend play and attends second grade.
options: Concrete operational stage: conservation and seriation are present, but she cannot isolate hypothetical variables
Formal operational stage: she should already isolate one pendulum variable at a time
Preoperational stage: conservation of liquid is expected to fail, yet appearance still dominates her answer
Sensorimotor stage: seriation is achieved before object permanence and does not require conservation
Trust versus mistrust: the pendulum result is an attachment finding rather than a cognitive stage
correctAnswer: Concrete operational stage: conservation and seriation are present, but she cannot isolate hypothetical variables
explanation: Conservation of liquid and seriation of sticks are concrete operational achievements, typical of the early school years. The pendulum task requires holding other variables constant and testing one at a time, which is formal operational and usually appears later. A nearby younger stage would fail the conservation she just passed. She is therefore in the concrete operational stage. Formal operational stage: she should already isolate one pendulum variable at a time describes the stage she has not reached; changing every variable at once is exactly the failure. Preoperational stage: conservation of liquid is expected to fail, yet appearance still dominates her answer does not fit, because she said the amount was unchanged and cited reversibility, so appearance did not dominate. Sensorimotor stage: seriation is achieved before object permanence and does not require conservation reverses development; object permanence is an infant achievement, and seriation comes much later. Trust versus mistrust: the pendulum result is an attachment finding rather than a cognitive stage imports an Erikson psychosocial crisis into a reasoning task about volume and variables.
question: Which of the following best interprets these tasks?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 4-year-old boy pretends a wooden block is a truck and talks about his grandmother, who is not in the room. When two equal rows of coins are spread so that one row looks longer, he insists that the longer-looking row has more coins. On a three-mountain model he points to his own view when asked what a doll seated on the opposite side sees. He does search under a cloth for a toy he watched you hide. His sentences are clear, and he is not yet in school.
options: Preoperational stage: symbolic play is present, but conservation and another person viewpoint fail
Concrete operational stage: he would pass conservation of number and the three-mountain task
Formal operational stage: pretend play appears only after abstract hypothetical reasoning
Sensorimotor stage: he would not yet show symbolic play about an absent person
Concrete operational success: finding a hidden toy means he can already conserve number
correctAnswer: Preoperational stage: symbolic play is present, but conservation and another person viewpoint fail
explanation: Symbolic pretend play and language about an absent person mark the preoperational years. Failing conservation of number, because the spread-out row looks like more, and failing the three-mountain task, because he reports only his own viewpoint, are the limits of that stage. A concrete operational child nearby in age would pass both of those tasks. Searching under a cloth shows object permanence, which he already achieved earlier and which does not move him into the next stage. Concrete operational stage: he would pass conservation of number and the three-mountain task is what he did not do. Formal operational stage: pretend play appears only after abstract hypothetical reasoning reverses the order; pretend play is early, and hypothetical reasoning is adolescent. Sensorimotor stage: he would not yet show symbolic play about an absent person fits an infant, not a child who talks about his grandmother and pretends with a block. Concrete operational success: finding a hidden toy means he can already conserve number treats object permanence as if it were conservation, which his coin answer shows he lacks.
question: Which of the following best interprets these tasks?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 14-month-old infant plays with toys while her mother sits nearby and sometimes brings a toy back to show her. When the mother steps out of the room, the infant cries and crawls to the door. When the mother returns, the infant reaches to be picked up, calms within about a minute, and goes back to the toys. She had resisted being held by a stranger a few minutes earlier. The mother has been the consistent caregiver since birth. The examiner wonders whether crying at the door means the attachment is insecure.
options: Secure attachment: she protests the separation and calms, then returns to exploration
Avoidant attachment: little protest and little seeking of comfort on reunion
Ambivalent attachment: she would remain inconsolable and angry after the caregiver returns
Disorganized attachment: freezing or contradictory approach and fear of the caregiver
Disinhibited social engagement: she would accept comfort equally from the stranger
correctAnswer: Secure attachment: she protests the separation and calms, then returns to exploration
explanation: Secure attachment uses the caregiver as a base. The infant explores while the mother is present, protests when she leaves, seeks contact when she returns, is comforted quickly, and resumes play. Crying at the door is the protest, not evidence against security. She also distinguishes her mother from a stranger. Avoidant attachment: little protest and little seeking of comfort on reunion is the pattern she did not show; an avoidant infant would keep playing and would not reach to be picked up. Ambivalent attachment: she would remain inconsolable and angry after the caregiver returns does not fit a child who calms within a minute. Disorganized attachment: freezing or contradictory approach and fear of the caregiver would look like approaching and then freezing or showing fear, which is not described. Disinhibited social engagement: she would accept comfort equally from the stranger is excluded by her resistance to the stranger and her selective comfort from her mother.
question: Which of the following best interprets the reunion behavior?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 3-year-old boy spent his first two years moving between institutions and had no consistent caregiver. In the exam room he climbs into the examiner lap within a minute, asks to go home with the examiner, and does not look back at the foster parent who brought him. He greeted the receptionist with the same immediate familiarity. He speaks in sentences and points to show the foster parent a toy, so social communication is not absent. There is no motor regression and no fever. The foster parent says this happens with every new adult. He is not afraid of the examiner.
options: Disinhibited social engagement after early absence of a selective attachment figure
Secure attachment, because friendliness with adults means the separation did no harm
Normal stranger anxiety, which would make him cling to the foster parent and refuse the examiner
Autism spectrum disorder, which would reduce social approach rather than produce indiscriminate approach
Avoidant attachment limited to one caregiver, which would not include leaving with a stranger just met
correctAnswer: Disinhibited social engagement after early absence of a selective attachment figure
explanation: After early care with no stable attachment figure, some children approach any adult, sit in a stranger lap, and are willing to leave with someone they just met. That indiscriminate pattern, repeated with the receptionist and the examiner, and without checking back with the foster parent, is disinhibited social engagement. Preserved sentences and pointing make a primary social-communication disorder less likely. Secure attachment, because friendliness with adults means the separation did no harm, misreads indiscriminate friendliness as security; a secure child prefers a familiar caregiver and uses that person as a base. Normal stranger anxiety, which would make him cling to the foster parent and refuse the examiner, is the opposite of climbing into a new lap. Autism spectrum disorder, which would reduce social approach rather than produce indiscriminate approach, is unlikely when he is socially eager, points to show toys, and speaks in sentences. Avoidant attachment limited to one caregiver, which would not include leaving with a stranger just met, describes coolness toward a specific caregiver, not a willingness to depart with every new adult.
question: Which of the following best interprets this approach to strangers?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 14-year-old boy has not started puberty. Testicular volume is 3 mL on each side. Height has tracked at the 5th percentile with a normal prepubertal velocity. Bone age is 11 years. His father did not shave until age 17 and was short until late in high school. The boy identifies coffee, smoke, and soap by smell without difficulty. There is no gynecomastia. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are low but appropriate for the bone age. He is worried that something is permanently wrong.
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty, with bone age delayed in keeping with late maturation
Central precocious puberty, which would show an advanced bone age and enlarged testes
Kallmann syndrome, which would include anosmia from failed migration of olfactory neurons
Klinefelter syndrome, which would show small firm testes, tall stature, and high gonadotropins
Familial short stature, which would show a bone age equal to chronologic age and puberty on time
correctAnswer: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty, with bone age delayed in keeping with late maturation
explanation: Constitutional delay is a late but intact maturational clock. Height tracks at a low percentile, velocity is normal for the prepubertal state, bone age is delayed toward the height age, a parent was a late bloomer, smell is intact, and gonadotropins fit the bone age rather than a broken axis. Puberty is expected to arrive late and then proceed. Central precocious puberty, which would show an advanced bone age and enlarged testes, is the opposite problem: early development, not absent development at 14. Kallmann syndrome, which would include anosmia from failed migration of olfactory neurons, is excluded by normal smell of coffee, smoke, and soap. Klinefelter syndrome, which would show small firm testes, tall stature, and high gonadotropins, is a primary testicular problem with elevated follicle-stimulating hormone, not low gonadotropins appropriate for a delayed bone age and a late-bloomer father. Familial short stature, which would show a bone age equal to chronologic age and puberty on time, fits short parents with a mature skeleton, not bone age 11 at chronologic age 14.
question: Which of the following best interprets the delayed puberty?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 7-year-old girl developed breast buds six months ago and is now Tanner breast stage 3. Height velocity over the recent interval is 9 cm per year. Bone age is 10 years. After gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation, luteinizing hormone rises into the pubertal range. She has no cafe-au-lait macule, no exposure to estrogen cream, and no vaginal bleeding. Headache and visual symptoms are absent. A relative calls this either a harmless early breast bud or a late-bloomer pattern.
options: Central precocious puberty from early gonadotropin release, with bone age advanced
Premature thelarche, which is isolated breast development with a normal bone age and normal growth velocity
Constitutional delay, which delays bone age and postpones puberty rather than advancing them
McCune-Albright syndrome, which is gonadotropin-independent and would not produce a pubertal luteinizing hormone rise
Premature adrenarche, which adds pubic hair from adrenal androgens without a pubertal luteinizing hormone response
correctAnswer: Central precocious puberty from early gonadotropin release, with bone age advanced
explanation: Breast development before age 8, rapid linear growth, and a bone age advanced to 10 years mean puberty is not only early but skeletally consequential. A pubertal luteinizing hormone rise after gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation shows the pituitary has been activated, so the process is central. Premature thelarche, which is isolated breast development with a normal bone age and normal growth velocity, is a toddler pattern of breast buds without a growth spurt or an advanced skeleton, unlike Tanner stage 3 and 9 cm per year. Constitutional delay, which delays bone age and postpones puberty rather than advancing them, cannot describe a 7-year-old who is already mid-pubertal. McCune-Albright syndrome, which is gonadotropin-independent and would not produce a pubertal luteinizing hormone rise, also brings cafe-au-lait macules and fibrous dysplasia, and the luteinizing hormone would stay prepubertal. Premature adrenarche, which adds pubic hair from adrenal androgens without a pubertal luteinizing hormone response, does not produce progressive breast development driven by a luteinizing hormone rise.
question: Which of the following best interprets the early breast development?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 17-year-old boy has no facial or axillary hair, a high voice, and testicular volume of 2 mL on each side. He cannot smell coffee or smoke and says he has never noticed odors. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are low, and testosterone is low. Karyotype is 46,XY. There is no gynecomastia. When he hops on one foot, the other foot moves with it. A clinician suggests this is only a late bloomer, or that small testes with low testosterone must be Klinefelter syndrome.
options: Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons with the olfactory axons
Klinefelter syndrome, which is primary hypogonadism with high gonadotropins and a 47,XXY line
Androgen insensitivity, which produces a phenotypic female because the receptor cannot respond
Constitutional delay alone, which preserves the sense of smell and eventually triggers puberty
5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which virilizes the body at puberty under testosterone itself
correctAnswer: Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons with the olfactory axons
explanation: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons migrate from the olfactory placode along olfactory axons. When that migration fails, puberty never starts from lack of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, the gonadotropins and testosterone stay low, and smell is lost. Mirror movements are part of the same Kallmann picture. The 46,XY karyotype and absent gynecomastia fit hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Klinefelter syndrome, which is primary hypogonadism with high gonadotropins and a 47,XXY line, would raise follicle-stimulating hormone and show an extra X, and smell would be normal. Androgen insensitivity, which produces a phenotypic female because the receptor cannot respond, does not produce a male phenotype with low testosterone. Constitutional delay alone, which preserves the sense of smell and eventually triggers puberty, cannot explain anosmia or synkinesia at age 17. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which virilizes the body at puberty under testosterone itself, allows a testosterone-mediated puberty and does not remove the sense of smell or suppress gonadotropins from birth of the axis.
question: Which of the following best interprets the missing puberty?

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: A 15-year-old girl is 142 cm tall and has a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and a coarctation of the aorta that was repaired in infancy. Breasts are Tanner stage 1, she has had no menarche, follicle-stimulating hormone is high, and estradiol is low. Ultrasound shows a small uterus and streak gonads. Karyotype is 45,X. She asks why puberty did not start. A relative wonders whether the problem is an androgen receptor, an extra X in the testes, or a missing gonadotropin-releasing hormone signal.
options: Ovarian dysgenesis with early loss of oocytes, so estrogen is not produced and gonadotropins rise
Androgen receptor resistance, which would leave testosterone unable to act in a 46,XY fetus
Seminiferous tubule hyalinization from an extra X chromosome, as in Klinefelter syndrome
Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which would lower follicle-stimulating hormone
Excess antimullerian hormone from functioning testes, which would remove the uterus
correctAnswer: Ovarian dysgenesis with early loss of oocytes, so estrogen is not produced and gonadotropins rise
explanation: A 45,X karyotype leads to loss of oocytes and streak gonads. Without ovarian estrogen, breasts and menses do not develop, and follicle-stimulating hormone rises because there is no feedback. A uterus is present because she never had testes to secrete antimullerian hormone. Short stature, neck webbing, and coarctation are the surrounding Turner phenotype, but the absent puberty itself is ovarian failure. Androgen receptor resistance, which would leave testosterone unable to act in a 46,XY fetus, produces a phenotypic female with testes, breasts from aromatized testosterone, and no uterus. Seminiferous tubule hyalinization from an extra X chromosome, as in Klinefelter syndrome, is a 47,XXY male problem, not a short girl with streak gonads. Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which would lower follicle-stimulating hormone, is Kallmann syndrome; her follicle-stimulating hormone is high, not low. Excess antimullerian hormone from functioning testes, which would remove the uterus, is incompatible with a visible uterus and streak gonads.
question: Which mechanism best accounts for the absent puberty?

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: An 18-year-old man is tall, with long arms, bilateral gynecomastia, and firm testes measuring about 4 mL. Two semen analyses show azoospermia. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are high, testosterone is low-normal, and a Barr body is present on a buccal smear. Smell is normal. Karyotype is 47,XXY. He has completed a male puberty that is incomplete at the testes. He wants to know why there are no sperm.
options: Hyalinization and fibrosis of the seminiferous tubules caused by the extra X chromosome
Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which would suppress both gonadotropins
Androgen receptor mutation, which would produce breasts in a phenotypic female without a uterus
45,X gonadal dysgenesis, which produces short stature, streak gonads, and a female phenotype
5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which blocks dihydrotestosterone but does not add a Barr body
correctAnswer: Hyalinization and fibrosis of the seminiferous tubules caused by the extra X chromosome
explanation: An extra X chromosome progressively destroys the seminiferous tubules by hyalinization and fibrosis, so sperm are absent and the testes stay small and firm. Follicle-stimulating hormone rises because inhibin and spermatogenesis fail, and Leydig cell dysfunction leaves testosterone low-normal with a high luteinizing hormone. The Barr body is the extra X. Gynecomastia reflects the altered testosterone-to-estrogen balance. Smell is normal, so this is not a migration defect. Failed migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which would suppress both gonadotropins, would lower luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, not raise them. Androgen receptor mutation, which would produce breasts in a phenotypic female without a uterus, is androgen insensitivity, not a tall man with testes and a Barr body. 45,X gonadal dysgenesis, which produces short stature, streak gonads, and a female phenotype, is Turner syndrome. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which blocks dihydrotestosterone but does not add a Barr body, does not create an XXY karyotype, high gonadotropins from tubular sclerosis, or gynecomastia as the main picture.
question: Which mechanism best accounts for the azoospermia?

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: A 16-year-old adolescent who has been raised as a girl has primary amenorrhea. Breasts are Tanner stage 4. Axillary and pubic hair are scant. The vagina ends in a blind pouch, and ultrasound shows no uterus. Gonads consistent with testes are undescended. Karyotype is 46,XY. Serum testosterone is in the adult male range, luteinizing hormone is elevated, and estradiol is measurable from peripheral conversion. She has no cyclic pelvic pain. Height is above average, and there is no webbed neck.
options: Androgen receptor defect: testosterone is aromatized to estrogen, while antimullerian hormone still suppresses the uterus
Mullerian agenesis: a 46,XX karyotype, normal female testosterone, and normal pubic hair
45,X ovarian dysgenesis: no spontaneous breast development, high follicle-stimulating hormone, and low estradiol
5-alpha-reductase deficiency: the phenotype virilizes at puberty and breasts do not develop
Kallmann syndrome: gonadotropins and testosterone are low, and a uterus would still be absent only if testes were present
correctAnswer: Androgen receptor defect: testosterone is aromatized to estrogen, while antimullerian hormone still suppresses the uterus
explanation: Complete androgen insensitivity is a 46,XY androgen receptor defect. The testes still secrete antimullerian hormone, so the uterus does not form, and they secrete testosterone, which cannot act on hair follicles or external male genitalia. Peripheral aromatization of that testosterone to estradiol produces breasts. Luteinizing hormone is high because androgen feedback at the receptor fails. That single mechanism accounts for both the breast development and the absent uterus. Mullerian agenesis: a 46,XX karyotype, normal female testosterone, and normal pubic hair removes the uterus but leaves ovaries, female-range testosterone, and normal sexual hair, unlike male-range testosterone and scant hair. 45,X ovarian dysgenesis: no spontaneous breast development, high follicle-stimulating hormone, and low estradiol is Turner syndrome, with streak gonads, short stature, and a uterus. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: the phenotype virilizes at puberty and breasts do not develop, because testosterone action is intact and only dihydrotestosterone was missing in fetal life. Kallmann syndrome: gonadotropins and testosterone are low, and a uterus would still be absent only if testes were present, but low testosterone would not create Tanner stage 4 breasts or a male-range testosterone level.
question: Which mechanism best accounts for the breasts and the absent uterus?

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: A 20-month-old girl has fallen from the 50th percentile to the 5th percentile for weight over four months. Height remains near the 50th percentile. She drinks large volumes of juice and eats little protein or fat. Development and the neurologic examination are normal. There is no diarrhea and no fever. Midparental height is average. A recent bone-age film is not delayed. Her parents ask whether this pattern means she needs growth hormone or has precocious puberty because a cousin was treated for early puberty.
options: Inadequate calories, which slow weight gain before they slow linear growth
Growth hormone deficiency, which slows linear growth and bone age while weight is relatively preserved
Constitutional delay, which is a later pubertal pattern with a delayed bone age and a late-bloomer family
Precocious puberty, which accelerates height velocity and advances the bone age
Hypothyroidism as the best fit, which would slow height at least as early as weight and delay the bone age
correctAnswer: Inadequate calories, which slow weight gain before they slow linear growth
explanation: When intake is short, weight percentile falls first and height is spared until the deficit is prolonged. Juice instead of protein and fat, a drop from the 50th to the 5th percentile for weight, height still at the 50th, and a bone age that is not delayed match inadequate calories. Growth hormone deficiency, which slows linear growth and bone age while weight is relatively preserved, would pull height down and delay the skeleton, often with a chubby appearance, not an isolated weight drop. Constitutional delay, which is a later pubertal pattern with a delayed bone age and a late-bloomer family, is not a diagnosis at 20 months with an on-time bone age and average parents. Precocious puberty, which accelerates height velocity and advances the bone age, speeds linear growth rather than dropping weight. Hypothyroidism as the best fit, which would slow height at least as early as weight and delay the bone age, would not leave height on the 50th percentile and the bone age on time in a child whose diet is plainly short on calories.
question: Which of the following best interprets the growth pattern?

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 6-year-old girl has two large cafe-au-lait macules with ragged borders, breast development, and one episode of vaginal bleeding. Bone age is 9 years. A femur radiograph shows fibrous dysplasia. After gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation, luteinizing hormone stays in the prepubertal range, while estradiol is high. She has not used estrogen cream or other exogenous hormones. There is no headache. A consultant suggests this is early activation of the pituitary and would respond to a long-acting gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist.
options: Peripheral precocious puberty from gonadotropin-independent ovarian estrogen secretion
Central precocious puberty, which would show a pubertal luteinizing hormone rise after stimulation
Premature thelarche, which would not advance bone age, cause bleeding, or include fibrous dysplasia
Constitutional delay, which delays skeletal maturation rather than advancing it
A pituitary process that continuous gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy would suppress
correctAnswer: Peripheral precocious puberty from gonadotropin-independent ovarian estrogen secretion
explanation: Cafe-au-lait macules with ragged borders, fibrous dysplasia, and early estrogen effects form the McCune-Albright pattern. Activating Gs signaling in the ovary produces estradiol without a pituitary signal. The prepubertal luteinizing hormone after stimulation, the high estradiol, vaginal bleeding, and bone age of 9 years at chronologic age 6 show peripheral, gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty. Central precocious puberty, which would show a pubertal luteinizing hormone rise after stimulation, is excluded by the flat luteinizing hormone response. Premature thelarche, which would not advance bone age, cause bleeding, or include fibrous dysplasia, is only isolated breast tissue in a younger child with a normal skeleton. Constitutional delay, which delays skeletal maturation rather than advancing it, is a late bone age, not bone age 9 at age 6. A pituitary process that continuous gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy would suppress is the wrong mechanism: continuous agonist exposure downregulates pituitary receptors and can treat central puberty, but it cannot turn off an ovary that is secreting estrogen on its own.
question: Which of the following best interprets the early bleeding and breast development?

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: An infant with atypical external genitalia was raised as a girl. At age 13 the voice deepens, the phallus enlarges, muscle mass increases, and breasts do not develop. Imaging shows no uterus. Karyotype is 46,XY. The ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone is markedly elevated. The child and parents are distressed that a body that looked female in infancy is masculinizing now. Smell is normal, and gonadotropins are in a pubertal male range rather than suppressed.
options: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: dihydrotestosterone was lacking in utero, while puberty proceeds under testosterone
Complete androgen insensitivity: breasts develop at puberty and the phallus does not virilize
45,X gonadal dysgenesis: a uterus is present, stature is short, and testosterone does not virilize the phenotype
Kallmann syndrome: the pubertal testosterone rise fails and anosmia is expected
21-hydroxylase deficiency: a 46,XX fetus is virilized in utero and a uterus is present
correctAnswer: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: dihydrotestosterone was lacking in utero, while puberty proceeds under testosterone
explanation: External male genitalia in the fetus depend on dihydrotestosterone, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase. Without that enzyme the newborn looks female or atypical, while testes still make antimullerian hormone, so there is no uterus, and the Wolffian ducts can respond to testosterone. At puberty the testosterone rise, which does not require dihydrotestosterone for muscle, voice, and phallic growth, virilizes the adolescent and does not produce breasts. An elevated testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone ratio is the laboratory counterpart. Complete androgen insensitivity: breasts develop at puberty and the phallus does not virilize, because the receptor itself is absent and testosterone is aromatized to estrogen. 45,X gonadal dysgenesis: a uterus is present, stature is short, and testosterone does not virilize the phenotype, which is Turner syndrome rather than a 46,XY adolescent with no uterus. Kallmann syndrome: the pubertal testosterone rise fails and anosmia is expected, so it cannot explain deepening voice and phallic growth with a normal sense of smell. 21-hydroxylase deficiency: a 46,XX fetus is virilized in utero and a uterus is present, the mirror image of a 46,XY adolescent who virilizes only at puberty and has no uterus.
question: Which mechanism best accounts for the infantile appearance and the pubertal virilization?

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: A newborn boy is virilized and in the second week becomes a salt-wasting shock with low sodium, high potassium, and hypoglycemia. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is very high. A student calls this 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency because the child is sick, and another says the blood pressure should be high.
question: Which enzyme failed, and why is the pressure low rather than high?
options: 21-hydroxylase; cortisol and aldosterone cannot be made, so salt is lost, while ACTH drives androgen buildup
11-beta hydroxylase; deoxycorticosterone excess causes hypertension and this salt-wasting picture
17-alpha hydroxylase; sex steroids are increased and potassium is high
Aromatase; estrogens are absent and aldosterone is the missing mineralocorticoid
5-alpha reductase; DHT is low so a newborn boy cannot virilize
correctAnswer: 21-hydroxylase; cortisol and aldosterone cannot be made, so salt is lost, while ACTH drives androgen buildup
explanation: 21-hydroxylase is required for cortisol and aldosterone. Its loss dumps precursors into androgens, so girls are virilized and boys can present in salt-wasting crisis with hyperkalemia. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the marker. 11-beta hydroxylase blocks cortisol but shunts to DOC, which causes hypertension, not salt wasting. 17-alpha hydroxylase blocks cortisol and sex steroids and leaves mineralocorticoid excess, so pressure is high and androgens are low. Aromatase deficiency affects estrogen, not this adrenal salt loss. 5-alpha reductase deficiency under-virilizes an XY infant; it does not cause a salt-wasting boy who is already virilized.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child is virilized and hypertensive. Sodium is not low. Deoxycorticosterone is high and renin is low. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is only modestly up compared with the huge DOC. A classmate remembers the salt-wasting infant and wants fludrocortisone as the main mineralocorticoid replacement.
question: Why is this child hypertensive, and why is fludrocortisone the wrong emphasis?
options: DOC, a mineralocorticoid made before the 11-beta block, expands volume; he needs glucocorticoid to turn off ACTH, not extra mineralocorticoid
He lacks aldosterone, so salt wasting is about to start and fludrocortisone is required
The enzyme block is 21-hydroxylase, which always causes hypertension
Renin is high, which proves renal artery stenosis as the cause of the virilization
DOC is a glucocorticoid only and cannot raise blood pressure
correctAnswer: DOC, a mineralocorticoid made before the 11-beta block, expands volume; he needs glucocorticoid to turn off ACTH, not extra mineralocorticoid
explanation: 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency stops cortisol and sends the pathway toward deoxycorticosterone, which acts like aldosterone. Volume is high, renin is suppressed, and there is no salt wasting. Glucocorticoid replacement suppresses ACTH and therefore the DOC drive. Adding fludrocortisone piles mineralocorticoid onto mineralocorticoid. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the salt-losing, low-pressure disease. Renin is low here, not high, and stenosis does not virilize. DOC has real mineralocorticoid activity, which is the whole mechanism.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A teenager has never menstruated, has hypertension, and has low potassium. She has little pubic hair. Cortisol is low, androgens are low, and mineralocorticoid metabolites are high. A pelvic exam is not the first issue; the blood pressure is. Someone suggests she has 21-hydroxylase deficiency because both are congenital adrenal hyperplasias.
question: What is overproduced, and why is puberty absent?
options: Corticosterone and DOC are overproduced and suppress renin; sex steroids cannot be made because 17-hydroxylation is required for them
Androgens are high, so she should be virilized
Aldosterone is directly high and sex steroids are normal
This is the salt-wasting form, so potassium should be high
17-hydroxyprogesterone is the dominant marker, as in 21-hydroxylase deficiency
correctAnswer: Corticosterone and DOC are overproduced and suppress renin; sex steroids cannot be made because 17-hydroxylation is required for them
explanation: 17-alpha hydroxylase is required to enter the cortisol and sex-steroid pathways. Block it and the adrenal makes mineralocorticoids, blood pressure rises, potassium falls, and there is no puberty because androgens and estrogens are not made. 21-hydroxylase deficiency does the opposite with androgens: virilization and, in the salt-losing form, low pressure. Androgens are low here, so she is not virilized. Aldosterone itself is often low because high DOC expands volume and suppresses renin; the active mineralocorticoid is DOC and corticosterone. Potassium is low, not high. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is not the marker; that steroid requires the enzyme she lacks.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A has a high cortisol that suppresses with low-dose dexamethasone and a high ACTH that is suppressible; she is depressed and drinks heavily. Patient B has a high cortisol that does not suppress with low dose but does with high dose, and ACTH is high. Patient C does not suppress even with high-dose dexamethasone and ACTH is low. All three look Cushingoid or are being tested for it.
question: Which lesions fit B and C?
options: B is a pituitary adenoma that still has some feedback; C is an adrenal tumor making cortisol and shutting off ACTH
B is an adrenal carcinoma because high-dose suppression means the adrenal is primary
C is a pituitary adenoma because ACTH is low
A has Cushing disease and should not have suppressed with low-dose dexamethasone
Ectopic ACTH suppresses with low-dose dexamethasone
correctAnswer: B is a pituitary adenoma that still has some feedback; C is an adrenal tumor making cortisol and shutting off ACTH
explanation: Low-dose dexamethasone suppression means the axis can still be turned off, which is pseudo-Cushing from depression or alcohol, patient A. Failure of low dose but success of high dose, with high ACTH, is a pituitary adenoma, Cushing disease. Failure of high dose with low ACTH is cortisol from the adrenal itself, which has turned the pituitary off. An adrenal cancer would not suppress and would have low ACTH, so calling B adrenal reverses the test. Low ACTH is not a pituitary tumor. Patient A did suppress, so this is not Cushing disease. Ectopic ACTH usually fails high-dose suppression and the ACTH is high, not low-dose suppressible.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman has fatigue, low sodium, high potassium, low glucose, and increased pigmentation in the palmar creases and a scar. ACTH is high and cortisol does not rise after a cosyntropin test. She has no cushingoid features. A student says the pigmentation means her pituitary is overproducing melanin directly from a melanoma.
question: Why is she pigmented, and why is potassium high?
options: High ACTH and its POMC cousin MSH darken the skin; the whole adrenal cortex is out, so aldosterone is low and potassium rises
Secondary adrenal insufficiency pigment is darker than primary because ACTH is higher
Potassium is high because cortisol excess dumps potassium in the urine
Cosyntropin failure means the pituitary cannot make ACTH
Pigmentation means she has Cushing disease and the ACTH stain is from cortisol
correctAnswer: High ACTH and its POMC cousin MSH darken the skin; the whole adrenal cortex is out, so aldosterone is low and potassium rises
explanation: Primary adrenal failure removes cortisol and aldosterone. Pituitary ACTH rises, and POMC products darken the skin. Hyperkalemia is the mineralocorticoid loss. Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH, no pigmentation, and aldosterone is largely intact because it is renin-driven, so potassium is usually normal. Cortisol excess wastes potassium; she has too little cortisol. Cosyntropin tests the adrenal response; failure with a high ACTH means the gland, not the pituitary, is dead. Cushing disease is cortisol excess, the opposite body habitus.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 45-year-old man has hypertension and a potassium of 2.9 mmol/L that is hard to replace. He is not on a diuretic. Plasma renin is low and aldosterone is high and does not suppress with salt. Metabolic alkalosis is present. A friend says the low renin means renal artery stenosis.
question: What is the lesion pattern, and why is renin low?
options: An adrenal aldosterone-producing adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia expands volume and shuts renin off
Renal artery stenosis raises renin and then aldosterone, so renin would be high
He has Bartter syndrome, which presents with hypertension
Low potassium proves cortisol excess from a pituitary tumor
ACE-inhibitor cough physiology is the cause of the low renin
correctAnswer: An adrenal aldosterone-producing adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia expands volume and shuts renin off
explanation: Primary aldosteronism makes aldosterone on its own. Sodium is retained, volume rises, renin falls, and potassium and hydrogen are wasted, so he is hypertensive, hypokalemic, and alkalotic. Renal artery stenosis is secondary aldosteronism: renin is high. Bartter and Gitelman waste salt and have normal or low blood pressure. Cushing can lower potassium but the screening pair here is high aldosterone with low renin, not a pituitary story. An ACE inhibitor raises renin by blocking feedback; it is not this picture.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Three thyrotoxic patients: A has a diffuse goiter, pretibial myxedema, and high radioiodine uptake. B had a sore throat and a tender gland, uptake is near zero, and thyroglobulin is high. C has no goiter, uptake is zero, and thyroglobulin is low. All have a low TSH and a high T4.
question: Who has Graves disease, and who is taking hormone?
options: A is Graves, TSH-receptor antibodies driving the gland; C is exogenous hormone because the gland is quiet and thyroglobulin is low
B is Graves because the gland hurts
C has thyroiditis because thyroglobulin is low when the gland is leaking
A has factitious thyrotoxicosis because uptake is high
All three need methimazole as the only distinction is cosmetic
correctAnswer: A is Graves, TSH-receptor antibodies driving the gland; C is exogenous hormone because the gland is quiet and thyroglobulin is low
explanation: Graves disease is stimulating antibody. The gland is working, so uptake is high, and the extrathyroidal signs are orbitopathy and pretibial myxedema. Subacute thyroiditis leaks stored hormone, uptake is low, thyroglobulin is high, and the gland is tender. Factitious hormone suppresses the gland, uptake is low, and thyroglobulin is low because the gland is not releasing its protein. A tender gland is thyroiditis, not Graves. Low thyroglobulin means the hormone did not come from the gland. High uptake means the gland is making hormone, the opposite of factitious disease. Methimazole blocks synthesis and helps Graves; it does not stop leak from thyroiditis or exogenous pills.

references.label: Ross DS et al. 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism. Thyroid 2016

scenario: A woman with Graves disease is planning pregnancy. She is on methimazole and euthyroid. She is told that in early pregnancy the antithyroid drug choice changes because of a rare scalp and choanal anomaly, and that later the drug may cross and make the fetus hypothyroid. She also has orbitopathy.
question: Which drug is preferred in the first trimester, and why is ablation not casual here?
options: Propylthiouracil is preferred in early pregnancy because methimazole is linked to aplasia cutis and choanal atresia; radioiodine is not used in pregnancy and can worsen orbitopathy around treatment
Methimazole is mandatory in the first trimester and PTU is banned for the whole pregnancy
Radioiodine ablation is the safest treatment once she has a positive pregnancy test
Both drugs block release only, so either is identical for the fetus
Orbitopathy is treated by making her hyperthyroid on purpose
correctAnswer: Propylthiouracil is preferred in early pregnancy because methimazole is linked to aplasia cutis and choanal atresia; radioiodine is not used in pregnancy and can worsen orbitopathy around treatment
explanation: Both thioamides block new hormone synthesis. Methimazole is generally preferred outside early pregnancy because PTU can cause severe hepatitis, but methimazole's teratogenicity in the first trimester makes PTU the early-pregnancy choice, with a later switch often discussed. Radioiodine destroys the gland and is contraindicated in pregnancy; it can also flare orbitopathy. The drugs are not identical for the fetus. Leaving her hyperthyroid to 'treat' the eyes is harmful; eye disease is managed alongside euthyroidism, not by withholding treatment.

references.label: Ross DS et al. 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism. Thyroid 2016

scenario: Patient A is 16, type 1, with glucose 420 mg/dL, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 8, and moderate ketones. Potassium is 5.4 mmol/L and he has not been eating. Patient B is 72, type 2, with glucose 900 mg/dL, pH 7.35, bicarbonate 20, osmolality 340, and almost no ketones. He is very dry and sleepy. Someone wants to start insulin in A before any fluid and without checking potassium again after insulin.
question: Why can A have a normal or high potassium and still need potassium, and why is B not in ketoacidosis?
options: Acidosis and low insulin shift potassium out of cells, so the serum number hides a total-body deficit; B still makes enough insulin to limit ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose
A high serum potassium means total-body potassium is high and replacement will cause arrhythmia
B must be in DKA because the glucose is higher
Insulin is started in A before fluids because glucose, not volume, is the first threat
Ketones are required for hyperosmolar coma
correctAnswer: Acidosis and low insulin shift potassium out of cells, so the serum number hides a total-body deficit; B still makes enough insulin to limit ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose
explanation: In DKA, potassium leaves cells with the acidosis and the insulin lack, so the serum can look normal or high while the body is depleted. Insulin drives potassium back in and can stop the heart if you do not replace it. Fluids come first. Patient B has hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: enough insulin remains to suppress most ketogenesis, so acidosis is mild, but glucose and osmolality are extreme. A high serum potassium is not a surplus. A higher glucose does not define DKA; ketones and acidosis do. Insulin before volume in a crashing dry patient is the wrong order. Ketones are exactly what HHS lacks.

references.label: American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026. Diabetes Care 2026

scenario: A woman with type 2 diabetes and an eGFR of 25 mL/min is scheduled for a contrast CT. She takes metformin and had a recent bout of vomiting. A student says metformin causes hypoglycemia like a sulfonylurea and that the kidney function does not matter.
question: What is the dangerous accumulation, and does metformin cause hypoglycemia alone?
options: Metformin can cause lactic acidosis when clearance is poor or tissue perfusion is low; by itself it does not raise insulin, so hypoglycemia is not its standalone effect
Metformin stimulates insulin release and is the main cause of fasting hypoglycemia
Contrast is irrelevant because metformin is metabolized by the liver only
Lactic acidosis is the sulfonylurea toxicity
An eGFR of 25 is a reason to increase the metformin dose
correctAnswer: Metformin can cause lactic acidosis when clearance is poor or tissue perfusion is low; by itself it does not raise insulin, so hypoglycemia is not its standalone effect
explanation: Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases insulin sensitivity. It is cleared by the kidney. When GFR is very low, or after contrast in someone at risk, or when perfusion is poor, lactate can accumulate. It does not squeeze insulin from the pancreas, so alone it rarely causes hypoglycemia. That hypoglycemia is the sulfonylurea and insulin problem. Contrast plus low GFR is exactly the hold-the-drug situation. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, not this lactate story. A lower GFR is a reason to stop or avoid the drug, not to raise it.

references.label: American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026. Diabetes Care 2026

scenario: An older man on glyburide is found confused with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. He ate little and took his usual dose. He wakes with dextrose and an hour later is hypoglycemic again. Renal function is reduced. A student gives one amp of dextrose and discharges him.
question: Why did the sugar return to low, and why is glyburide a poor choice here?
options: Sulfonylureas keep potassium channels closed and insulin secretion going for many hours; glyburide is long-acting and renally cleared, so one glucose dose does not end the episode
Glyburide wears off in minutes, so recurrent lows mean he took insulin secretly
Dextrose stimulates further sulfonylurea release from the bottle, which is the mechanism
Hypoglycemia from this class is impossible if he still has a pancreas
Reduced kidney function shortens glyburide action
correctAnswer: Sulfonylureas keep potassium channels closed and insulin secretion going for many hours; glyburide is long-acting and renally cleared, so one glucose dose does not end the episode
explanation: Sulfonylureas close the beta-cell K-ATP channel, calcium enters, and insulin is released regardless of the current glucose once the drug is on board. Glyburide lasts and accumulates when the kidneys fail, which is why it is a bad drug in older adults. He needs observation and repeated glucose, sometimes octreotide, not a doorway discharge. A short action would not explain the relapse. Dextrose does not release more tablets. The whole toxicity requires a pancreas that can still be forced to secrete. Low GFR prolongs, not shortens, the effect.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: Patient A has a high calcium, low phosphate, high PTH, and a bone film with subperiosteal resorption. Patient B has a squamous lung cancer, high calcium, low PTH, and low phosphate. Patient C has high calcium, high phosphate, low PTH, and a history of eating supplements. Patient D has sarcoidosis, high calcium, low PTH, and a high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
question: Who has primary hyperparathyroidism, and who is making vitamin D outside the kidney's usual control?
options: A is a parathyroid adenoma; D has granulomatous 1-alpha hydroxylase activity that is not turned off by calcium
B has primary hyperparathyroidism because the cancer secretes PTH
C has humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy because both minerals are high
D has hypoparathyroidism because PTH is low
A should have a high phosphate because PTH holds phosphate in the blood
correctAnswer: A is a parathyroid adenoma; D has granulomatous 1-alpha hydroxylase activity that is not turned off by calcium
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium, lowers phosphate, and the PTH is high; bone is resorbed. PTHrP from squamous cancer imitates PTH on bone and kidney but the real PTH is suppressed. Milk-alkali or vitamin D excess raises both calcium and phosphate and suppresses PTH. Sarcoid macrophages make 1,25-vitamin D on their own, so calcium rises and PTH falls, and the active vitamin D is high. Cancer does not raise the PTH assay in the usual PTHrP case. High calcium with high phosphate is not PTHrP, which wastes phosphate. Low PTH with high calcium is appropriate suppression, not hypoparathyroidism, which would have low calcium. PTH dumps phosphate in the urine, so phosphate is low, not high.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A short child with short fourth metacarpals has a low calcium, a high phosphate, and a high PTH. Infused PTH does not raise urinary cAMP. A classmate with a surgical thyroidectomy has the same minerals but a low PTH. The mother has the same hand shape and a normal calcium.
question: Where is the resistance, and why can the mother look different?
options: The kidney Gs protein does not answer PTH, so cAMP does not rise; the gene is imprinted and the maternal allele matters, so a parent can carry the phenotype with or without the biochemistry
The parathyroids are absent, so PTH should be low
Vitamin D poisoning explains the low calcium and high PTH
This is hypoparathyroidism because the minerals match a low PTH patient
Urinary cAMP should fall in normal people given PTH, so the test was misread
correctAnswer: The kidney Gs protein does not answer PTH, so cAMP does not rise; the gene is imprinted and the maternal allele matters, so a parent can carry the phenotype with or without the biochemistry
explanation: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type Ia is end-organ resistance. PTH is high and cannot lower phosphate or raise calcium, and exogenous PTH does not generate cAMP. Albright hereditary osteodystrophy can appear in relatives; GNAS imprinting means the maternal allele is the one that matters in the kidney, so family members can share the body habitus with different labs. Absent parathyroids would lower PTH, which is the post-surgical classmate. Vitamin D poisoning raises calcium. The minerals look like hypoparathyroidism but the high PTH is the separator. Normal kidneys increase cAMP when PTH is infused.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Six hours after a total thyroidectomy a woman has perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign. Calcium is low and PTH is low. Phosphate is high. She is not septic. A student blames hungry bone from a longstanding parathyroid adenoma because the surgery was a thyroidectomy for cancer and the parathyroids were at risk.
question: What was removed or stunned, and why is phosphate high?
options: The parathyroids were removed or ischemic, so PTH is gone, bone and kidney release less calcium, and the kidney holds phosphate
Hungry bone keeps PTH high and phosphate low
Hypocalcemia after neck surgery is from high calcitonin that lasts for months
A high phosphate means vitamin D toxicity
Chvostek sign is specific for hypokalemia
correctAnswer: The parathyroids were removed or ischemic, so PTH is gone, bone and kidney release less calcium, and the kidney holds phosphate
explanation: PTH normally raises calcium and dumps phosphate. Without it, calcium falls, phosphate rises, and neuromuscular irritability appears soon after surgery. Hungry bone after parathyroidectomy for longstanding hyperparathyroidism also drops calcium, but PTH is not low in the same way at the moment of cure if residual glands work, and the classic immediate low PTH is gland injury. Calcitonin is not the lasting cause. Vitamin D toxicity raises calcium. Chvostek sign is facial twitching from low calcium, not potassium.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A student is asked why muscle takes up glucose after a meal but the liver's main glucose transporter does not wait for insulin. She says both tissues use GLUT4. A patient with a rare insulin-receptor mutation has high insulin, high glucose, and acanthosis.
question: Which transporter is insulin-dependent, and what does the receptor mutation prove?
options: GLUT4 in muscle and fat is moved to the membrane by insulin signaling; liver GLUT2 is constitutive. Receptor failure causes hyperglycemia despite high insulin
GLUT2 is the insulin-regulated transporter in muscle
The liver cannot take up glucose unless insulin opens GLUT4
High insulin with high glucose means the pancreas has failed
Acanthosis nigricans means insulin levels are low
correctAnswer: GLUT4 in muscle and fat is moved to the membrane by insulin signaling; liver GLUT2 is constitutive. Receptor failure causes hyperglycemia despite high insulin
explanation: Insulin binds its receptor, a tyrosine kinase, and in muscle and adipose tissue sends GLUT4 to the surface. Liver and beta cells use GLUT2, which is not parked waiting for insulin; the liver's insulin effect on glucose is mostly enzyme regulation. A receptor mutation is insulin resistance: glucose stays high while insulin is high, and acanthosis tracks that high insulin. GLUT2 is not the regulated muscle transporter. The liver does take up glucose without a GLUT4 step. High insulin means the pancreas is working, which is the opposite of type 1 failure. Acanthosis is a sign of high, not low, insulin.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman is mid-cycle. Estradiol has been high for two days. The LH surge is starting. A student says estrogen always inhibits LH, so a surge is impossible, and that progesterone was the hormone that triggered ovulation. Basal body temperature has not risen yet.
question: What switched, and what raises the temperature after ovulation?
options: Sustained high estradiol becomes positive feedback at the pituitary and hypothalamus and triggers the LH surge; progesterone from the corpus luteum then raises temperature
Estrogen is only inhibitory, so the surge is FSH from the ovary
Progesterone triggers the LH surge and temperature falls after ovulation
The LH surge follows menstruation by one day
Ovulation is caused by a drop in estradiol to zero
correctAnswer: Sustained high estradiol becomes positive feedback at the pituitary and hypothalamus and triggers the LH surge; progesterone from the corpus luteum then raises temperature
explanation: Low or moderate estrogen inhibits gonadotropins. When estradiol stays high through the late follicular phase, feedback flips and LH surges, which ovulates the follicle. After ovulation the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which is thermogenic, so the temperature rise is a post-ovulation sign, not the trigger. Calling estrogen only inhibitory misses the switch. FSH does not surge as the ovulatory signal in that way. Progesterone is not the pre-ovulatory trigger, and temperature rises rather than falls. The surge is mid-cycle, not the day after menses. Estradiol is high, not zero, when the surge starts.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman has irregular menses, acne, and hirsutism. LH is high relative to FSH. The ovaries are enlarged with many small follicles. She is insulin resistant. A student says the androgens come from an adrenal tumor because DHEA-S must be the source whenever hair grows, and that FSH is high.
question: Why is LH high relative to FSH, and where are the androgens from in this common disease?
options: Insulin and high LH drive theca-cell androgens; follicles do not mature well because FSH action is relatively low, and an adrenal tumor is not required
FSH is higher than LH, which luteinizes many follicles
Androgens come only from a cortisol-producing adenoma
Insulin resistance lowers ovarian androgen production
Regular monthly ovulation is the definition of this physiology
correctAnswer: Insulin and high LH drive theca-cell androgens; follicles do not mature well because FSH action is relatively low, and an adrenal tumor is not required
explanation: In PCOS, LH is disproportionately high and pushes theca cells to make androgens. FSH is relatively low, so many follicles stall. Hyperinsulinemia amplifies ovarian androgen production and lowers sex-hormone binding globulin. Most hirsutism of this pattern is ovarian, and a very high DHEA-S would be the adrenal-tumor clue, which is not this story. FSH is not the dominant gonadotropin here. A cortisol adenoma is Cushing syndrome. Insulin resistance increases, not lowers, the androgen drive. Ovulation is infrequent, which is why menses are irregular.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman has galactorrhea and amenorrhea. Prolactin is high and a pituitary MRI shows a small adenoma. LH and FSH are low. She is not pregnant. A student says high prolactin should increase GnRH because lactation and fertility go together, and recommends dopamine as the drug that would raise prolactin further.
question: How does prolactin stop menses, and what does a dopamine agonist do?
options: Prolactin suppresses GnRH, so gonadotropins fall and ovulation stops; dopamine agonists such as cabergoline lower prolactin because dopamine is the physiologic brake
Prolactin stimulates GnRH, so LH should be high
Dopamine agonists are used to increase prolactin in a prolactinoma
Amenorrhea with galactorrhea is primary ovarian failure, so FSH is high
A pituitary adenoma that makes prolactin always presents with bitemporal hemianopia first
correctAnswer: Prolactin suppresses GnRH, so gonadotropins fall and ovulation stops; dopamine agonists such as cabergoline lower prolactin because dopamine is the physiologic brake
explanation: High prolactin turns down GnRH. Without pulsatile GnRH, LH and FSH fall and the ovary is quiet, so menses stop and milk can be present. Dopamine from the hypothalamus inhibits lactotrophs, so a dopamine agonist treats the adenoma. The fertility-and-lactation intuition is backward for the GnRH effect. A dopamine agonist does not raise prolactin. Primary ovarian failure would raise FSH. A microadenoma often has no visual-field cut; that finding is a macroadenoma clue, not a requirement.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: Family A has hyperparathyroidism, a pituitary prolactinoma, and a pancreatic gastrinoma. Family B has medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. Family C has medullary thyroid cancer, pheo, and mucosal neuromas, with a marfanoid habitus and no hyperparathyroidism as the lead feature.
question: Which genes and which family gets thyroidectomy based on the RET risk?
options: A is MEN1 (menin); B is MEN2A and C is MEN2B, both RET, and medullary thyroid cancer risk drives early thyroidectomy
All three are MEN1 because each has an endocrine tumor
MEN2B has hyperparathyroidism as its defining parathyroid disease and no neuromas
Pheochromocytoma belongs only to MEN1
Medullary thyroid cancer is a follicular-cell cancer treated with radioiodine as the inherited lesion
correctAnswer: A is MEN1 (menin); B is MEN2A and C is MEN2B, both RET, and medullary thyroid cancer risk drives early thyroidectomy
explanation: MEN1 is parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas, the menin gene. MEN2 is RET. 2A adds hyperparathyroidism to medullary thyroid cancer and pheo. 2B has medullary thyroid cancer, pheo, and mucosal neuromas, and is marfanoid, without the parathyroid disease as its signature. The thyroid cancer is C-cell, calcitonin-producing, and the reason gene carriers lose the thyroid early. Not every endocrine cluster is MEN1. 2B is the neuroma family. Pheo is the MEN2 tumor, not the MEN1 one. Follicular cells make papillary and follicular cancers; medullary cancer does not take up iodine the way those do.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man has paroxysms of headache, palpitations, and hypertension. Plasma metanephrines are high. A surgeon plans a resection. A student starts a beta blocker the night before for the tachycardia and the pressure rises further. He has not received an alpha blocker.
question: Why did the pressure rise, and what must come first?
options: Blocking beta-2 vasodilation while alpha constriction is unopposed raises pressure; phenoxybenzamine or another alpha block comes before any beta blocker
Beta blockers are the first and only preoperative drug
