Alpha blockade would worsen the tachycardia and is saved for after removal
Metanephrines are a thyroid marker, so this is a thyroid storm protocol
The pressure rise means the tumor is not catecholamine-secreting
correctAnswer: Blocking beta-2 vasodilation while alpha constriction is unopposed raises pressure; phenoxybenzamine or another alpha block comes before any beta blocker
explanation: Pheochromocytoma pours out epinephrine and norepinephrine. Alpha receptors constrict; beta-2 receptors dilate in some beds. If you block beta first, dilation is lost and alpha constriction is unopposed, so pressure climbs. Irreversible alpha blockade, volume replacement, then a beta blocker if the heart rate needs it, is the order. Beta blockade is not the opening drug. Alpha blockade is preoperative, not something you skip until the gland is out. Metanephrines are catecholamine metabolites, not a thyroid test. The rise is exactly what a catecholamine tumor does when beta-blocked first.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A toddler has a huge liver, severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and high triglycerides. Muscle cramps with brief exercise are absent. Glucose-6-phosphatase is the enzyme under discussion. A student picks McArdle disease because both are glycogenoses.
question: Why can this child not free glucose, and why is McArdle the wrong organ?
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase in liver is required to release free glucose; McArdle is muscle phosphorylase, with cramps and no hypoglycemia
McArdle disease causes fasting hypoglycemia and a big liver
Von Gierke disease is a lysosomal maltase defect that enlarges the heart
The lactic acid means he has too much glucose-6-phosphatase
Branching enzyme deficiency presents with this severe fasting hypoglycemia as its classic form
correctAnswer: Glucose-6-phosphatase in liver is required to release free glucose; McArdle is muscle phosphorylase, with cramps and no hypoglycemia
explanation: Von Gierke disease traps glucose-6-phosphate in the liver. Glycogen builds, free glucose cannot be released, and the phosphate is shunted to lactate and to the pentose pathway that feeds uric acid, with lipid following. McArdle disease cannot break muscle glycogen, so brief exercise causes cramps and myoglobinuria, and the blood glucose is maintained by the liver. Pompe disease is lysosomal acid maltase and hits the heart. The enzyme is missing, not overactive. Andersen branching-enzyme disease causes cirrhosis and abnormal glycogen, not this classic fasting biochemical storm.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A teenager gets cramps and burgundy urine after a short sprint. The forearm exercise test does not raise lactate. He can sometimes continue after a brief rest, the second wind. Between sprints his blood glucose is normal and the liver is not enlarged.
question: Which enzyme, and why does a second wind happen?
options: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase is missing, so anaerobic glycogen cannot make lactate; blood-borne fuels after a few minutes bypass the missing enzyme
Liver glucose-6-phosphatase is missing, so sprints cause hypoglycemia as the first sign
Acid maltase is missing, so the ECG is the test of choice for the burgundy urine
Lactate should rise more than normal when phosphorylase is gone
The urine color is bilirubin from hemolysis of G6PD deficiency only
correctAnswer: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase is missing, so anaerobic glycogen cannot make lactate; blood-borne fuels after a few minutes bypass the missing enzyme
explanation: McArdle disease is muscle phosphorylase deficiency. Glycogen cannot enter glycolysis in muscle, so lactate does not rise with ischemic exercise and ATP fails, cramping the muscle and spilling myoglobin. After a few minutes, liver glucose and fatty acids delivered by blood take over, which is the second wind. The liver enzyme of von Gierke disease would cause fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, which he does not have. Pompe disease is a floppy infant or cardiomyopathy, not sprint myoglobinuria. Lactate stays flat, which is the test. Myoglobin, not bilirubin, colors the urine.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child becomes profoundly hypoglycemic during a gastroenteritis when he stops eating, and he has no ketones in the urine. Muscle weakness is present. A medium-chain triglyceride supplement is being discussed because medium-chain fats do not need the carnitine shuttle. He does not have a big liver from von Gierke disease.
question: Why are ketones absent, and why do medium-chain fats bypass the block?
options: Long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria without carnitine palmitoyltransferase, so the liver cannot make ketones; medium-chain fats enter without that shuttle
Ketones are absent because he has too much insulin from an insulinoma during the illness
Medium-chain fats require more carnitine than long-chain fats
Hypoglycemia with no ketones is the definition of von Gierke disease
Carnitine carries glucose into the mitochondria
correctAnswer: Long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria without carnitine palmitoyltransferase, so the liver cannot make ketones; medium-chain fats enter without that shuttle
explanation: Beta oxidation and ketone production need fatty acids inside mitochondria. The carnitine shuttle, including CPT-I and CPT-II, carries long-chain acyl groups in. A block presents as hypoketotic hypoglycemia when fasting removes dietary carbohydrate, plus weak muscles. Medium-chain fatty acids skip the shuttle, which is why that nutrition is used. An insulinoma would suppress ketones but is not a carnitine story and not a fasting-illness pattern with a shuttle bypass. Medium chains need the shuttle less, not more. Von Gierke disease has lactate and a huge liver and can still make ketones from fat. Carnitine does not carry glucose.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A fair-haired infant who missed the newborn screen is irritable and later intellectually delayed. The diaper has a musty smell. Phenylalanine is high and tyrosine is low. A student says he needs a high-phenylalanine diet to replace the missing amino acid, and that tyrosine is essential only in healthy children.
question: Which enzyme failed, and which amino acid becomes essential?
options: Phenylalanine hydroxylase or its biopterin cofactor failed; tyrosine must be supplied and phenylalanine restricted
Tyrosinase failed, so this is albinism and the diet is irrelevant
Homogentisate oxidase failed, so urine turns black
Cystathionine synthase failed, so methionine is low and phenylalanine is a bystander
A high-phenylalanine diet prevents the intellectual disability
correctAnswer: Phenylalanine hydroxylase or its biopterin cofactor failed; tyrosine must be supplied and phenylalanine restricted
explanation: Phenylalanine cannot become tyrosine. It and its metabolites accumulate, which injures the developing brain and causes the musty odor and pale pigment because tyrosine is short for melanin. Treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet plus tyrosine, which has become essential. Tyrosinase deficiency is albinism without this amino-acid pair and without the musty delay. Homogentisate oxidase is alkaptonuria. Cystathionine synthase is homocystinuria. Feeding more phenylalanine is the exposure that causes the injury.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A tall child has a downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, and a clot in a leg vein. Homocysteine is high. A classmate with Marfan syndrome has an upward lens dislocation, a normal intellect, and an aortic root at risk. Someone prescribes a low-methionine plan for the Marfan patient.
question: Which enzyme and which direction of the lens separate them?
options: Cystathionine synthase deficiency causes downward dislocation and thrombosis; Marfan is fibrillin with upward dislocation and no homocysteine clot
Both are fibrillin defects and the lens direction is random
Homocystinuria dislocates the lens upward
Marfan syndrome causes fair hair and a musty urine
Thrombosis means the child has too little homocysteine
correctAnswer: Cystathionine synthase deficiency causes downward dislocation and thrombosis; Marfan is fibrillin with upward dislocation and no homocysteine clot
explanation: Classic homocystinuria cannot condense homocysteine with serine. Homocysteine injures vessels and the brain, and the lens zonules fail downward. Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue microfibril disease: upward lens dislocation, aortic aneurysm, and normal intelligence, without a clotting amino acid. The lens direction is the clinical separator, not a coin flip. Upward dislocation is Marfan. A musty smell is PKU. The clot is from too much homocysteine, not too little.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A male infant becomes lethargic as feeds increase. Ammonia is very high, BUN is low, and orotic acid is high in the urine. There is no megaloblastic anemia. A sister is healthy. A student picks orotic aciduria because orotic acid is high, and plans uridine only.
question: Which cycle is blocked, and why is this not hereditary orotic aciduria?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase is missing, so carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis and makes orotic acid; the emergency is hyperammonemia, and orotic aciduria the disease also has megaloblastic anemia and no ammonia crisis
Arginase deficiency, which has a high BUN
CPS-I deficiency, which also raises orotic acid
The urea cycle is intact and the ammonia is from liver failure with a high BUN
Uridine alone treats the X-linked ammonia crisis
correctAnswer: Ornithine transcarbamylase is missing, so carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis and makes orotic acid; the emergency is hyperammonemia, and orotic aciduria the disease also has megaloblastic anemia and no ammonia crisis
explanation: OTC is X-linked. Carbamoyl phosphate cannot enter the urea cycle, ammonia rises, and the excess carbamoyl phosphate makes orotic acid. Hereditary orotic aciduria is a pyrimidine-synthesis defect with megaloblastic anemia and growth failure, and it does not present as a neonatal ammonia crisis; uridine helps that disease, not this one. Arginase deficiency is a later, different urea-cycle picture and does not raise BUN; BUN is low when the cycle is blocked. CPS-I deficiency raises ammonia but not orotic acid, because carbamoyl phosphate itself is not made. This is not intact-cycle liver failure. The treatment of the crisis is ammonia removal, not uridine monotherapy.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A newborn on milk becomes jaundiced, vomits, and has a reducing sugar in the urine that is not glucose on a glucose oxidase strip. E. coli sepsis is a worry. Cataracts are starting. The enzyme that makes galactose-1-phosphate is the one named in the severe form, and milk is stopped.
question: What accumulates, and why is the urine trick useful?
options: Galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol accumulate because galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase is missing; the urine reduces copper but is not glucose
Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates after the first milk feed
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency presents on the first day of milk with cataracts
The reducing sugar is glucose, so the oxidase strip should have been positive
Stopping milk is useless because lactose is not the source of galactose
correctAnswer: Galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol accumulate because galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase is missing; the urine reduces copper but is not glucose
explanation: Classic galactosemia lacks GALT. Galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to liver, kidney, and brain, and galactitol swells the lens. Milk lactose is glucose plus galactose, so stopping milk stops the source. The urine has galactose, a reducing sugar that glucose oxidase ignores. Hereditary fructose intolerance needs fructose, not the first milk. Von Gierke disease is a fasting glycogen problem, not cataracts from milk. A negative glucose oxidase strip is the point of the test. Lactose is exactly the dietary source.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A baby is fine on breast milk and becomes hypoglycemic and vomits when fruit juice and sucrose are added. The liver is tender and phosphate is low. Aldolase B is the enzyme. A parent was told this is galactosemia because both are sugar diseases of infants.
question: Why did milk spare him, and what traps the phosphate?
options: Milk has no fructose; aldolase B failure traps fructose-1-phosphate and consumes phosphate, which blocks glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Breast milk is rich in fructose, so the story is impossible
Galactosemia presents only after juice and spares milk
Hexokinase is the missing enzyme, so fructose never gets phosphorylated
Hypoglycemia means he needs more sucrose
correctAnswer: Milk has no fructose; aldolase B failure traps fructose-1-phosphate and consumes phosphate, which blocks glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
explanation: Sucrose and fruit contain fructose. Aldolase B splits fructose-1-phosphate. Without it the phosphate ester accumulates, inorganic phosphate falls, and the liver cannot run glycogen breakdown or gluconeogenesis, so glucose falls. Breast milk does not contain fructose, which is why he was well at first. Galactosemia is triggered by milk, the opposite timing. The phosphorylating enzyme works; the cleavage enzyme does not. More sucrose is the poison.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man on spironolactone for heart failure develops tender breast tissue. A second man takes finasteride for prostatic hyperplasia and is told his PSA and his scalp hair may change. A student says both drugs block the androgen receptor.
question: Which receptor or enzyme does each drug hit?
options: Spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor as well as the mineralocorticoid receptor; finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase and lowers DHT without blocking the androgen receptor
Finasteride is an androgen-receptor blocker and spironolactone only blocks 5-alpha reductase
Both inhibit aromatase, so estrogen falls and breasts shrink
Gynecomastia from spironolactone means the dose is subtherapeutic
Finasteride raises DHT, which shrinks the prostate
correctAnswer: Spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor as well as the mineralocorticoid receptor; finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase and lowers DHT without blocking the androgen receptor
explanation: Spironolactone's off-target androgen-receptor block is why men get gynecomastia. Finasteride and dutasteride block conversion of testosterone to the more potent DHT in prostate and hair follicle. Testosterone itself can still bind the androgen receptor, which is a different drug class (flutamide, spironolactone). Swapping the mechanisms swaps the side effects you warn about. They are not aromatase inhibitors; aromatase inhibition would lower estrogen. Breast tenderness is a real effect, not a sign of a tiny dose. Finasteride lowers DHT, which is how the prostate shrinks.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man with type 1 diabetes is put on propranolol for tremor. During an insulin reaction he does not feel the usual pounding heart or tremor, and he is sweaty and confused by the time anyone notices. A nonselective beta blocker was chosen. A student says beta blockers raise glucose and cannot mask a low.
question: Which warning symptoms are blocked, and which one remains?
options: Tremor and tachycardia are beta-adrenergic and are blunted; sweating is cholinergic and can remain, and recovery from hypoglycemia is also slowed because beta-2 helps counter-regulation
Sweating is the symptom beta blockers remove, while tremor remains
Propranolol causes hypoglycemia by releasing insulin
Selective and nonselective agents are identical for this warning
Masking means the glucose number on the meter rises falsely
correctAnswer: Tremor and tachycardia are beta-adrenergic and are blunted; sweating is cholinergic and can remain, and recovery from hypoglycemia is also slowed because beta-2 helps counter-regulation
explanation: The adrenergic warning of hypoglycemia is a beta effect: shake and a fast heart. Propranolol blocks it, so the patient skips the early alarm and presents confused. Sweating is muscarinic and often persists, which is the clue that remains. Nonselective blockade also impairs glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis that depend on beta-2. Sweating is not the blocked symptom. Propranolol does not release insulin the way a sulfonylurea does. Beta-1 selective drugs are somewhat less guilty, so they are not identical. The meter still reads a true low; the mask is symptomatic, not analytic.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A woman on lisinopril has a dry cough and a normal chest radiograph. She stops the drug and the cough ends. She later becomes pregnant while a relative restarts her on the same pill from an old bottle. She is in the second trimester.
question: Why the cough, and why must the drug stop in pregnancy?
options: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, which coughs; in pregnancy they injure the fetal kidney and cause oligohydramnios, so they are stopped
The cough is from low bradykinin and is treated by raising the dose
ARBs cause the same cough as often as ACE inhibitors because both raise bradykinin equally
ACE inhibitors are first-line antihypertensives throughout pregnancy
Fetal injury is limited to the first 48 hours after conception and the second trimester is safe
correctAnswer: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, which coughs; in pregnancy they injure the fetal kidney and cause oligohydramnios, so they are stopped
explanation: ACE normally degrades bradykinin. Inhibit it and bradykinin builds up in the lung and triggers a dry cough that goes away when the drug stops. The same blockade of angiotensin II formation is catastrophic for the fetal renal circulation later in pregnancy: oligohydramnios, skull and renal malformation. Raising the dose would worsen the cough. ARBs block the receptor and do not raise bradykinin the same way, so cough is much less common, but they are also teratogenic. They are contraindicated in pregnancy, not first-line. Injury continues through the second and third trimesters, which is why a leftover bottle is an emergency stop.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A pregnant woman on levothyroxine feels well but her TSH has risen above the pregnancy target. Estrogen is high and thyroxine-binding globulin is high. Free T4 is drifting down. A student says she needs less hormone because TBG is high and total T4 will look high even if she is hypothyroid.
question: Why does the dose usually rise?
options: High TBG binds more hormone, and pregnancy increases clearance and volume; she needs more levothyroxine so free hormone and TSH stay normal. A high total T4 can hide a low free level
Pregnancy lowers TBG, so the dose is cut in half
TSH is an unreliable pregnancy lab and should be ignored
Levothyroxine is stopped in pregnancy because it does not cross any relevant pathway to the fetus
Free T4 falling means she is hyperthyroid and the dose is too high
correctAnswer: High TBG binds more hormone, and pregnancy increases clearance and volume; she needs more levothyroxine so free hormone and TSH stay normal. A high total T4 can hide a low free level
explanation: Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin. More hormone is bound, free hormone tends to fall, TSH rises, and the replacement dose is increased, often early in pregnancy. Total T4 rises with the binding protein and is a trap if you treat the total and not the free level and the TSH. TBG goes up, not down. TSH remains the guide, with pregnancy-specific ranges. Maternal thyroid hormone matters for the fetus, especially early, and is not stopped. A falling free T4 is hypothyroidism, not excess.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation has a low TSH and a high free T4. One mechanism discussed is iodine load causing hyperthyroidism in a nodular gland, and another is thyroiditis from the drug. A student says amiodarone only causes hypothyroidism because it blocks conversion of T4 to T3, so a low TSH is impossible.
question: Which statement is right?
options: Amiodarone can cause either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism; blocked T4-to-T3 conversion can raise T4, but a suppressed TSH means real thyrotoxicosis that still has to be sorted into iodine-induced versus destructive
Amiodarone never affects the thyroid because it contains no iodine
A low TSH on amiodarone is always hypothyroidism
Type 1 and type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis are treated identically with high-dose hormone replacement
Stopping the interpretation at the deiodinase block is enough when TSH is suppressed
correctAnswer: Amiodarone can cause either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism; blocked T4-to-T3 conversion can raise T4, but a suppressed TSH means real thyrotoxicosis that still has to be sorted into iodine-induced versus destructive
explanation: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and also inhibits peripheral deiodinase. Hypothyroidism is common, especially where iodine is sufficient. Hyperthyroidism also occurs: type 1 is extra synthesis in a nodular or Graves gland, type 2 is destructive thyroiditis. A low TSH is not hypothyroidism. The drug is loaded with iodine. High-dose levothyroxine is the wrong direction for thyrotoxicosis. The deiodinase effect can confuse total and free levels, but a suppressed TSH is not dismissed as a lab quirk.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 64-year-old man with a urinary-source fever has a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg after fluids. Cardiac output is high, systemic vascular resistance is low, and the skin is warm. A second patient after a large anterior myocardial infarction is cold, with low cardiac output and high systemic vascular resistance. Both have lactate elevation.
question: Which profile is the septic patient, and why does warm skin matter?
options: High output and low resistance is vasodilation from sepsis; cold low-output high-resistance shock is cardiogenic pump failure
Both profiles are hypovolemia, and skin temperature does not matter
Low resistance means tamponade because the heart cannot fill
High cardiac output excludes shock even if the pressure is 78 mm Hg
Cardiogenic shock has low resistance because the heart releases nitric oxide
correctAnswer: High output and low resistance is vasodilation from sepsis; cold low-output high-resistance shock is cardiogenic pump failure
explanation: Septic shock is distributive: inflammatory mediators drop systemic vascular resistance, cardiac output is often high, and the skin is warm. Cardiogenic shock is a failed pump, so output is low, the body clamps down, resistance is high, and the skin is cold. Calling both hypovolemia misses the output and resistance split. Tamponade is obstructive, with low output and equalization of diastolic pressures, not low resistance with warm skin. A pressure of 78 mm Hg with lactate is shock even if output is high; the tissues are under-perfused because pressure, not just output, is inadequate. Cardiogenic vasoconstriction raises resistance; it does not lower it.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man two weeks after a viral illness has hypotension, jugular venous distention, and muffled sounds. Pulsus paradoxus is present. Cath shows diastolic pressures equal in the right atrium, right ventricle, and left ventricle. A student calls it septic shock because he is febrile.
question: What limits filling, and which shock numbers are the opposite of sepsis?
options: Fluid under pressure around the heart equalizes diastolic filling; output falls and resistance rises, unlike warm vasodilated sepsis
A ruptured valve causes a wide pulse pressure and a new diastolic murmur as the main finding
Sepsis and tamponade share high cardiac output, so antibiotics are the only next step
Pulsus paradoxus means the systolic pressure rises on inspiration
Equal diastolic pressures are the definition of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
correctAnswer: Fluid under pressure around the heart equalizes diastolic filling; output falls and resistance rises, unlike warm vasodilated sepsis
explanation: Tamponade, often from pericarditis or bleeding, stops the heart from filling. Diastolic pressures equalize, stroke volume falls, and the body vasoconstricts, so this is obstructive shock with low output and high resistance. Sepsis is the opposite resistance pattern and is warm. A ruptured valve gives a loud murmur and a different pressure tracing, not equalization and muffled sounds. Antibiotics do not drain the pericardium. Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated drop in systolic pressure on inspiration. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is dynamic outflow obstruction, not equal diastolic pressures.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Minutes after a peanut exposure a teenager has hives, wheezing, vomiting, and a blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg. A classmate who fainted at the sight of blood is pale, bradycardic, and has no rash or wheeze, and he wakes as soon as he is flat. The nurse reaches for diphenhydramine first for the teenager.
question: What is the first drug for the teenager, and why is the fainting friend different?
options: Intramuscular epinephrine for IgE-mediated anaphylaxis; the friend has a vasovagal reflex with bradycardia and no allergic findings, so epinephrine is not his treatment
Diphenhydramine first, because histamine block reverses shock
A glucocorticoid first, because it acts in minutes on the airway
Epinephrine for both, because any loss of consciousness is anaphylaxis
Atropine for the teenager because anaphylaxis causes bradycardia as the first sign
correctAnswer: Intramuscular epinephrine for IgE-mediated anaphylaxis; the friend has a vasovagal reflex with bradycardia and no allergic findings, so epinephrine is not his treatment
explanation: Anaphylaxis is IgE-triggered mast-cell release with airway and shock. Intramuscular epinephrine is first because it supports pressure and opens the airway; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and do not treat the shock. A vasovagal faint is bradycardia and pallor without urticaria or wheeze and resolves when supine. Diphenhydramine does not restore circulation. Steroids act over hours, not minutes. Epinephrine for a simple faint is the wrong drug and the wrong diagnosis. Anaphylactic shock is typically tachycardic, not a primary atropine problem.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

blueprintTopic: Type I versus type III hypersensitivity
scenario: Patient A wheezes and gets hives within minutes of penicillin. Patient B, ten days into a drug for a long infection, has fever, joint pain, and a falling complement with a rash, and the symptoms began long after the first dose. A student calls both immediate allergy and stops at antihistamines for both.
question: Which immune mechanisms fit?
options: A is IgE on mast cells; B is immune-complex disease with complement consumption, days to weeks after antigen
Both are IgE, and complement falls in classic anaphylaxis as the rule
B is delayed T-cell contact dermatitis, which consumes complement
A is cytotoxic IgG against red cells because it happened fast
Serum sickness is a type II disease of a single cell surface
correctAnswer: A is IgE on mast cells; B is immune-complex disease with complement consumption, days to weeks after antigen
explanation: Type I is immediate: IgE cross-linking, histamine, minutes. Type III is immune complexes depositing in joints, skin, and vessels, consuming complement, typically a week or more into exposure. Antihistamines do not treat serum sickness. Anaphylaxis does not present as a complement-consuming arthritis ten days later. Contact dermatitis is type IV, T-cell, and does not drop complement this way. Fast hemolysis is type II but is not hives and wheeze. Serum sickness is not a single-cell type II target.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A nurse develops an itchy rash only where nickel touches the skin, peaking two days later. A different patient has a firm red nodule two days after a tuberculosis skin test. Neither had symptoms in the first hour. A student labels both as IgE because they are skin findings.
question: What cell mediates both, and why is the timing the clue?
options: Previously sensitized T cells activate macrophages over one to two days; there is no immediate mast-cell phase
IgE, because all rashes are type I
Immune complexes, because complement is required for a PPD
IgG against keratinocytes, a type II blister in the first minutes
Neutrophils only, with no memory, which is why it recurs at the same site
correctAnswer: Previously sensitized T cells activate macrophages over one to two days; there is no immediate mast-cell phase
explanation: Contact dermatitis and the tuberculin reaction are type IV. Memory T cells see antigen and recruit macrophages; the reaction is delayed, not present in the first minutes. IgE reactions are immediate. A PPD is not an immune-complex complement event. Type II keratinocyte attack is pemphigus-family disease, not a nickel rash at 48 hours. The recurrence at a known site is memory, which neutrophils alone do not provide.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Minutes into a red-cell transfusion a patient has fever, back pain, dark urine, and oozing from the IV site. The direct antiglobulin test is positive and hemoglobinuria is present. A clerical check shows the unit was labeled for another patient. A nurse suggests slowing the rate and continuing because fever during transfusion is common.
question: What is lysing the cells, and why is continuing the unit wrong?
options: Preformed ABO IgM fixes complement and lyses donor cells intravascularly; the unit is stopped because this is hemolysis, not a trivial cytokine fever
The reaction is allergic urticaria, so slowing the rate is enough
TRALI is the cause whenever urine turns dark
IgA deficiency causes this back pain and hemoglobinuria
A febrile nonhemolytic reaction drops haptoglobin and causes oozing
correctAnswer: Preformed ABO IgM fixes complement and lyses donor cells intravascularly; the unit is stopped because this is hemolysis, not a trivial cytokine fever
explanation: ABO incompatibility is type II intravascular hemolysis from complement-fixing IgM. Fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and coagulopathy mean the transfusion stops immediately and the identity is rechecked. A simple allergic reaction is hives without dark urine. TRALI is noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, not hemoglobinuria. IgA deficiency causes anaphylaxis when IgA in plasma is given, not this hemolytic picture. A febrile nonhemolytic reaction is cytokine-mediated, the Coombs test stays negative, and it does not lyse cells or start DIC.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An hour after plasma, a patient is hypoxic with bilateral infiltrates and a normal heart size. Blood pressure is not high and he was not volume overloaded before the unit. A second patient, known to have heart failure, gets several units and develops hypoxia, hypertension, and an elevated BNP.
question: Which is antibody-mediated lung injury, and which is overload?
options: The first is TRALI from donor antibodies activating recipient neutrophils; the second is circulatory overload
Both are ABO hemolysis because hypoxia followed a transfusion
The first is cardiogenic because any post-transfusion infiltrate is the heart
The second is TRALI because heart-failure patients cannot get fluid overload
Diuretics are first-line for TRALI and harmful in overload
correctAnswer: The first is TRALI from donor antibodies activating recipient neutrophils; the second is circulatory overload
explanation: TRALI is noncardiogenic edema during or soon after transfusion, often from donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies. The heart is not the problem, pressures are not those of failure, and diuretics are not the treatment. TACO is too much volume for a weak heart: hypertension, high BNP, and a response to diuretics. Hypoxia alone is not hemolysis. Calling every infiltrate cardiogenic misses a normal heart size and normal filling story. Heart-failure patients are exactly who overload. Diuretics help overload and do not fix capillary leak from TRALI.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A was in a house fire, has a headache, a normal pulse oximeter reading, and cherry-red skin; the calculated oxygen saturation from a co-oximeter is low. Patient B, pulled from the same fire, has a profound lactic acidosis, a bitter-almond odor, and a normal arterial oxygen tension. His venous blood looks arterial.
question: Which toxin binds hemoglobin, and which blocks cytochrome oxidase?
options: A is carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and shifts the remaining curve left; B is cyanide, which stops aerobic respiration so oxygen is not used
Both are cyanide, and the pulse oximeter reliably shows the oxygen deficit
A is methemoglobin because the skin is red
B should receive methylene blue as the specific antidote
Carbon monoxide lowers dissolved arterial oxygen tension, which is why the ABG PaO2 falls
correctAnswer: A is carbon monoxide, which binds hemoglobin and shifts the remaining curve left; B is cyanide, which stops aerobic respiration so oxygen is not used
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity and makes standard pulse oximetry look falsely normal; co-oximetry shows the gap, and the remaining hemoglobin holds oxygen too tightly. Cyanide poisons complex IV, cells cannot use oxygen, lactate rises, and venous blood stays oxygenated. A pulse oximeter does not detect carbon monoxide. Cherry skin is not methemoglobin; methemoglobin is chocolate-brown and cyanotic. Methylene blue treats methemoglobin, not cyanide; cyanide is treated with hydroxocobalamin. Dissolved PaO2 stays normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because that number is not hemoglobin-bound oxygen.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man who took a topical anesthetic for a procedure is cyanotic and chocolate-brown blood is drawn. Arterial oxygen tension is normal and the pulse oximeter sits near 85 percent and does not rise with oxygen. He is not short of breath from lung disease on exam.
question: What is the pigment, and what is the antidote?
options: Iron is oxidized to Fe3+ and cannot bind oxygen; methylene blue reduces it back via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase
This is carbon monoxide, treated with methylene blue
Cyanide turns blood chocolate and is treated with oxygen alone
Methylene blue is contraindicated and the treatment is pralidoxime
A normal PaO2 rules out any hemoglobin problem
correctAnswer: Iron is oxidized to Fe3+ and cannot bind oxygen; methylene blue reduces it back via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase
explanation: Methemoglobin is ferric heme. It does not carry oxygen and shifts the curve, so the patient is cyanotic with chocolate blood while dissolved PaO2 is normal. Methylene blue is the electron donor that lets the cell reduce the iron. Carbon monoxide is cherry-red, not chocolate, and is treated with oxygen, not methylene blue. Cyanide does not make chocolate blood and is not fixed by oxygen alone. Pralidoxime is for organophosphates. A normal PaO2 only says dissolved oxygen is fine; it says nothing about hemoglobin that cannot carry it.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A woman took a large amount of acetaminophen 10 hours ago. She feels nauseated but the liver enzymes are only just rising. A level plots above the treatment line. A student wants to wait for fulminant failure before giving an antidote, and suggests N-acetylcysteine works by binding the parent drug in the stomach.
question: What is the toxic metabolite, and how does the antidote work now?
options: NAPQI is normally glutathione-conjugated; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and can still help after absorption, so you do not wait for failure
The parent drug is directly toxic to the liver and charcoal at 10 hours is the only antidote
N-acetylcysteine is useless once the drug is absorbed
Fomepizole blocks CYP2E1 as the first-line specific antidote
Rising enzymes mean the injury is finished and glutathione no longer matters
correctAnswer: NAPQI is normally glutathione-conjugated; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and can still help after absorption, so you do not wait for failure
explanation: CYP2E1 makes NAPQI. Glutathione detoxifies it; overdose exhausts glutathione and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is given based on the nomogram or a dangerous history, not after transplant-level failure. Charcoal only helps very early and does not replace the antidote at 10 hours. The antidote still works after absorption because it restores the cofactor, not because it binds drug in the gut. Fomepizole is for toxic alcohols. Early enzyme rise is the start of injury, which is why the antidote is given now.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A teenager after a large aspirin ingestion is tachypneic. Arterial pH is 7.48, PaCO2 is 18 mm Hg, and the anion gap is 22. A student sees the high pH and says there is no acidosis, so bicarbonate is unnecessary. He is getting sleepy.
question: What two acid-base processes are present, and why does sleepiness change the plan?
options: A respiratory alkalosis from medullary stimulation plus an anion-gap metabolic acidosis; tiring means he may lose the respiratory compensation and needs urgent alkalinization and possibly dialysis
A pure metabolic alkalosis, so ammonium chloride is the treatment
A pure respiratory acidosis, because aspirin depresses ventilation first
The anion gap is from methanol only, and fomepizole replaces bicarbonate
Sleepiness is reassurance that the drug is wearing off
correctAnswer: A respiratory alkalosis from medullary stimulation plus an anion-gap metabolic acidosis; tiring means he may lose the respiratory compensation and needs urgent alkalinization and possibly dialysis
explanation: Salicylate directly stimulates breathing, so CO2 falls and pH may look alkalemic, while uncoupling and acids open the anion gap. The alkalemia hides the metabolic acidosis if you only read pH. When he tires, ventilation falls, CO2 rises onto the existing acidosis, and pH crashes. Bicarbonate alkalinizes serum and urine to keep the drug ionized and out of the brain. Ammonium chloride would worsen acidosis. Early aspirin overdose hyperventilates; it does not start as CO2 retention. Fomepizole does not treat salicylate. Sleepiness is CNS toxicity, not recovery.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man from a party where antifreeze was stored has drunken behavior without much ethanol on the breath, an osmolar gap, and later an anion-gap acidosis. Urine shows envelope crystals and calcium is low. A friend who drank windshield fluid is blind with the same gaps and no oxalate crystals.
question: Which alcohol is which, and what blocks alcohol dehydrogenase for both?
options: Ethylene glycol makes oxalate crystals and hypocalcemia; methanol makes formic acid and blindness; fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase for both
Methanol causes oxalate crystals; ethylene glycol causes blindness
Ethanol is the treatment because it speeds formation of the toxic acids
Fomepizole induces alcohol dehydrogenase so the acids are cleared faster
An osmolar gap without acidosis means the ingestion is over and no antidote is needed
correctAnswer: Ethylene glycol makes oxalate crystals and hypocalcemia; methanol makes formic acid and blindness; fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase for both
explanation: Both parent alcohols are osmotically active and not very acidic. Alcohol dehydrogenase makes the toxic acids: oxalic acid from ethylene glycol, which precipitates calcium oxalate and drops calcium, and formic acid from methanol, which injures the optic nerve. Fomepizole blocks that enzyme. Swapping the end-organs is the classic miss. Ethanol can compete for the enzyme but it does not speed safe clearance of the acids; it occupies the enzyme. Fomepizole inhibits, not induces. An early osmolar gap before the gap acidosis is exactly when you block the enzyme, not a reason to watch.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A toddler in an old house has abdominal pain, constipation, a foot drop, and a microcytic anemia. The smear shows basophilic stippling. A lead level is high. A student wants deferoxamine because the anemia looks like iron overload, and another suggests dimercaprol in peanut oil without asking about allergy.
question: Which enzyme step is blocked, and which chelators fit?
options: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase; succimer is oral chelation for children and EDTA is used for more severe disease, while deferoxamine is the iron chelator
Lead blocks globin synthesis only, so a chelator cannot help
Deferoxamine is first-line for lead because both metals are divalent
Basophilic stippling is specific for folate deficiency
Wrist or foot drop means a central cord syrinx, not a neuropathy
correctAnswer: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase; succimer is oral chelation for children and EDTA is used for more severe disease, while deferoxamine is the iron chelator
explanation: Lead blocks heme synthesis at ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, so protoporphyrin builds and stippled red cells appear. The neuropathy is motor, classically wrist or foot drop, with abdominal pain and constipation. Succimer is the oral chelator used in children; calcium EDTA is for higher burdens. Deferoxamine chelates iron, not lead. The anemia is a production problem, not iron overload. Stippling is classic for lead, not the smear of folate deficiency. A syrinx is a central-cord sensory cape, not this systemic picture.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A toddler ate his mother's prenatal tablets. He is vomiting blood, then seems better, then becomes hypotensive with a metabolic acidosis and a high anion gap. The abdominal film shows tablets. A student reaches for N-acetylcysteine because the mother also mentioned headaches.
question: What is the chelator, and why is the quiet phase a trap?
options: Deferoxamine chelates iron; the latent phase can precede shock and liver failure, so improvement does not mean the ingestion is over
Deferoxamine is for lead, and iron is watched unless he seizes
N-acetylcysteine is the specific iron antidote
The quiet hours mean the tablets were not absorbed
Alkalinization of urine is the primary removal strategy for iron
correctAnswer: Deferoxamine chelates iron; the latent phase can precede shock and liver failure, so improvement does not mean the ingestion is over
explanation: Iron is directly corrosive and mitochondrial-toxic. After the first vomiting there is often a lull, then shock, acidosis, and liver injury. Deferoxamine binds iron (the urine turns vin rose). The lull is not clearance. Deferoxamine is not the lead chelator. N-acetylcysteine is for acetaminophen. Visible tablets and a lull still mean a dangerous ingestion. Urinary alkalinization is a salicylate and phenobarbital idea, not how iron is removed.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A young woman has episodes of painful swelling of the bowel and one episode of airway swelling, without hives. Attacks follow dental work. Complement C4 is low between stories you are given, and C1 inhibitor function is low. Epinephrine and antihistamines did little for the last abdominal attack. Her father had the same illness.
question: What is missing, and why do antihistamines fail?
options: C1 inhibitor is low or dysfunctional, so bradykinin accumulates; this is not histamine edema, so antihistamines and steroids miss the mechanism
IgE is elevated and antihistamines are first-line specific therapy
C3 is the deficient protein, and swelling is from infection only
Terminal complement is gone, so she is at risk for Neisseria and the swelling is meningococcemia
ACE inhibitors treat this disease by lowering bradykinin
correctAnswer: C1 inhibitor is low or dysfunctional, so bradykinin accumulates; this is not histamine edema, so antihistamines and steroids miss the mechanism
explanation: C1 inhibitor normally brakes the complement and kallikrein-kinin cascades. Without it, bradykinin increases vascular permeability. There are no hives because histamine is not the mediator, which is why epinephrine and antihistamines disappoint. C4 is consumed and is a screening clue. This is not atopic IgE disease. C3 deficiency presents with pyogenic infection, not hereditary angioedema. Terminal-complement deficiency is Neisseria susceptibility. ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin and can provoke angioedema; they are not the treatment.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 19-year-old has a second episode of meningococcal bacteremia. He recovered from the first. CH50 is very low. Antibody levels to vaccines are normal and he makes pus. A student diagnoses chronic granulomatous disease because the infections are bacterial.
question: Which proteins are missing, and why is CGD unlikely?
options: C5 through C9 form the membrane attack complex; without it Neisseria recur. CGD is a phagocyte oxidative-burst defect and presents with catalase-positive abscesses and fungal disease, not isolated Neisseria
C1 inhibitor deficiency causes recurrent meningococcus
Selective IgA deficiency is the usual cause of recurrent Neisseria sepsis
A low CH50 with normal vaccine antibodies means he cannot make immunoglobulin
Terminal complement deficiency blocks pus formation
correctAnswer: C5 through C9 form the membrane attack complex; without it Neisseria recur. CGD is a phagocyte oxidative-burst defect and presents with catalase-positive abscesses and fungal disease, not isolated Neisseria
explanation: The membrane attack complex lyses Neisseria. Recurrent meningococcus with a dead CH50 and intact antibodies points there. Chronic granulomatous disease fails the oxidative burst, so catalase-positive organisms and fungi cause abscesses and granulomas; a nitroblue tetrazolium or dihydrorhodamine test would be abnormal, and isolated Neisseria is the wrong signature. C1 inhibitor deficiency is angioedema. IgA deficiency is mucosal and transfusion reactions, not this bacteremia. He makes antibody, so the low CH50 is complement consumption or a component deficiency, not agammaglobulinemia. Pus formation is a leukocyte problem, as in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, not MAC loss.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A boy has recurrent abscesses with Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus and a family of maternal uncles with the same history. Dihydrorhodamine testing shows no oxidative burst. Catalase-negative streptococci have been less of a problem. A student prescribes a terminal-complement workup as the only test.
question: What enzyme is missing, and why do catalase-positive organisms win?
options: NADPH oxidase cannot make superoxide; catalase-positive organisms destroy the hydrogen peroxide the host might have borrowed, so they survive inside the phagocyte
Myeloperoxidase deficiency is the usual cause of this severe phenotype
He cannot diapedese, so there is no pus and the burst test is normal
Adenosine deaminase is missing, so only viral infections occur
The burst is intact and the test result was described backward
correctAnswer: NADPH oxidase cannot make superoxide; catalase-positive organisms destroy the hydrogen peroxide the host might have borrowed, so they survive inside the phagocyte
explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease is NADPH oxidase failure, often X-linked. No superoxide is made. Organisms that bring their own catalase degrade whatever peroxide leaks in, so Staph and Aspergillus thrive. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is usually mild. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency has sky-high neutrophils, no pus, and a normal burst. Adenosine deaminase deficiency is a form of SCID with viral and opportunistic disease. The test showed no burst; that is the diagnosis, not a reversed result.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An infant had delayed separation of the umbilical cord and now has a high neutrophil count in the blood with no pus at a skin infection. Wound cultures grow bacteria. A Rebuck skin window shows neutrophils do not arrive. Oxidative burst testing is normal.
question: Which molecule is missing?
options: CD18, the beta-2 integrin, so leukocytes cannot leave the blood
NADPH oxidase, so the burst test should have failed
C5, so he cannot make the membrane attack complex
IgG, so the cord separation is a B-cell problem
Selectin ligands are increased, which traps cells in the tissue
correctAnswer: CD18, the beta-2 integrin, so leukocytes cannot leave the blood
explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 loses CD18. Neutrophils cannot crawl out of vessels, so the blood count is high, tissues have no pus, the cord separates late, and a skin window stays empty. The burst is normal, which excludes chronic granulomatous disease. C5 deficiency does not trap neutrophils in the blood. Immunoglobulin is not the adhesion molecule, and cord separation is the classic adhesion clue. The problem is too little trafficking, not excess selectin.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Infant A has no thymic shadow, low calcium, a conotruncal heart defect, and viral and fungal infections, with low T cells. Infant B has almost no T or B cells, low lymphocytes on the newborn count, and infections with bacteria, viruses, and fungi, and the thymus is small from lack of lymphocytes rather than a field defect. Infant A has no hypocalcemia twin in infant B.
question: Which embryologic field failed in A, and what cell lines failed in B?
options: A failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches; B has a combined lymphocyte precursor defect such as a cytokine-receptor or ADA problem
Both lack only B cells, so immunoglobulins are the whole story
A is Bruton agammaglobulinemia, which includes hypocalcemia
B has a pure neutrophil adhesion defect and a normal lymphocyte count
The heart defect in A is an incidental PDA and the thymus is normal
correctAnswer: A failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches; B has a combined lymphocyte precursor defect such as a cytokine-receptor or ADA problem
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is a third-and-fourth pouch field defect: no thymus, no parathyroids, and conotruncal anomalies such as tetralogy or interrupted arch, so T cells fail and calcium is low. SCID is a combined T and B failure from defects such as the common gamma chain or adenosine deaminase, with low lymphocytes and infections of every class. B-cell-only disease would spare the viral and fungal pattern and the calcium. Bruton disease is boys with absent B cells after maternal IgG wanes, not hypocalcemia. Adhesion deficiency raises the neutrophil count and does not empty the lymphocyte count. The cardiac lesion is part of the field defect, not a coincidence.

references.label: Sadler TW. Langman's Medical Embryology. 15th ed. Wolters Kluwer 2023

scenario: A man with gout and a kidney transplant is started on allopurinol for tophi. He already takes azathioprine. Two weeks later his white count crashes and he has mouth ulcers. The gout pain is better. A student says the cytopenia is from colchicine, which he is not taking, or that allopurinol only affects uric acid and cannot touch a transplant drug.
question: Why did the marrow fail?
options: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine from azathioprine, so the active metabolite soars
Allopurinol induces CYP3A4 and lowers azathioprine levels, so the marrow finding is unrelated
The interaction is with penicillin, not a thiopurine
Tophi mean he needed a higher azathioprine dose, which is why the count fell
Xanthine oxidase inhibition reduces 6-MP effect, so leukopenia means a different drug was stopped
correctAnswer: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine from azathioprine, so the active metabolite soars
explanation: Azathioprine becomes 6-mercaptopurine, and xanthine oxidase helps clear it. Allopurinol blocks that enzyme, the thiopurine level rises, and the marrow dies. This is a classic lethal interaction. Induction of CYP would lower levels, the opposite of marrow failure. The interacting drug is the thiopurine, not penicillin. Raising azathioprine because of tophi would be a second error; the tophi are why allopurinol was added, and the dose of azathioprine must be cut sharply or the drug changed. Blocking xanthine oxidase increases, not reduces, 6-MP effect.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

blueprintTopic: Do not start allopurinol alone in a hot joint
scenario: A man has a red hot first toe. Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are in the joint and the gram stain is negative. A clinician starts allopurinol today and no anti-inflammatory. The next day the toe is worse. He has no azathioprine on his list. Serum uric acid was normal during the attack.
question: Why did the toe flare, and what should have come first?
options: A sudden drop in urate destabilizes crystals; treat the flare with an anti-inflammatory first, and a normal uric acid during an attack does not exclude gout
A normal uric acid rules out gout, so the crystals were artifact
Allopurinol is an anti-inflammatory and should calm the joint within hours
Negative birefringence means pseudogout, so allopurinol is the correct specific drug
Gram-negative stain means antibiotics are unnecessary only if allopurinol is started
correctAnswer: A sudden drop in urate destabilizes crystals; treat the flare with an anti-inflammatory first, and a normal uric acid during an attack does not exclude gout
explanation: Starting urate-lowering therapy during an unprotected flare can mobilize crystals and worsen pain. An NSAID, colchicine, or a steroid covers the flare; allopurinol is prevention, not the acute drug, and if it is started it needs cover. Uric acid often falls during an acute attack, so a normal level does not throw out crystals you already saw. Allopurinol is not an anti-inflammatory. Pseudogout is rhomboid and positively birefringent. A negative gram stain supports a crystal diagnosis only together with the crystals; it is not a reason that allopurinol treats infection.

references.label: FitzGerald JD et al. 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care Res 2020

scenario: An older woman has a swollen knee after a parathyroidectomy left her calcium unstable. Crystals are rhomboid and blue when parallel to the compensator. The joint fluid gram stain is negative and the glucose is normal. She has no podagra. A student calls it gout because the knee is hot.
question: Which crystal, and which associated disease fits the neck surgery?
options: Calcium pyrophosphate; pseudogout tracks with hyperparathyroidism and the birefringence is positive, the opposite of urate
Monosodium urate, because any hot knee in an older adult is gout
Cholesterol crystals from osteoarthritis, which are strongly negatively birefringent needles
Hydroxyapatite, which is easy to see as rhomboids on plain light microscopy
Septic arthritis, because a hot knee with crystals cannot also be infected so the gram stain was enough
correctAnswer: Calcium pyrophosphate; pseudogout tracks with hyperparathyroidism and the birefringence is positive, the opposite of urate
explanation: CPPD crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent (blue when aligned with the compensator). They favor the knee and associate with hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, and age. Urate needles are negatively birefringent and yellow when parallel, and they love the first toe. A hot joint is not specific. Cholesterol crystals are not this birefringence pattern. Hydroxyapatite is not brightly visible on compensated polarized light the way these are. Crystals do not rule out infection; a gram stain and culture still matter, but this vignette's crystal and the parathyroid history are CPPD.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 62-year-old with a prosthetic knee has fever and a joint he cannot move. He has had gout before. A clinician starts colchicine and skips a tap because the last attack looked the same. The skin over the joint is hot and he looks ill. There is no rash of gonorrhea and no recent viral illness.
question: What is the danger of treating this as gout without fluid?
options: A septic joint, including around hardware, destroys cartilage in hours and can look like a crystal flare; fluid for gram stain and culture has to come before assuming crystals
Colchicine covers Staphylococcus, so the tap can wait a week
Prosthetic joints do not get infected after the first month
Fever means the diagnosis is gout, because infection does not cause fever
Gonorrhea is the only organism that infects a knee, and he has no rash so infection is impossible
correctAnswer: A septic joint, including around hardware, destroys cartilage in hours and can look like a crystal flare; fluid for gram stain and culture has to come before assuming crystals
explanation: You cannot tell a septic knee from a crystal flare by history, especially in someone who has had both risks. Cartilage dies quickly and hardware infections need a tap, culture, and often surgery. Colchicine does not treat bacteria. Prostheses remain infected risk forever, not only in the first month. Fever fits infection at least as well as gout. Staphylococcus and streptococci infect native and prosthetic knees; gonorrhea is a cause in younger sexually active patients, not the only organism, and absence of a rash does not clear the joint.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A is 45 with flaccid blisters, a positive Nikolsky sign, and oral erosions. Immunofluorescence shows net-like IgG around keratinocytes. Patient B is 78 with tense blisters, a negative Nikolsky sign, and a linear band of IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. He has no oral lesions. A student uses steroids the same way and says the antibody target is identical.
question: Which proteins were attacked?
options: A is desmoglein inside the epidermis; B is hemidesmosome proteins at the basement membrane
Both are hemidesmosomes, which is why Nikolsky is positive in both
A is a subepidermal split, so the blisters should be tense
B is desmoglein 3, the mucosal pemphigus target
Immunofluorescence that is linear means the antibody is between keratinocytes
correctAnswer: A is desmoglein inside the epidermis; B is hemidesmosome proteins at the basement membrane
explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris antibodies hit desmoglein, the glue between keratinocytes. The split is shallow, blisters are flaccid, the roof shears off (Nikolsky), the mouth is involved, and immunofluorescence is a net around cells. Bullous pemphigoid antibodies hit hemidesmosomes. The split is under the epidermis, blisters are tense, Nikolsky is negative, the mouth is usually spared, and immunofluorescence is a line at the base. The targets are not the same, which is why the exams look different. A positive Nikolsky and flaccid bullae are intraepidermal, not subepidermal. Desmoglein 3 is the pemphigus mucosal antigen, not pemphigoid. A linear band is the basement membrane, not the net of pemphigus.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man has intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the elbows and knees. Skin biopsy immunofluorescence shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. He has chronic bloating. A student calls it herpes simplex because the vesicles are grouped, and another calls it bullous pemphigoid because IgA and IgG are both antibodies.
question: What is the associated gut disease, and why is the immunofluorescence specific?
options: Celiac disease; IgA against epidermal transglutaminase sits in the papillae, and the gut disease is gluten
Herpes simplex, which deposits granular IgA
Bullous pemphigoid, which is granular IgA at the papillae
Dermatitis herpetiformis is IgG around keratinocytes
The gut disease is ulcerative colitis, treated with gluten loading
correctAnswer: Celiac disease; IgA against epidermal transglutaminase sits in the papillae, and the gut disease is gluten
explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin of celiac disease. Granular IgA in the dermal papillae is the finding, and the itch is out of proportion to what you see. Gluten drives it. Herpes simplex is a virus, not an IgA papillary deposit. Pemphigoid is linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. Net-like IgG is pemphigus. Ulcerative colitis is not this rash, and gluten is removed, not loaded.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Newborn A was stuck at the shoulder and keeps the arm adducted, internally rotated, and the elbow extended, with an intact hand. Newborn B was pulled up by the arm and has a clawed hand and, on the same side, a small pupil and a mild ptosis. A student says both are C5-C6 because both followed a delivery.
question: Which roots, and why the pupil?
options: A is upper trunk C5-C6; B is lower trunk C8-T1, and T1 sympathetics to the eye are torn with it
A is C8-T1 because the elbow is extended
B is an isolated oculomotor palsy from birth trauma
Both are radial nerve injuries in the axilla
A Horner syndrome means the upper trunk, because the sympathetics exit at C5
correctAnswer: A is upper trunk C5-C6; B is lower trunk C8-T1, and T1 sympathetics to the eye are torn with it
explanation: Erb palsy is the waiter's-tip posture: loss of shoulder abduction and external rotation and of elbow flexion, from C5-C6, typically shoulder dystocia. Klumpke is the claw hand of the intrinsic muscles, C8-T1, from upward traction, and the T1 white ramus to the cervical sympathetics is why the pupil is small. Same delivery story does not mean the same roots. An extended elbow is weak biceps, an upper trunk sign. The pupil in this setting is a Horner syndrome, not a third-nerve palsy, which would dilate the pupil and paralyze the eye. The radial nerve does not claw the hand or shrink the pupil. Sympathetics for the eye leave the cord around T1, not C5.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A cannot extend the wrist and has sensory loss on the back of the hand after a mid-humerus fracture. Patient B cannot spread the fingers and has numb little finger after an elbow injury. Patient C cannot oppose the thumb and has numb index and middle fingers, worse at night.
question: Which nerves?
options: A radial, B ulnar, C median
A ulnar, B radial, C musculocutaneous
A median, because wrist drop is a median nerve sign
B median, because finger spread is the thenar pad
C ulnar, because night hand pain is the ulnar tunnel
correctAnswer: A radial, B ulnar, C median
explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove and extends the wrist and fingers; a humeral shaft fracture drops the wrist and numbs the dorsal hand. The ulnar nerve supplies interossei, so spread is lost, and it feels the little finger. The median nerve supplies thenar opposition and the palmar thumb-index-middle sensation; night pain is carpal tunnel. Swapping radial and ulnar swaps wrist drop and claw. Wrist drop is not median. Finger spread is dorsal interossei, ulnar, not thenar. Night symptoms in the median digits are carpal tunnel, not the ulnar nerve at Guyon canal.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A teenage boy has a dull thigh pain that is worse at night and gone after ibuprofen. Imaging shows a small cortical nidus with a lot of surrounding bone. He has no fever and a normal white count. A student calls it osteomyelitis because night pain means infection, and another calls it osteosarcoma because he is young.
question: What is the lesion, and why does the NSAID response matter?
options: Osteoid osteoma; the nidus makes prostaglandin, which is why NSAIDs abolish the night pain, and the lesion is small and benign
Osteosarcoma, which is relieved completely by one dose of ibuprofen and has a tiny nidus
Ewing sarcoma, which is a small nidus without an onion-skin reaction as its classic film
Osteomyelitis, because any night pain with a normal white count is infection
Osteochondroma, a cartilage-capped projection that hurts at night and vanishes with NSAIDs
correctAnswer: Osteoid osteoma; the nidus makes prostaglandin, which is why NSAIDs abolish the night pain, and the lesion is small and benign
explanation: Osteoid osteoma is a small benign nidus of osteoid. Prostaglandins drive the night pain, so NSAIDs are dramatically effective, which is the clinical clue. Osteosarcoma is a large destructive metaphyseal mass, not an NSAID-cured nidus. Ewing sarcoma is a diaphyseal small-round-cell tumor with onion-skin periosteum and systemic symptoms. Osteomyelitis has fever, an elevated count or inflammatory markers, and does not vanish with one anti-inflammatory. Osteochondroma is a bony spur with a cartilage cap, usually painless unless the stalk is bumped.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Teen A has a destructive mass at the distal femur metaphysis, a sunburst periosteal reaction, and a Codman triangle. Teen B has a diaphyseal femoral lesion, fever, onion-skin periosteum, and a translocation involving the EWS gene. Both are limping. A student calls both osteomyelitis because teens get bone pain.
question: Which cells, and which one is related to the marrow round-cell family?
options: A is malignant osteoid from osteosarcoma; B is a small round blue cell Ewing tumor
Both make osteoid, and the EWS translocation is the osteosarcoma gene
B is osteoid osteoma because it is in the femur
A is Ewing because sunburst means layers of periosteum
Codman triangle is specific for infection and excludes tumor
correctAnswer: A is malignant osteoid from osteosarcoma; B is a small round blue cell Ewing tumor
explanation: Osteosarcoma is a metaphyseal tumor of teenagers that makes osteoid, lifts periosteum into a Codman triangle, and throws a sunburst of bone. Ewing sarcoma is a diaphyseal neuroectodermal small round cell tumor, t(11;22) EWS-FLI1, with onion-skin periosteum and fever that mimics osteomyelitis. They are not the same gene or the same matrix. Location in the femur does not make Ewing an osteoid osteoma. Sunburst is osteosarcoma; onion skin is Ewing. A Codman triangle is periosteum lifted by tumor or sometimes infection, not a finding that clears a mass of being cancer.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 28-year-old woman has knee pain. The film shows a lytic lesion reaching the epiphysis of the distal femur, abutting the joint, with a soap-bubble look. She is skeletally mature. A student calls it osteosarcoma because it is near the knee, and another calls it a unicameral bone cyst because it is lucent.
question: Where must this tumor be, and why is age a clue?
options: Giant cell tumor sits in the epiphysis of a closed-growth-plate adult; osteosarcoma prefers the metaphysis of a teenager
Giant cell tumor is diaphyseal in children with open plates
A soap-bubble epiphyseal lesion is an osteoid osteoma nidus
Unicameral cysts reach the articular surface in 30-year-olds
Epiphyseal location means Ewing sarcoma
correctAnswer: Giant cell tumor sits in the epiphysis of a closed-growth-plate adult; osteosarcoma prefers the metaphysis of a teenager
explanation: Giant cell tumor of bone is the epiphyseal lucent lesion of young adults after the plate closes, often around the knee. The 'soap bubble' is the description. Osteosarcoma is metaphyseal and makes bone in adolescents. An osteoid osteoma is a tiny cortical nidus, not a bubbly epiphyseal mass. Simple cysts are metaphyseal in children and do not cross to the joint like this. Ewing is diaphyseal.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 16-year-old has a hard painless bump on the distal femur that points away from the knee. The cap is cartilage and is continuous with the marrow cavity. It has not grown since he stopped growing. A student wants a radical resection because every cartilage cap is a chondrosarcoma.
question: What is the lesion, and when does the cap become worrying?
options: It is an osteochondroma, a benign growth-plate cartilage rest; a thick or growing cap after skeletal maturity raises concern for chondrosarcoma
Any cartilage cap is chondrosarcoma at diagnosis
Continuity with the marrow means osteosarcoma
Painful night nidus is the usual presentation
The lesion points toward the joint if it is benign
correctAnswer: It is an osteochondroma, a benign growth-plate cartilage rest; a thick or growing cap after skeletal maturity raises concern for chondrosarcoma
explanation: Osteochondroma is a bony spur capped by cartilage, continuous with the medullary canal, aimed away from the joint, and it stops growing when the plate closes. Malignant change is uncommon and is suspected if the cap thickens or growth continues in an adult, not because cartilage is present at all. Marrow continuity is the benign osteochondroma feature, not osteosarcoma. Night pain relieved by NSAIDs is osteoid osteoma. Benign osteochondromas point away from the physis/joint.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child with sickle cell disease has a swollen, tender femur and fever. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that produces hydrogen sulfide. He has had prior pain crises. A student treats this as a vaso-occlusive crisis only, because fever can occur in crisis, and names Staphylococcus as the only bone organism in sickle cell disease.
question: Which organism is classic here, and why is 'just a crisis' unsafe?
options: Salmonella; infarcted gut and bone in sickle cell disease make Salmonella osteomyelitis the classic gram-negative, and fever plus focal bone findings need more than fluids
Staphylococcus is the only organism, so a gram-negative rod is a contaminant
Pseudomonas from a nail through a sneaker, which is this patient's exposure
Crisis fluid alone treats bacterial osteomyelitis
Hydrogen sulfide production is the lab signature of Streptococcus
correctAnswer: Salmonella; infarcted gut and bone in sickle cell disease make Salmonella osteomyelitis the classic gram-negative, and fever plus focal bone findings need more than fluids
explanation: Most osteomyelitis is still Staphylococcus, but sickle cell disease is the exception people are tested on: Salmonella. Functional asplenia and infarcted bone are the setup. A focal hot bone with fever is not written off as a pain crisis. A gram-negative rod that makes H2S is Salmonella, not a contaminant you ignore. Pseudomonas is the sneaker puncture, which is not the history. Fluids do not treat osteomyelitis. Streptococcus does not give the H2S Salmonella signature.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A young man has a tibial fracture in a cast. Pain is severe and worse when the toes are stretched. The foot is pale only late. Pulses are still present. A student says pulses must be lost before you open the compartments, and offers more opioid instead.
question: What is dying, and why are pulses the wrong trigger?
options: Muscle and nerve inside a closed compartment are ischemic at pressures well below arterial pressure, so pulses can remain; pain on passive stretch is the sign to open the cast and the fascia
Absent pulses are required before fasciotomy
Pain relieved by a reasonable opioid dose excludes compartment syndrome
The artery is blocked, which is why pulses stay normal
Stretching the toes should relieve ischemic muscle pain
correctAnswer: Muscle and nerve inside a closed compartment are ischemic at pressures well below arterial pressure, so pulses can remain; pain on passive stretch is the sign to open the cast and the fascia
explanation: Compartment pressure can collapse capillaries and kill muscle while arterial pulses persist, because arterial pressure is higher than the compartment. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch come first; pulselessness is late. Waiting for a lost pulse waits too long. Opioids that do not touch the pain are a clue, not a treatment. Pulses are present precisely because the artery is not yet occluded. Passive stretch hurts; it does not relieve the ischemia.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man fell on an outstretched hand and has pain in the anatomic snuffbox. Initial radiographs are normal. He is told it is a sprain and not immobilized. Two months later the proximal pole of the scaphoid is sclerotic.
question: Why did the proximal pole die?
options: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a waist fracture isolates the proximal pole
The distal pole is the one that necroses because blood enters proximally
A normal first film excludes a scaphoid fracture
Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid is from a radial artery laceration only
Snuffbox pain is the lunate, which has a rich dual supply that never necroses
correctAnswer: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a waist fracture isolates the proximal pole
explanation: Radial artery branches enter the scaphoid from the distal end. A fracture through the waist cuts the proximal fragment off its blood, and avascular necrosis follows. The distal pole is the side that still has vessels. Early films miss scaphoid fractures, which is why snuffbox tenderness is immobilized even when the x-ray is normal. The mechanism is intraosseous retrograde flow, not only a cut artery in the open wound. The lunate can necrose (Kienbock) but snuffbox tenderness is the scaphoid, and the lunate is not immune.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child falls off a swing and has a swollen elbow. The hand is pale and the radial pulse is weak. He cannot flex the index finger well when asked to make the OK sign, and sensation is reduced on the palmar index finger. A student says the ulnar nerve is the one at risk because the elbow is the ulnar groove.
question: Which artery and nerve are in danger?
options: The brachial artery and the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, in a supracondylar humerus fracture
The ulnar nerve and the ulnar artery, because all elbow injuries hit the cubital tunnel
The radial nerve in the spiral groove, which flexes the index finger
The axillary nerve, which supplies the OK sign
A weak pulse is normal after any pediatric elbow sprain and needs no reduction
correctAnswer: The brachial artery and the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, in a supracondylar humerus fracture
explanation: Supracondylar fractures displace the distal fragment and stretch the brachial artery and the median nerve where they cross the elbow. The anterior interosseous nerve is motor to flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index, so the OK sign fails, often without a dramatic sensory loss, though palmar sensation can suffer if the main median nerve is involved. The ulnar nerve is the risk at the medial epicondyle and the cubital tunnel, not the classic supracondylar vascular injury. The radial nerve extends the wrist; it does not flex the index tip. The axillary nerve is shoulder abduction and the lateral shoulder patch. A weak pulse with pallor is ischemia until the fracture is reduced.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Boy A is 13, overweight, and has a weeks-long limp with the hip held in external rotation. The ice-cream scoop of the femoral head has slipped off the neck. Boy B is 6, thinner, and has a painless limp with a flattened femoral head. A student orders the same immediate pinning story for both and calls both infection.
question: Which child has a slip that can threaten the blood supply if missed, and which has osteonecrosis of the epiphysis as the disease itself?
options: A is slipped capital femoral epiphysis and needs urgent stabilization; B is Legg-Calve-Perthes, idiopathic osteonecrosis in a younger child
Both are septic hips and need drainage tonight
B is the SCFE because he is younger
A can bear weight so the slip is stable and follow-up in six months is fine
