Perthes disease is a slipped epiphysis on the x-ray
correctAnswer: A is slipped capital femoral epiphysis and needs urgent stabilization; B is Legg-Calve-Perthes, idiopathic osteonecrosis in a younger child
explanation: SCFE is an adolescent, often heavy, whose proximal femoral epiphysis slides. Even a stable-seeming slip is pinned so it does not go on and so osteonecrosis is limited. Perthes is younger children, the head itself necroses and flattens, and the treatment is containment, not the same emergency pin. Infection is a different acute picture. Age runs the other way: SCFE is the teenager. Delayed follow-up of a slip risks further displacement. The Perthes film is a collapsed head, not a slip off the neck.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Woman A is 72, has a vertebral compression fracture, normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal PTH, and a low DEXA T-score. Woman B has bone pain, low vitamin D, low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH, and Looser zones. A student says both have weak bone so both get the same vitamin D lecture and neither has a mineralization problem.
question: Which matrix is normal, and which is unmineralized?
options: A has normally mineralized bone that is simply less of it; B has osteoid that never mineralized because vitamin D and mineral were short
Both have unmineralized osteoid
A has osteomalacia because the T-score is low
B has osteoporosis because calcium is low
PTH is low in vitamin D deficiency
correctAnswer: A has normally mineralized bone that is simply less of it; B has osteoid that never mineralized because vitamin D and mineral were short
explanation: Osteoporosis is less bone of normal composition, so calcium and phosphate labs are normal and the T-score is low; fractures are vertebral and hip. Osteomalacia is soft bone: vitamin D deficiency drops calcium and phosphate, PTH rises, and osteoid does not mineralize, with Looser zones. They are not the same lecture. A low T-score without mineral abnormalities is osteoporosis, not osteomalacia. Low calcium is the osteomalacia direction, not the definition of osteoporosis. Vitamin D deficiency raises PTH; it does not suppress it.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An older man has a large skull, hearing loss, and a warm bowed tibia. Calcium is normal. Alkaline phosphatase is very high and the other liver enzymes are normal. A student calls it prostate cancer because ALP can rise in bone metastases, and he wants a PSA only.
question: What is the bone doing, and which later tumor is the rare fear?
options: Chaotic osteoclast then osteoblast activity makes woven bone and a huge ALP; osteosarcoma is the rare late tumor, and isolated ALP with this shape is Paget disease
Paget disease lowers ALP because bone is quiet
Hearing loss means the cranial nerves are compressed by a meningioma as the usual Paget story is false
Normal calcium excludes Paget disease
Prostate metastases bow one tibia and spare the calcium while isolating ALP from the rest of the liver panel as their classic first sign
correctAnswer: Chaotic osteoclast then osteoblast activity makes woven bone and a huge ALP; osteosarcoma is the rare late tumor, and isolated ALP with this shape is Paget disease
explanation: Paget disease is disordered resorption and formation. The bone is vascular and mosaic, ALP from osteoblasts is high, and calcium stays normal unless the patient is immobilized. Skull enlargement compresses cranial nerve VIII. A late risk is osteosarcoma in pagetic bone. ALP is high, not low. The hearing loss is foraminal crowding from bone, which is part of the disease. Normal calcium is expected. Prostate cancer can raise ALP when it is in bone, but the enlarged skull and bowed warm tibia are the Paget pattern, not a reason to stop at PSA.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman on alendronate for osteoporosis is told to take it upright with water and to wait before breakfast. She has severe reflux. After years of IV zoledronic acid for a different indication she develops exposed jaw bone after an extraction, and a classmate has an atypical femoral fracture. A student says these drugs build a lot of normal new bone and can be taken lying down.
question: How do they work, and why the instructions?
options: They bind hydroxyapatite and kill osteoclasts, so turnover falls; esophageal irritation is why she stays upright, and long use rarely causes osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical fractures because bone becomes too quiet
Bisphosphonates activate osteoclasts, which is why the jaw dies
They can be swallowed lying down because they are not acidic to the esophagus
Atypical femoral fractures mean the dose is too low
Osteonecrosis of the jaw is the expected effect of a two-week course
correctAnswer: They bind hydroxyapatite and kill osteoclasts, so turnover falls; esophageal irritation is why she stays upright, and long use rarely causes osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical fractures because bone becomes too quiet
explanation: Bisphosphonates stop osteoclasts. Bone density rises because resorption falls, not because a burst of healthy formation occurs. The pill can ulcerate the esophagus, so she stays up and takes it on an empty stomach. Years of potent drug, especially IV, plus a dental extraction, is the jaw osteonecrosis setting. Suppressed turnover is also why an atypical femur fracture, a stress fracture of too-quiet bone, occurs. They do not activate osteoclasts. Lying down is exactly the wrong instruction. An atypical fracture is over-suppression, not under-dosing. Jaw osteonecrosis is rare and late, not a two-week effect.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A woman cannot take a bisphosphonate. One option is a RANKL antibody. Another is a daily PTH analog. She has a history of skeletal radiation. A student says both drugs are anabolic and both are safe after radiation, and that stopping the antibody has no rebound.
question: Which drug builds bone by a pulse of PTH, and which risk fits the antibody?
options: Teriparatide is intermittent PTH and is anabolic, and it is avoided after skeletal radiation or Paget disease because of osteosarcoma concern; denosumab blocks RANKL, and stopping it can rebound fractures
Denosumab is a PTH analog
Teriparatide blocks RANKL
Both may be used freely after radiation to bone
Continuous high PTH and once-daily teriparatide have the same anabolic effect
correctAnswer: Teriparatide is intermittent PTH and is anabolic, and it is avoided after skeletal radiation or Paget disease because of osteosarcoma concern; denosumab blocks RANKL, and stopping it can rebound fractures
explanation: A daily pulse of PTH analog favors osteoblasts. Continuous PTH, as in hyperparathyroidism, favors resorption. That is why teriparatide is anabolic and why it is not the same as a high PTH disease. It carries a rodent osteosarcoma signal, so radiation and Paget disease are avoidance settings. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL, so osteoclasts are not activated. It is antiresorptive. When it is stopped, turnover rebounds and vertebral fractures can follow, so it is not a drug you halt without a plan. Calling both anabolic and both radiation-safe swaps them.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 74-year-old woman cannot lift her shoulders because of pain and stiffness in the morning. Strength testing once she is past the pain is actually normal. CK is normal and ESR is 90. She has a new headache. A student diagnoses polymyositis and orders a muscle biopsy first, and skips the headache.
question: What is the disease pair, and why is the biopsy the wrong first move?
options: Polymyalgia rheumatica with possible giant-cell arteritis; the muscle is not necrotic so CK is normal, and the headache needs steroids promptly to protect vision rather than a wait for biopsy of muscle
Polymyositis, because shoulder pain means inflamed muscle and CK should be ignored
Statin myopathy, because the ESR is high
A normal CK excludes vasculitis
Giant-cell arteritis is a disease of people under 50
correctAnswer: Polymyalgia rheumatica with possible giant-cell arteritis; the muscle is not necrotic so CK is normal, and the headache needs steroids promptly to protect vision rather than a wait for biopsy of muscle
explanation: Polymyalgia is pain and stiffness of shoulders and hips in an older adult, with a high ESR and a normal CK, because the muscle itself is not the inflamed tissue. Giant-cell arteritis travels with it. A new headache is a vision-threatening arteritis until proven otherwise, and steroids are not delayed for a muscle biopsy. Polymyositis has true weakness and a high CK. Statin myopathy raises CK and does not raise the ESR into this range as its signature. A normal CK is expected in vasculitis of this type and does not clear the temporal artery. Giant-cell arteritis is a disease of older adults.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 24-year-old man has low back pain that is worse in the morning, better with movement, and wakes him in the second half of the night. Chest expansion is reduced. He had a red eye last year. A student calls it a herniated disc because he is young, and orders bed rest.
question: Which HLA and which spinal finding fit, and why is rest wrong?
options: HLA-B27; the entheses and sacroiliac joints are inflamed, and activity helps, whereas a disc is worse with sitting and flexion and is not a systemic eye disease
HLA-DR4, the rheumatoid association, as the cause of sacroiliitis
Rest is the treatment of inflammatory back pain
Anterior uveitis means infection, so the back pain is septic
Reduced chest expansion is asthma, unrelated to the spine
correctAnswer: HLA-B27; the entheses and sacroiliac joints are inflamed, and activity helps, whereas a disc is worse with sitting and flexion and is not a systemic eye disease
explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is an HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis. Inflammation is at entheses and the sacroiliac joints, morning stiffness improves with use, and anterior uveitis is the eye clue. Costovertebral fusion limits chest expansion. A disc herniation is mechanical, worse with flexion and sitting, and has no uveitis. HLA-DR4 is rheumatoid arthritis, a peripheral synovial disease. Bed rest stiffens inflammatory back pain further. One red eye in this pattern is uveitis, not a reason to call the spine septic. The chest finding is thoracic spine and rib joint fusion.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A has morning stiffness for two hours, boggy MCP and PIP joints, and spares the DIPs. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are positive. Patient B is 70, has DIP Heberden nodes, a short-lived morning ache, and a knee that hurts with walking. A student says both are wear-and-tear and both should have a positive anti-CCP.
question: Which joint and which antibody separate them?
options: A is synovial pannus of rheumatoid arthritis, MCP and PIP, anti-CCP specific; B is cartilage loss of osteoarthritis at DIPs and the knee, antibody negative
Osteoarthritis hits the MCP joints and lasts all morning
Anti-CCP is the osteoarthritis screening test
Rheumatoid arthritis prefers the DIP joints
Heberden nodes are rheumatoid nodules
correctAnswer: A is synovial pannus of rheumatoid arthritis, MCP and PIP, anti-CCP specific; B is cartilage loss of osteoarthritis at DIPs and the knee, antibody negative
explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune synovitis. Pannus invades cartilage, morning stiffness is prolonged, MCPs and PIPs are involved, DIPs are spared, and anti-CCP is specific. Osteoarthritis is mechanical cartilage failure: DIPs, PIPs, first CMC, knees, and hips, with brief stiffness and bony nodes, and no anti-CCP. Wear-and-tear does not explain an hour of stiffness and boggy MCPs. Anti-CCP is not an OA test. DIPs are the OA joint, not the rheumatoid one. Heberden nodes are osteophytes, not rheumatoid nodules.

references.label: Fraenkel L et al. 2021 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis. Arthritis Care Res 2021

scenario: A fellow remembers 'yellow when parallel' but swaps the crystal. Under the compensator, needles parallel to the axis are yellow and perpendicular needles are blue. The patient has podagra. Another slide of rhomboids from a knee turns blue when parallel.
question: Which crystal is yellow when parallel?
options: Monosodium urate is negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel; calcium pyrophosphate is the blue-when-parallel rhomboid
Calcium pyrophosphate is yellow when parallel
Both crystals are yellow when parallel and the shape does not matter
Urate is positively birefringent
The color depends on the gram stain, not the compensator
correctAnswer: Monosodium urate is negatively birefringent, yellow when parallel; calcium pyrophosphate is the blue-when-parallel rhomboid
explanation: Negative birefringence means the crystal is yellow when its long axis is parallel to the compensator. That is urate, and the shape is a needle, and the toe is the joint. CPPD is positive, blue when parallel, and rhomboid, usually the knee. Swapping the color swaps the disease. Shape and color both matter. Urate is the negatively birefringent one. The compensator, not the gram stain, assigns the color.

references.label: FitzGerald JD et al. 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care Res 2020

scenario: A child has fractures of brittle marble bone, cranial nerve crowding, and a low blood count. The marrow cavity is filled with unresorbed primary spongiosa. Carbonic anhydrase II is mentioned. A student says osteoclasts are overactive because the bones are dense.
question: What failed, and why is the marrow crowded?
options: Osteoclasts cannot acidify the resorption pit without carbonic anhydrase II, so bone is not carved out and the marrow has no room
Osteoblasts have failed, so bone is thin
The disease is osteoporosis, which also fills the marrow with bone
Cranial nerves are spared because the foramina widen
Dense bone means resorption is increased
correctAnswer: Osteoclasts cannot acidify the resorption pit without carbonic anhydrase II, so bone is not carved out and the marrow has no room
explanation: Osteoclasts need acid to dissolve hydroxyapatite. Carbonic anhydrase II supplies the protons. Without it, bone is made and not removed, foramina narrow, nerves are compressed, and the marrow cavity never opens, so pancytopenia follows. Osteoblasts are working; that is why bone accumulates. Osteoporosis is too little bone. Foramina get smaller, not larger. Density here is failed resorption, not extra resorption.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has short limbs, a normal trunk, and a large head with frontal bossing. A parent has the same proportions. Intelligence is normal. The growth-plate cartilage fails to proliferate. A student calls it cretinism because both can be short, and another calls it osteogenesis imperfecta because the limbs are short.
question: Which receptor is constitutively active?
options: FGFR3, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, is overactive; this is not a thyroid or collagen-brittle-bone disease
A mutated collagen I gene, which causes blue sclerae and fractures as the main picture
FGFR3 loss of function, which would lengthen the limbs
Thyroid hormone receptor blockade, with delayed bone age as the only growth-plate lesion
The trunk is short and the limbs are normal
correctAnswer: FGFR3, which inhibits chondrocyte proliferation, is overactive; this is not a thyroid or collagen-brittle-bone disease
explanation: Achondroplasia is activating FGFR3. The receptor's normal job is to slow the growth plate, so a receptor stuck on makes short limbs (rhizomelic) with a relatively normal trunk and a large head. It is autosomal dominant. Cretinism is hypothyroidism, with delayed bones and a different body proportion and developmental delay. Osteogenesis imperfecta is collagen I, fractures, and blue sclerae, not this proportion with normal intelligence as the lead. Loss of FGFR3 would not suppress the plate. The limbs are the short part.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A toddler is yanked by the hand, then will not use the arm, and holds it slightly flexed and pronated. There is no swelling and radiographs are normal. A student orders an MRI for a supracondylar fracture because the child will not move the elbow.
question: What slipped, and what is the maneuver?
options: The radial head slipped out of the annular ligament; supination and flexion reduce it
The ulnar nerve dislocated and needs surgical transposition
This is a scaphoid fracture, so a cast for two weeks without reduction is enough
The distal humerus is displaced and the pulse must be checked as the only lesion
Pronation is the reduction maneuver that seats the radial head
correctAnswer: The radial head slipped out of the annular ligament; supination and flexion reduce it
explanation: Nursemaid's elbow is subluxation of the radial head from the annular ligament after longitudinal traction. The child refuses the arm, films are normal, and reduction is supination with flexion. The ulnar nerve is not out of its groove. A scaphoid fracture is a fall on the hand in an older child or adult, with snuffbox pain. A supracondylar fracture swells and threatens the pulse; a normal film and a traction history are the radial head. The reduction supinates; pronation is not the seating maneuver.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 60-year-old cannot start abduction of the shoulder and has pain at night. When the arm is passively lifted past 30 degrees he can hold it up using the deltoid. Drop-arm test is positive. A student says the deltoid is torn because abduction is weak, and another says the subscapularis because that is the supraspinatus neighbor.
question: Which tendon starts abduction?
options: Supraspinatus starts the first degrees of abduction; deltoid takes over after, so a cuff tear shows up when initiation fails
Deltoid initiates abduction and supraspinatus only lifts past 90 degrees
Subscapularis abducts the shoulder
Biceps long head is the only abductor
A positive drop-arm test means the axillary nerve is out and the cuff is intact
correctAnswer: Supraspinatus starts the first degrees of abduction; deltoid takes over after, so a cuff tear shows up when initiation fails
explanation: Supraspinatus seats the humeral head and starts abduction. Past about 15 degrees the deltoid can continue, which is why passive assistance lets him hold the arm up and why he cannot begin the motion himself. Night pain and a drop when he lowers the arm are the cuff. The deltoid is working if he can hold the arm once it is up. Subscapularis internally rotates. The long head of biceps is a humeral-head depressor, not the abductor you are testing. Drop-arm is the cuff, not an isolated axillary nerve lesion, which would atrophy the deltoid and numb the lateral shoulder.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A soccer player is clipped from the lateral side. The knee opens medially, the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive, and the joint locks. A student says the lateral collateral ligament is the one that opens with a valgus force, and that a positive Lachman is the posterior cruciate.
question: Which three structures?
options: Medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and anterior cruciate ligament
Lateral collateral, lateral meniscus, and posterior cruciate
Anterior cruciate only, because Lachman ignores the collateral ligaments
Posterior cruciate, because the tibia slides backward on a positive anterior drawer
Medial collateral alone, because locking means a bone bruise and not a meniscus
correctAnswer: Medial collateral ligament, medial meniscus, and anterior cruciate ligament
explanation: A lateral blow is a valgus force. It opens the medial side, tearing the medial collateral ligament, and can continue through the medial meniscus and the ACL. That is the unhappy triad. Lachman and anterior drawer pull the tibia forward, which is the ACL, not the PCL. The lateral collateral resists varus. A positive Lachman is not a collateral test, but the valgus opening is. Anterior drawer is forward, not backward. Locking and joint-line pain are the meniscus, not a bruise you can ignore.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has had several fractures with minimal force, blue sclerae, and hearing loss starting to appear. A parent was investigated for abuse. Teeth are imperfect. The collagen is type I. A student says the blue sclerae are from Ehlers-Danlos type collagen III and that child abuse is still the only explanation because the genes cannot break bone.
question: Which collagen, and why is abuse the differential rather than the only answer?
options: Type I collagen is defective, so bone is brittle and sclerae are thin and blue; abuse must be considered but the systemic findings point to osteogenesis imperfecta
Type III collagen, which causes hollow organs to rupture as the bone disease
Type II collagen, the cartilage collagen of Stickler syndrome only
Blue sclerae are diagnostic of copper deficiency
Fractures with a genetic disease exclude any need to think about abuse
correctAnswer: Type I collagen is defective, so bone is brittle and sclerae are thin and blue; abuse must be considered but the systemic findings point to osteogenesis imperfecta
explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen disease. Bone matrix is weak, sclerae show the choroid through thin collagen, teeth and hearing can fail. Multiple fractures raise abuse, and abuse is still considered, but blue sclerae, family pattern, and dental findings are the disease. Type III collagen is vascular Ehlers-Danlos, hollow-organ rupture. Type II is cartilage. Blue sclerae are not the copper-deficiency sign (that is Menkes kinky hair and vascular tortuosity). A genetic brittle-bone disease does not mean you never consider trauma; it means you do not stop there.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A young man has translucent skin, easy bruising, and a ruptured colon during a minor illness. Hypermobile joints are present but the emergency is the vessel and the bowel. A student says this is the same type I collagen disease as brittle bones.
question: Which collagen failed?
options: Type III collagen in vessels and hollow organs
Type I collagen, so the next finding should be blue sclerae and a femoral fracture as the lead
Type IV collagen, so the glomerulus is the organ that ruptured
Fibrillin, so the lens should dislocate upward as the required companion
Type II collagen, so the annulus of the disc is the only tissue at risk
correctAnswer: Type III collagen in vessels and hollow organs
explanation: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos is type III collagen. Arteries and the bowel rupture, skin is thin, and bruising is easy. Classic hypermobile forms are other collagen types and are not the rupture disease. Type I is bone and sclera. Type IV is basement membrane, Goodpasture and Alport, not a colonic perforation. Fibrillin is Marfan syndrome. Type II is cartilage.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

blueprintTopic: Gout negative birefringence trap already used
scenario: A patient with recurrent gout and uric acid kidney stones is choosing a prevention drug. He under-excretes uric acid and his GFR is normal. He wants a drug that increases uric acid excretion. He has no history of overproduction from tumor lysis. A student offers probenecid and also offers it to a different patient whose GFR is 20 mL/min and who already makes stones.
question: Who can use a uricosuric, and who should not?
options: Probenecid blocks proximal reabsorption of urate and can help an under-excretor with a normal kidney and no stones; it is a poor choice when GFR is low or when stones are already forming, where allopurinol lowers production
Probenecid is safe in uric acid stone formers because it dissolves stones by raising urine urate
Allopurinol increases uric acid excretion
A GFR of 20 is the best setting for probenecid
Under-excretors should receive rasburicase as daily oral therapy
correctAnswer: Probenecid blocks proximal reabsorption of urate and can help an under-excretor with a normal kidney and no stones; it is a poor choice when GFR is low or when stones are already forming, where allopurinol lowers production
explanation: Probenecid inhibits URAT1, so less urate is reabsorbed and more appears in the urine. That helps someone who under-excretes, if the kidney works and the urine will not be flooded into new stones. Stones and a low GFR are reasons to use a xanthine oxidase inhibitor instead. Raising urine urate does not treat existing stones; it can make them. Allopurinol decreases production, it does not increase excretion. Probenecid needs a working tubule, so GFR 20 is the wrong patient. Rasburicase is an IV recombinant uricase for tumor lysis, not a daily gout pill.

references.label: FitzGerald JD et al. 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care Res 2020

scenario: A man takes colchicine for an acute gout flare and develops profuse diarrhea. The joint is improving. He asks how a drug that does not lower uric acid can help, and whether the diarrhea means he should double the dose. He is also on a strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitor.
question: What does colchicine bind, and why is the inhibitor dangerous?
options: It binds tubulin and blocks neutrophil migration; diarrhea is toxicity, and a strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitor raises the level enough to cause marrow and muscle failure
It inhibits xanthine oxidase, so diarrhea means uric acid is falling correctly
Doubling the dose is the way to treat the diarrhea
Colchicine is safe with any CYP inhibitor because it is renally inert
Neutrophils use microtubules only for antibody production, which is irrelevant to the joint
correctAnswer: It binds tubulin and blocks neutrophil migration; diarrhea is toxicity, and a strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitor raises the level enough to cause marrow and muscle failure
explanation: Colchicine caps microtubules. Neutrophils cannot crawl into the joint, which is the anti-inflammatory effect, and it does not change the uric acid pool. The gut lining also depends on microtubules, so diarrhea is a dose-limiting toxicity, not a sign of success to chase with more drug. Clearance depends on CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein; inhibitors such as clarithromycin can cause fatal marrow suppression and rhabdomyolysis. It is not a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. The dose is reduced or stopped when diarrhea starts, not doubled.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A woman has proximal weakness, a heliotrope rash on the eyelids, and scaly red papules on the knuckles. CK is high. She is 58 and has not had a cancer screen. A student calls it eczema of the hands and age-related weakness, and skips the malignancy question. A biopsy pattern discussed is perimysial inflammation.
question: What are the knuckle lesions, and why does age matter?
options: Gottron papules with a heliotrope rash are dermatomyositis; in adults it is associated with malignancy, and the inflammation is perimysial and perifascicular, unlike endomysial polymyositis
These rashes are psoriasis, and CK is high from a statin she is not taking
Polymyositis has the heliotrope rash and no cancer link
Perimysial inflammation is the polymyositis pattern
Adult dermatomyositis does not change cancer screening
correctAnswer: Gottron papules with a heliotrope rash are dermatomyositis; in adults it is associated with malignancy, and the inflammation is perimysial and perifascicular, unlike endomysial polymyositis
explanation: Gottron papules are the knuckle rash of dermatomyositis, and the violaceous eyelids are heliotrope. Proximal weakness and a high CK complete it. Adults with dermatomyositis have an increased rate of underlying cancer, so the age is a reason to look, not to call it eczema. Psoriasis does not raise CK or weaken the shoulders in this pattern. Polymyositis lacks the rash. The perimysial, perifascicular atrophy pattern is dermatomyositis; endomysial inflammation is polymyositis. Skipping screening misses the association.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: After a cardiac arrest a man can move his face and hands poorly but the arms and legs nearer the trunk are weaker in a band, and he is not hemiplegic on one side only. Blood pressure had been unrecordable for several minutes. A student calls it an MCA stem stroke because the hands are weak.
question: Which arterial territory failed?
options: The border zones between ACA, MCA, and PCA, which are the last fields perfused when pressure collapses
A single lenticulostriate lacune, which weakens the proximal arm only
The anterior spinal artery, because trunk weakness means the cord
Both MCAs, which would spare the shoulder and hip girdle
The basilar artery, because watershed infarcts are brainstem
correctAnswer: The border zones between ACA, MCA, and PCA, which are the last fields perfused when pressure collapses
explanation: When mean pressure falls, the tissue between the major cerebral arteries dies first. The homunculus is hit in the shoulder and hip more than the hand, the classic man-in-a-barrel, after hypotension. An MCA stem stroke is unilateral and hits face and hand hardest. A lacune is a small deep pure-motor lesion, not a bilateral proximal band. The anterior spinal artery is the cord, and the history is a cerebral low-flow event. Bilateral MCA infarction would devastate language and face-hand cortex, not selectively the watershed band. Watershed infarcts from hypotension are hemispheric cortical borders, not the basilar artery.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man with poorly controlled diabetes has a third-nerve palsy with a spared pupil and pain around the eye. He has no headache of sudden onset and no aneurysm risk story beyond age. Glucose is 340 mg/dL. A student sends him for emergency coiling because any third-nerve palsy is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
question: Why is the pupil the deciding sign?
options: Microvascular ischemia hits the central motor fibers and spares the superficial pupil fibers; a compressing aneurysm hits the pupil early
A spared pupil proves an aneurysm because the pupil fibers are deep
Diabetes dilates the pupil first and leaves the eye muscles for later
Coiling is required whenever glucose is high
Pain around the eye means migraine and excludes a nerve palsy
correctAnswer: Microvascular ischemia hits the central motor fibers and spares the superficial pupil fibers; a compressing aneurysm hits the pupil early
explanation: Pupil fibers travel on the outside of the third nerve. Ischemia in a small vessel, as in diabetes, infarcts the core and spares the pupil, so a painless or moderately painful pupil-sparing palsy in a person with diabetes is microvascular until a reason says otherwise. An aneurysm compresses the outside and blows the pupil, especially with a thunderclap headache. This vignette spared the pupil and has marked hyperglycemia, so emergency coiling is the wrong default. Diabetes does not dilate the pupil first. High glucose is the risk for ischemia, not an indication to coil. Pain can occur with microvascular third-nerve palsy and does not by itself mean migraine or exclude the localization.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A man has lightning pains in the legs, wide-based gait, and a slap as the foot hits the ground. Pupils accommodate but do not react to light. Vibration is gone at the toes. RPR is positive. A student calls it B12 deficiency only, because the dorsal columns are involved, and skips the pupil.
question: Which columns, and what is the pupil?
options: Dorsal roots and columns from neurosyphilis, with an Argyll Robertson pupil; B12 can hit the same columns but does not make that pupil
Spinothalamic tracts only, which carry vibration
A midbrain Parinaud lesion, which is the Argyll Robertson pupil
Negative RPR excludes syphilis if the columns are involved
The foot slap is cerebellar, so proprioception is intact
correctAnswer: Dorsal roots and columns from neurosyphilis, with an Argyll Robertson pupil; B12 can hit the same columns but does not make that pupil
explanation: Tabes dorsalis is tertiary syphilis destroying dorsal roots. Proprioception is lost, gait slaps, and pain is lightning-like. The Argyll Robertson pupil accommodates to near but does not react to light. B12 deficiency also hits dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts but does not create that pupil, so stopping at B12 misses the RPR. Vibration is dorsal column, not spinothalamic. Parinaud syndrome is upgaze failure from a pineal mass, not this pupil. A positive RPR is the clue, not a negative one. The slap is sensory ataxia from lost position sense, not a cerebellar hemisphere.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A patient on clozapine has a fever and a sore throat. The absolute neutrophil count is 400. He is not rigid. A student stops the drug for neuroleptic malignant syndrome because any fever on an antipsychotic is that syndrome, and he plans to restart the same dose next week if the fever fades.
question: What monitoring rule was broken?
options: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so fever means hold the drug and do not restart casually; rigidity is what would suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Fever on clozapine is always neuroleptic malignant syndrome even with a soft tone
The neutrophil count is unrelated to clozapine
Restarting at the same dose the next week is safe after agranulocytosis
Agranulocytosis is the haloperidol toxicity, and clozapine is the drug that treats it
correctAnswer: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so fever means hold the drug and do not restart casually; rigidity is what would suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation: Clozapine requires neutrophil monitoring because it can empty the marrow. A fever and a count of 400 is agranulocytosis until proven otherwise, and the drug stays stopped under a registry, not a casual restart. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is rigidity, high CK, and bradyreflexia, which this vignette does not have. The count is the point of the monitoring. Restarting immediately recreates the injury. Clozapine is the antipsychotic that causes this marrow toxicity; it is not the treatment for it.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: Twelve hours after a thunderclap headache, CT is negative and the cerebrospinal fluid is yellow after centrifugation, with a red-cell count that does not fall between tube 1 and tube 4. A student says the yellow color is a traumatic tap because there are red cells.
question: How do you tell a traumatic tap from blood that has been there for hours?
options: Xanthochromia is bilirubin from blood broken down in the CSF, and a stable red-cell count across tubes fits subarachnoid blood; a traumatic tap clears and is not xanthochromic that early
A falling red-cell count from tube 1 to tube 4 proves subarachnoid hemorrhage
Xanthochromia appears within five minutes of a traumatic tap
A negative CT at 12 hours never needs a lumbar puncture
Yellow CSF is only from a high protein of Guillain-Barre
correctAnswer: Xanthochromia is bilirubin from blood broken down in the CSF, and a stable red-cell count across tubes fits subarachnoid blood; a traumatic tap clears and is not xanthochromic that early
explanation: Blood that has sat in the CSF for hours is metabolized to bilirubin, which yellows the supernatant. A traumatic tap introduces fresh blood that clears across successive tubes and has not had time to become xanthochromic. A count that stays high is not the clearing pattern. Xanthochromia is not an instant tap artifact. CT misses some bleeds, which is why the puncture still matters. High protein can yellow the fluid in other diseases, but not with this headache and a persistent red-cell count.

references.label: Hoh BL et al. 2023 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Stroke 2023

scenario: A man with leukemia starts chemotherapy and the uric acid soars. Joints are not yet hot. A student waits for a flare before lowering urate and offers probenecid as the emergency drug. The risk discussed is tumor lysis, not an underexcretor with a normal kidney.
question: Which drug lowers the existing urate load fastest in tumor lysis, and why is probenecid wrong?
options: Rasburicase oxidizes uric acid to allantoin; probenecid only blocks reabsorption and cannot handle a sudden production flood with a threatened kidney
Probenecid is the tumor-lysis drug because it increases excretion
Allopurinol dissolves crystals already formed within an hour
Rasburicase is an oral daily gout preventive
Tumor lysis lowers uric acid, so no drug is needed
correctAnswer: Rasburicase oxidizes uric acid to allantoin; probenecid only blocks reabsorption and cannot handle a sudden production flood with a threatened kidney
explanation: Tumor lysis dumps purines and uric acid can precipitate in the kidney. Rasburicase is a recombinant uricase that converts uric acid to soluble allantoin and is used for that emergency. Probenecid increases urinary urate and is the wrong direction when the kidney is about to be clogged. Allopurinol blocks new formation and does not remove uric acid already present nearly as fast, and it does not melt a joint in an hour. Rasburicase is IV for lysis, not a daily tablet. Uric acid rises in tumor lysis; that is the problem.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: After a pelvic fracture a woman cannot extend the knee and has numb skin on the anterior thigh and medial leg. Hip adduction is intact. A student says the obturator nerve, because the pelvis was injured, and another says the sciatic nerve because the leg feels wrong.
question: Which nerve extends the knee?
options: The femoral nerve, from L2-L4, innervates quadriceps and the saphenous skin; obturator adducts the thigh
The obturator nerve extends the knee
The sciatic nerve is the only knee extensor
The tibial nerve supplies the quadriceps
Medial leg numbness is the sural nerve, which is femoral
correctAnswer: The femoral nerve, from L2-L4, innervates quadriceps and the saphenous skin; obturator adducts the thigh
explanation: Femoral nerve injury loses knee extension and sensation on the anterior thigh and the medial leg via the saphenous nerve. Adduction is obturator and is intact here, so the pelvis injury did not pick the obturator. The sciatic nerve flexes the knee (hamstrings) and moves the foot; it does not extend the knee. The tibial nerve is a sciatic division below the knee. The sural nerve is sensory on the lateral foot, not the medial leg.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man was struck on the lateral knee. He cannot dorsiflex or evert the foot, and the dorsum of the foot is numb. Inversion and plantarflexion are intact. A student diagnoses a tibial nerve injury because the foot is weak.
question: Which nerve, and why is inversion spared?
options: The common peroneal nerve at the fibular head; inversion is tibial (tibialis posterior), so it survives
The tibial nerve, which dorsiflexes the foot
The femoral nerve, which everts the foot
Loss of eversion with spared inversion is a pure tibial lesion
Plantarflexion is peroneal, so it should have been lost
correctAnswer: The common peroneal nerve at the fibular head; inversion is tibial (tibialis posterior), so it survives
explanation: The common peroneal nerve wraps the fibular neck. It dorsiflexes and everts and feels the dorsum of the foot. A foot drop is the result. Tibialis posterior, the inverter, is tibial and deep in the calf, so inversion remains and tells you the tibial nerve is working. The tibial nerve plantarflexes. The femoral nerve does not reach the foot everters. Loss of eversion is peroneal, not tibial. Plantarflexion should be spared in an isolated peroneal injury, which matches the vignette.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 68-year-old has knee pain that is worse with use and better with rest. Morning stiffness lasts ten minutes. The film shows joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophytes. A student expects a positive anti-CCP and prolonged morning stiffness because the knee is damaged.
question: What is the tissue that failed?
options: Articular cartilage, with secondary bony overgrowth; this is osteoarthritis, antibody negative, with brief stiffness
Synovial pannus, which prefers the DIP joints as its first site
Anti-CCP positive disease, because osteophytes are rheumatoid nodules
Crystal disease, because sclerosis means urate
Septic cartilage destruction, because stiffness of ten minutes is inflammatory
correctAnswer: Articular cartilage, with secondary bony overgrowth; this is osteoarthritis, antibody negative, with brief stiffness
explanation: Osteoarthritis is cartilage wear. The bone responds with sclerosis and osteophytes, stiffness is short, and use hurts more than rest. Rheumatoid pannus causes prolonged stiffness and hits MCPs, not a mechanically painful knee with osteophytes as the whole story. Anti-CCP is not positive in ordinary OA, and osteophytes are not nodules. Sclerosis is not urate. Ten minutes of stiffness is mechanical, not the hour-long inflammatory pattern or an infected joint.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A young man had bloody diarrhea two weeks ago. He now has an arthritis of the knee, painful heels, and a rash on the glans. He also has red eyes. HLA-B27 is positive. A student starts antibiotics for the knee as if it were septic only, and calls it rheumatoid arthritis because more than one system is involved.
question: What is the syndrome, and is the joint the infected site?
options: Reactive arthritis after an infection, sterile synovitis with enthesitis and uveitis or circinate balanitis; the knee is not where the bacteria are living
Septic arthritis from ongoing bacteremia, so the diarrhea organism is in the synovial fluid
Rheumatoid arthritis, which follows dysentery and prefers the DIP joints
Gout, because HLA-B27 is the gout gene
Antibiotics for the old diarrhea will reverse the sterile synovitis the same day
correctAnswer: Reactive arthritis after an infection, sterile synovitis with enthesitis and uveitis or circinate balanitis; the knee is not where the bacteria are living
explanation: Reactive arthritis follows Chlamydia or a gut infection by days to weeks. The joint is sterile inflammation, often with Achilles enthesitis, uveitis, and keratoderma or circinate balanitis, and HLA-B27 is enriched. Antibiotics for a septic knee are the wrong model once the fluid is sterile and the cluster is present. Rheumatoid arthritis is not a post-dysentery DIP disease. HLA-B27 is the spondyloarthritis gene, not gout. Treating the resolved diarrhea does not instantly clear the immune synovitis.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A valgus stress opens the knee on the medial side. Varus stress is stable. There is no locking. Lachman is negative. A student diagnoses an ACL tear because the knee opened, and another says the lateral collateral ligament fails under valgus.
question: Which ligament failed?
options: The medial collateral ligament resists valgus; a negative Lachman means the ACL is holding
The lateral collateral ligament resists valgus
The ACL is the only restraint to valgus opening
A negative Lachman confirms an ACL tear
Opening on valgus is the medial meniscus alone
correctAnswer: The medial collateral ligament resists valgus; a negative Lachman means the ACL is holding
explanation: Valgus opens the medial side and tests the MCL. Varus tests the LCL. Lachman tests the ACL and is negative here, so the cruciate is not the structure that opened. The LCL does not resist valgus. The ACL is an anterior restraint, not the collateral that stops side-to-side opening. A negative Lachman is a reassuring ACL exam, not a tear. Isolated opening without locking is the ligament, not a bucket-handle meniscus.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A 6-year-old has fever and refuses to walk. The proximal tibial metaphysis is tender. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. The growth plate is still open. A student says infection starts in the epiphysis because that is where the blood supply ends in adults.
question: Why the metaphysis in a child?
options: Metaphyseal arteries are slow-flow end arteries against the open plate, so bacteria settle there; the plate blocks spread into the joint in many bones
Children seed the diaphysis first, like Ewing sarcoma
An open growth plate lets infection into the joint in every bone, including the knee, as the first rule without exception
Staphylococcus avoids the metaphysis
Adults and children have the same intracapsular metaphysis at the tibia
correctAnswer: Metaphyseal arteries are slow-flow end arteries against the open plate, so bacteria settle there; the plate blocks spread into the joint in many bones
explanation: In children the nutrient artery ends in slow loops at the metaphysis next to the physis, which is a baffle. Staphylococcus seeds those loops. The plate usually stops pus from entering the joint, except where the metaphysis is intracapsular, such as the hip. Diaphysis is the Ewing location, not the typical hematogenous start. The knee's tibial metaphysis is extracapsular, so the hip exception is not the tibial rule. Staphylococcus is exactly the organism that settles there. Adult vascular anatomy across a closed plate is different, and the tibia is not the intracapsular hip.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man of northern European ancestry has a cord in the palm that pulls the ring finger into flexion. He cannot flatten the hand on the table. Sensation is normal and there is no night pain. A student calls it a trigger finger because the finger sticks, and another calls it an ulnar claw from a nerve.
question: What is contracting?
options: The palmar fascia, not a tendon or a nerve; sensation is intact so this is not an ulnar neuropathy
The flexor tendon nodule of trigger finger, which locks and then snaps
An ulnar nerve palsy, which numbs the little finger and weakens spread
A Dupuytren cord is a rheumatoid swan-neck deformity
Normal sensation means the median nerve is the one that is trapped
correctAnswer: The palmar fascia, not a tendon or a nerve; sensation is intact so this is not an ulnar neuropathy
explanation: Dupuytren contracture is myofibroblast thickening of the palmar fascia, often the ring finger, and the table-top test fails. It is not a tendon. Trigger finger snaps and locks from a flexor tendon nodule at the A1 pulley and does not pull the finger down at rest the same way. Ulnar claw comes with sensory loss and weak interossei. Swan-neck is a rheumatoid tendon balance problem, hyperextension of the PIP. Intact sensation argues against a nerve entrapment; the median nerve would numb the radial digits and is not this cord.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A patient is given a long course of a fluoroquinolone and then ruptures an Achilles tendon while stepping off a curb. He is also on a corticosteroid. A student says quinolones only bother cartilage in children and cannot affect an adult tendon.
question: What did the antibiotic do?
options: Fluoroquinolones raise the risk of tendon rupture, especially with steroids and in older adults; the Achilles is the classic tendon
Only children get quinolone toxicity, and it is limited to teeth
Corticosteroids protect tendons from quinolones
The rupture is an expected effect of penicillin, which he was not taking
Tendon rupture from this class occurs only in the first hour of the first dose
correctAnswer: Fluoroquinolones raise the risk of tendon rupture, especially with steroids and in older adults; the Achilles is the classic tendon
explanation: Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendinopathy and rupture, Achilles most often, and the risk climbs with age and corticosteroids. The warning is not limited to growing cartilage in children, which is a separate concern. Steroids add risk; they do not protect. Penicillin is not the tendon drug. Rupture can occur during or months after the course, not only in the first hour.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A football player had a deep thigh bruise. Three weeks later a firm mass is in the muscle and the film shows bone forming at the periphery of the mass, not in the center. A student calls it osteosarcoma because bone is present in muscle and wants an amputation.
question: Why is the zoning the clue that this is benign?
options: Myositis ossificans matures from the outside in after trauma; osteosarcoma is the reverse, with bone more central and a soft periphery
Any bone in muscle is osteosarcoma
Peripheral maturation means a high-grade sarcoma
The mass should be biopsied in the center first because the edge is the most malignant
Trauma cannot trigger bone formation in muscle
correctAnswer: Myositis ossificans matures from the outside in after trauma; osteosarcoma is the reverse, with bone more central and a soft periphery
explanation: After a contusion, heterotopic bone can form in muscle. It ossifies at the periphery first, a zonal pattern that says benign repair. Osteosarcoma is most mature at the center and invasive at the edge. Calling all extra bone a sarcoma leads to a mutilating operation for a process that often settles. Peripheral bone is the reassuring pattern, not the high-grade one. A biopsy of the center of myositis ossificans looks cellular and can be overcalled; the zoning on the film is what saves the diagnosis. Trauma is exactly the trigger.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A runner has burning on the sole and a positive Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus. Ankle dorsiflexion is strong and the dorsum of the foot feels normal. A student diagnoses a peroneal nerve palsy because the foot hurts.
question: Which nerve is trapped?
options: The tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel, which supplies the sole
The deep peroneal nerve, which feels the sole
The sural nerve, behind the lateral malleolus, as the sole's only supply
The femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
Dorsiflexion weakness is required for a tibial lesion
correctAnswer: The tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel, which supplies the sole
explanation: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole. Entrapment burns the plantar skin and Tinel sign is there. Dorsiflexion and dorsal sensation are peroneal and are intact, so this is not a fibular-head lesion. The deep peroneal nerve is the first web space on the dorsum. The sural nerve is lateral foot skin. The femoral nerve does not reach the sole. Tibial lesions weaken plantarflexion and toe flexion, not dorsiflexion.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: An older woman has bony swelling of the DIP joints and the PIP joints, and the first carpometacarpal joint hurts when she opens a jar. MCP joints are normal. Stiffness lasts a few minutes. A student looks for ulnar deviation and anti-CCP.
question: What are the DIP nodes called, and why are the MCPs reassuring?
options: Heberden nodes at the DIP and Bouchard nodes at the PIP are osteoarthritis; MCP disease would suggest an inflammatory arthritis
Ulnar deviation is the osteoarthritis pattern
Anti-CCP should be positive in DIP disease
The first CMC joint is spared in osteoarthritis
Minutes of stiffness mean rheumatoid arthritis
correctAnswer: Heberden nodes at the DIP and Bouchard nodes at the PIP are osteoarthritis; MCP disease would suggest an inflammatory arthritis
explanation: Osteoarthritis nodes are Heberden at the DIP and Bouchard at the PIP, and the base of the thumb is a classic site. MCPs are spared, which is the opposite of rheumatoid arthritis, where MCPs and PIPs dominate and DIPs are spared. Ulnar deviation is a rheumatoid deformity. Anti-CCP belongs to rheumatoid arthritis. The first CMC is involved, not spared. Brief stiffness is mechanical.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man dislocates his shoulder anteriorly. After reduction he cannot abduct the arm in the range the deltoid should cover once it is started, and a patch on the lateral shoulder is numb. Wrist extension is normal. A student says the radial nerve is out because the shoulder was injured.
question: Which nerve, and which muscle?
options: The axillary nerve, from the surgical neck region, supplies deltoid and the lateral shoulder skin; the radial nerve would drop the wrist
The radial nerve, which numbs a nickel-sized lateral shoulder patch
The long thoracic nerve, which abducts the shoulder
The suprascapular nerve, which is the only abductor and has a skin branch to the shoulder badge
Anterior dislocation spares the axillary nerve by definition
correctAnswer: The axillary nerve, from the surgical neck region, supplies deltoid and the lateral shoulder skin; the radial nerve would drop the wrist
explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation and surgical-neck fractures threaten the axillary nerve. Deltoid abduction and the regimental-badge sensation are lost. Wrist extension is radial and is intact, so the radial nerve is not the one injured. The radial sensory patch is the dorsal hand, not the lateral shoulder. The long thoracic nerve protracts and stabilizes the scapula via serratus; winging is its sign. Suprascapular nerve supplies supra- and infraspinatus and has no badge of skin. Anterior dislocation is exactly when the axillary nerve is at risk.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Lesion A is a pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on the upper lip of a fair-skinned man. Lesion B is a crusted ulcer on the ear of a man with a long sun exposure, growing faster, and the biopsy shows keratin pearls. A student calls both melanoma because both are on sun-exposed skin.
question: Which is locally destructive but almost never metastasizes?
options: The pearly lesion is basal cell carcinoma; the keratin-pearl ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma, which can metastasize
Both metastasize early to regional nodes as their usual course
Keratin pearls define basal cell carcinoma
A pearly rolled border is melanoma
Sun exposure protects against both
correctAnswer: The pearly lesion is basal cell carcinoma; the keratin-pearl ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma, which can metastasize
explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, pearly with telangiectasias, and it invades locally, rarely metastasizing. Squamous cell carcinoma makes keratin pearls, can arise in sun-damaged skin or scars, and does metastasize. Melanoma is a pigmented, ABCDE lesion of melanocytes, not these two. Keratin pearls are squamous. A rolled pearly border is basal cell. Ultraviolet light is the shared risk, not a protection.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A dark irregular mole is excised. The report argues about Clark versus Breslow. One margin description is a thickness of 3 mm. A student says the radial diameter on the skin is the number that decides prognosis, and that depth does not matter once the cells are malignant.
question: What measurement drives prognosis?
options: Breslow thickness, how deep the melanoma invades in millimeters, outweighs the width on the surface
The horizontal diameter is the sole prognostic number
Clark level is a millimeter measurement identical to Breslow
Depth does not matter if the color is uniform
A thicker tumor has a better prognosis because it has declared itself
correctAnswer: Breslow thickness, how deep the melanoma invades in millimeters, outweighs the width on the surface
explanation: Breslow depth is the strongest simple histologic predictor: deeper invasion means higher metastatic risk. The ugly width on the skin is how you notice it, not the number that sets prognosis. Clark level is an anatomic layer, not a millimeter scale, and Breslow has largely superseded it. Color irregularity is a detection clue, not a substitute for depth. Thicker tumors do worse, not better.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman has been on prednisone 20 mg daily for eight months for a vasculitis. She has a new vertebral fracture. Calcium is normal. A student says steroids only cause osteoporosis after a decade, and that they increase intestinal calcium absorption.
question: How do glucocorticoids weaken bone?
options: They decrease intestinal calcium absorption, increase urinary calcium loss, and suppress osteoblasts, so fracture risk rises within months
They increase osteoblast activity and bone density
Fractures require ten years of exposure
A normal serum calcium means the bone is unaffected
Steroids raise vitamin D action on the gut
correctAnswer: They decrease intestinal calcium absorption, increase urinary calcium loss, and suppress osteoblasts, so fracture risk rises within months
explanation: Glucocorticoids are a leading cause of secondary osteoporosis. They cut gut calcium absorption, waste calcium in urine, and turn off osteoblast bone formation, with more resorption early. Vertebral fractures happen early, not only after a decade. Serum calcium can stay normal while the skeleton is losing mineral, just as in primary osteoporosis. They impair, not enhance, vitamin D-mediated absorption.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: After an axillary lymph-node dissection a woman cannot push her arm forward against a wall without the scapula lifting off the chest. Shoulder shrug is intact. A student blames the dorsal scapular nerve and the trapezius.
question: Which nerve and muscle?
options: The long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior; trapezius winging would weaken the shrug via the accessory nerve
The accessory nerve, because shrug is lost in serratus injury
The thoracodorsal nerve, which wings the scapula
The axillary nerve, which protracts the scapula
Serratus anterior retracts the scapula
correctAnswer: The long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior; trapezius winging would weaken the shrug via the accessory nerve
explanation: Serratus anterior holds the scapula to the chest during forward push. The long thoracic nerve runs on the chest wall and is vulnerable in axillary surgery. Shrug is trapezius, accessory nerve, and it is intact, so this is not that palsy. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid. Serratus protracts and stabilizes; it does not retract.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man tries to make a fist and the index and middle fingers stay extended while the ring and little fingers flex. Sensation is reduced on the palmar thumb, index, and middle fingers. The injury is at the elbow, not the wrist. A student calls it an ulnar claw because the hand looks abnormal.
question: Which nerve, and why is the elbow level important?
options: The median nerve, which supplies the forearm finger flexors to digits 2 and 3; an ulnar claw is the opposite posture and is worse when the ulnar nerve fails more proximally for different muscles
The ulnar nerve, because digits 4 and 5 are the ones that stay extended
The radial nerve, because extended fingers mean wrist extensors
A wrist-level median injury produces the same loss of finger flexion
Benediction on attempting a fist is the resting claw of an ulnar palsy
correctAnswer: The median nerve, which supplies the forearm finger flexors to digits 2 and 3; an ulnar claw is the opposite posture and is worse when the ulnar nerve fails more proximally for different muscles
explanation: When the median nerve is out at the elbow, flexor digitorum superficialis and the median half of profundus are weak, so the patient cannot flex digits 2 and 3 when asked to make a fist. That active posture is the 'hand of benediction.' An ulnar claw is a resting posture of digits 4 and 5 from lost intrinsics, and those fingers are the ones that still flexed here. The radial nerve extends the wrist and MCP joints; it is not this sensory pattern. At the wrist the median nerve has already given off the forearm flexors, so a carpal-tunnel lesion does not block finger flexion. The test was an attempted fist, not the resting ulnar claw.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A student is asked why the liver can take up glucose only when the blood level is high after a meal, while muscle and brain phosphorylate glucose even when the level is low. She says both tissues use the same hexokinase with the same Km. A rare mutation of the beta-cell glucose sensor causes mild fasting hyperglycemia inherited from one parent.
question: Which enzyme is the high-Km sensor?
options: Glucokinase in liver and beta cells has a high Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so it works when glucose is high; hexokinase has a low Km and is product-inhibited
Hexokinase is the high-Km liver enzyme
Glucokinase is switched off by insulin
A glucokinase mutation lowers fasting glucose
Brain hexokinase stops working at normal glucose so the brain depends on glucokinase
correctAnswer: Glucokinase in liver and beta cells has a high Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so it works when glucose is high; hexokinase has a low Km and is product-inhibited
explanation: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) is the liver and beta-cell enzyme. Its high Km means it is active when glucose is abundant after a meal, and product inhibition does not shut it off, so the liver can keep taking glucose up to store glycogen. Hexokinase in muscle and brain has a low Km, works at fasting glucose, and is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. Calling them the same enzyme misses the sensor role. Glucokinase is induced in the fed state; it is not turned off by insulin. Heterozygous glucokinase mutations cause stable mild hyperglycemia (MODY2), not hypoglycemia. The brain relies on low-Km hexokinase so it is fed at ordinary glucose levels.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: In the fed state, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is high in the liver and glycolysis runs. In fasting, glucagon raises cAMP and the bifunctional enzyme switches. A student says fructose-2,6-bisphosphate inhibits PFK-1, and that glucagon increases glycolysis.
question: What does fructose-2,6-bisphosphate do to PFK-1, and what does glucagon do to it?
options: It activates PFK-1, pushing glycolysis; glucagon, via phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme, lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate so gluconeogenesis can proceed
It inhibits PFK-1, so the fed state is gluconeogenesis
Glucagon raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
PFK-1 is the gluconeogenic enzyme that makes glucose from lactate
The bifunctional enzyme is only in muscle, so the liver does not switch
correctAnswer: It activates PFK-1, pushing glycolysis; glucagon, via phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme, lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate so gluconeogenesis can proceed
explanation: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the feed-forward activator of phosphofructokinase-1, the committed step of glycolysis, and it inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. In the fed state insulin favors the kinase half of PFK-2 and the activator rises. Glucagon phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme, the phosphatase half wins, the activator falls, and the liver makes glucose. The student reversed both arrows. PFK-1 is glycolytic, not the enzyme that releases free glucose. The liver is exactly where this switch matters for blood glucose; muscle PFK-2 is regulated differently and does not run gluconeogenesis.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man with alcohol use disorder is given glucose and becomes confused with lactic acidosis and a low transketolase activity that corrects when a cofactor is added. Pyruvate is high. A student replaces biotin because carboxylases use it, and another gives riboflavin only.
question: Which cofactor is missing for both pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase?
options: Thiamine pyrophosphate; without it pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and the pentose pathway's transketolase fails
Biotin, the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase
Cobalamin, which is required for the decarboxylation of pyruvate
Pyridoxine, the cofactor that adds the acetyl group to coenzyme A
Glucose loading is safe before this vitamin because the enzymes do not use it
correctAnswer: Thiamine pyrophosphate; without it pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and the pentose pathway's transketolase fails
explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase needs thiamine, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD. Thiamine deficiency blocks pyruvate entry, lactate rises, and transketolase in the pentose pathway is the lab that improves when thiamine is added. Biotin is for carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase, not the dehydrogenase. B12 is for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase. Pyridoxine is transamination. Giving glucose before thiamine drives the blocked enzyme and can precipitate Wernicke injury.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: After 24 hours without food, a healthy student's insulin is low and glucagon is high. The liver is exporting glucose and making ketones. Muscle is using fatty acids. A classmate says the brain is using fatty acids directly and that insulin should be high because starvation is a stress.
question: What does the liver export, and what can the brain use?
options: The liver releases glucose from glycogen and gluconeogenesis and exports ketone bodies; the brain uses glucose and, later, ketones, not free fatty acids
Muscle glycogen keeps the blood glucose normal for days
High insulin in fasting drives ketogenesis
Fatty acids cross the blood-brain barrier as the main fuel on day one
Glucagon stores glycogen
correctAnswer: The liver releases glucose from glycogen and gluconeogenesis and exports ketone bodies; the brain uses glucose and, later, ketones, not free fatty acids
explanation: Low insulin and high glucagon turn on hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ketogenesis. Muscle glycogen is for the muscle; it does not maintain blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. Fatty acids are a fuel for muscle but do not meaningfully feed the brain. Ketones do. Insulin is low in fasting; high insulin would suppress ketogenesis and is the fed state. Glucagon promotes glycogen breakdown, not storage.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: During a sprint, muscle makes lactate. The liver turns that lactate back into glucose and sends it out. A student says the muscle itself runs gluconeogenesis and that the liver makes lactate as its main export during a sprint.
question: Which tissue releases lactate, and which makes the glucose?
options: Muscle (and red cells) release lactate; the liver uses lactate for gluconeogenesis, the Cori cycle
The liver releases lactate and muscle makes glucose
Lactate is a dead-end that cannot re-enter metabolism
Gluconeogenesis in muscle supplies the blood glucose of a sprint
The cycle costs no ATP, so it is free energy
correctAnswer: Muscle (and red cells) release lactate; the liver uses lactate for gluconeogenesis, the Cori cycle
explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis in muscle ends at lactate. The liver, which has the gluconeogenic enzymes including glucose-6-phosphatase, rebuilds glucose and returns it. Muscle cannot release free glucose. Lactate is a substrate, not a dead end. Assigning gluconeogenesis to muscle is the trap. The cycle costs ATP in the liver, which is why it shifts the energy burden off the exercising muscle rather than creating free energy.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man on a statin has less endogenous cholesterol made in the liver. LDL receptors on the liver increase. A student says statins block absorption of dietary cholesterol in the gut, and that less intracellular cholesterol would decrease LDL receptors.
question: What enzyme is blocked, and why do LDL receptors rise?
options: HMG-CoA reductase is blocked; the hepatocyte senses less cholesterol and puts more LDL receptors on the surface, clearing LDL from blood
Statins inhibit PCSK9 as their only action
Blocking the reductase raises intracellular cholesterol
LDL receptors fall when synthesis is blocked, so blood LDL rises
The enzyme blocked is lipoprotein lipase
correctAnswer: HMG-CoA reductase is blocked; the hepatocyte senses less cholesterol and puts more LDL receptors on the surface, clearing LDL from blood
explanation: The committed step of cholesterol synthesis is HMG-CoA reductase. Statins inhibit it. Lower cholesterol in the liver cell activates SREBP, which increases LDL-receptor expression, and blood LDL falls. That is not a block of intestinal absorption (ezetimibe) and not a direct PCSK9 inhibitor, although low cholesterol biology intersects that pathway. Synthesis falls, so intracellular cholesterol falls, it does not rise. Fewer receptors would raise blood LDL, the opposite of the drug's effect. Lipoprotein lipase clears chylomicrons and VLDL triglycerides.

references.label: Vanderah TW, Katzung BG. Katzung's Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 16th ed. McGraw Hill 2024

scenario: A 12-year-old has tendon xanthomas and an LDL cholesterol of 420 mg/dL. A parent had a heart attack at 40. Triglycerides are normal. A student calls it familial chylomicronemia because the number is high, and expects pancreatitis rather than coronary disease as the childhood emergency.
question: What is missing, and which lipid is high?
options: LDL receptors are absent or defective, so LDL cannot be cleared; triglycerides are not the particle in trouble
Lipoprotein lipase is missing, so chylomicrons cause pancreatitis
HDL is the particle that is markedly high
Tendon xanthomas are the sign of low LDL
The inheritance is autosomal recessive only, so a parent should be unaffected
correctAnswer: LDL receptors are absent or defective, so LDL cannot be cleared; triglycerides are not the particle in trouble
explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia is LDL-receptor (or apoB, or PCSK9) disease. LDL stays in the blood, tendons collect cholesterol, and coronary disease comes early. Heterozygotes already have very high LDL; homozygotes are worse. Chylomicronemia is lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency: sky-high triglycerides, pancreatitis, and eruptive xanthomas, not this LDL number with normal triglycerides. HDL is not the elevated particle. Xanthomas mean cholesterol is high. A parent with early disease fits dominant inheritance.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: On day three of a fast, a student's brain is using ketone bodies. The liver is making them but a biopsy discussion says the liver cannot oxidize them for its own ATP in the same way. A student says the liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase, which is why ketones are made in muscle.
question: Why can the liver not consume the ketones it exports?
options: The liver lacks thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase), so it cannot turn acetoacetate into acetoacetyl-CoA
The liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase, so it cannot make ketones
Muscle is the only tissue that makes ketone bodies
The brain cannot use ketones at any time
Ketogenesis is turned on by insulin
correctAnswer: The liver lacks thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase), so it cannot turn acetoacetate into acetoacetyl-CoA
explanation: Hepatocytes make acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate from HMG-CoA and export them. They lack the transferase that other tissues use to activate acetoacetate, so the liver does not burn its own ketones. HMG-CoA synthase is present in liver mitochondria and is required to make ketones; saying the liver lacks it reverses production and consumption. Muscle uses ketones and fatty acids; it is not the factory. After a couple of days the brain does use ketones, which spares glucose. Ketogenesis is a low-insulin, high-glucagon state.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has hypoketotic hypoglycemia when ill, elevated CK, and low free carnitine. Medium-chain fats are tolerated better than long-chain fats. A student gives him a high long-chain fat diet because fats are the treatment for a fasting problem, and says ketones should be high if hypoglycemia is real.
question: Why are ketones low, and why are long-chain fats the wrong meal?
options: Long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria without carnitine, so the liver cannot make ketones and the muscle cannot oxidize fat; medium chains bypass the shuttle
High ketones are required to diagnose a fatty-acid oxidation defect
Carnitine carries glucose, so low carnitine blocks glycolysis only
A high long-chain fat load restocks carnitine
Medium-chain fats need more carnitine than palmitate
correctAnswer: Long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria without carnitine, so the liver cannot make ketones and the muscle cannot oxidize fat; medium chains bypass the shuttle
explanation: Carnitine is required for the shuttle of long-chain acyl groups. Without it, beta oxidation fails, ketones are not made, glucose is the only fuel and runs out, and muscle is weak. That is hypoketotic hypoglycemia, the opposite of a high-ketone diabetic state. Carnitine does not carry glucose. Eating more long-chain fat gives substrate he cannot oxidize. Medium-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria without the carnitine shuttle, which is why they are the fat that is tolerated.

references.label: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A toddler who had a viral illness and stopped eating is found lethargic. Glucose is 30 mg/dL, urine ketones are absent, and the acylcarnitine profile shows medium-chain species. He had seemed well between illnesses. A student treats this as ordinary diabetic ketoacidosis because the child is ill and hypoglycemic.
question: What cannot be oxidized, and why is the illness the trigger?
options: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is missing, so medium-chain fats stall and ketones are not made when fasting removes carbohydrate
Insulin is high, as in diabetic ketoacidosis, and ketones should be large
The defect appears only after a high-carbohydrate meal
MCAD deficiency raises ketones higher than DKA
Between illnesses he should be chronically hypoglycemic every hour
correctAnswer: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is missing, so medium-chain fats stall and ketones are not made when fasting removes carbohydrate
explanation: MCAD deficiency blocks beta oxidation in the middle of the chain. When an illness stops feeding, hepatic ketogenesis fails and glucose falls without ketones, which can cause sudden death. Diabetic ketoacidosis has high ketones and, usually, high glucose. The danger is fasting, not a carbohydrate load. Ketones are inappropriately low, not higher than DKA. Between fasts he can look well, which is why the newborn screen and the illness history matter.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Two infants have high ammonia and low BUN after protein feeds. Infant A has low orotic acid. Infant B, a boy, has high orotic acid and no megaloblastic anemia. A student treats both as orotic aciduria with uridine and says the urea cycle is intact because orotic acid is a pyrimidine.
question: Which enzyme is out in the boy?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase; carbamoyl phosphate spills into orotic acid. Infant A is earlier, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, so orotic acid is not made
Both lack orotidine decarboxylase, the megaloblastic disease
Arginase deficiency raises orotic acid and BUN
OTC deficiency lowers orotic acid
Uridine monotherapy clears the ammonia in OTC deficiency
correctAnswer: Ornithine transcarbamylase; carbamoyl phosphate spills into orotic acid. Infant A is earlier, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, so orotic acid is not made
explanation: If carbamoyl phosphate is made but cannot enter the urea cycle at OTC, it leaks into pyrimidine synthesis and orotic acid rises, with hyperammonemia and no megaloblastic anemia. If CPS-I itself fails, carbamoyl phosphate is not made, so orotic acid stays low and ammonia still rises. Hereditary orotic aciduria is a later pyrimidine-synthesis defect with megaloblastic anemia and no ammonia storm.
