scenario: A smoker has a central lung mass, profound weakness, and a very high cortisol that does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. ACTH is high. Another smoker has a peripheral lung mass, high calcium, low PTH, and no bone metastases on the scan. A student says both secrete PTH and both will suppress with high-dose steroid.
question: Which tumor secretes what?
options: Small-cell carcinoma secretes ACTH; squamous carcinoma secretes PTHrP, which suppresses real PTH
Both secrete PTH
Squamous carcinoma secretes ACTH and suppresses with dexamethasone
High-dose dexamethasone suppresses ectopic ACTH
PTHrP raises PTH on the assay
correctAnswer: Small-cell carcinoma secretes ACTH; squamous carcinoma secretes PTHrP, which suppresses real PTH
explanation: Small-cell lung cancer is central and neuroendocrine and makes ACTH. Ectopic ACTH usually does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone, unlike a pituitary adenoma. Squamous cancer is often peripheral or central and makes PTHrP, which acts like PTH but is not detected as PTH, so the PTH assay is low and calcium is high without bone metastases. They are not the same peptide. Squamous cancer is the calcium tumor, not the ACTH one. Ectopic ACTH resists high-dose suppression. PTHrP does not raise the PTH assay.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man with metastatic cancer loses fat and muscle despite a feeding plan. He is not simply starving in a way that the body can adapt by lowering metabolic rate. A student says the loss is only reduced intake, and that TNF lowers metabolic rate.
question: What cytokine drives this, and how is it different from starvation?
options: TNF and related cytokines raise metabolic rate and waste both fat and muscle; starvation preferentially uses fat and lowers the metabolic rate
Starvation and cachexia are identical metabolically
TNF increases appetite
Muscle is spared in cachexia
Feeding fully reverses cytokine cachexia the way it reverses pure starvation
correctAnswer: TNF and related cytokines raise metabolic rate and waste both fat and muscle; starvation preferentially uses fat and lowers the metabolic rate
explanation: Cancer cachexia is inflammatory. TNF (cachectin), IL-1, and IL-6 raise resting energy expenditure and break down muscle as well as fat. Simple starvation lowers the metabolic rate and prefers fat while sparing protein longer. The patterns are not identical. TNF suppresses appetite and still wastes tissue beyond intake. Muscle is not spared. Calories help starvation more completely than they reverse a cytokine-driven cachexia.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child burns severely in little sun and has many skin cancers. Nucleotide excision repair of thymine dimers is broken. Another family has colon cancers and a broken mismatch-repair gene. A student says both cannot repair double-strand breaks, the BRCA job, and that thymine dimers are a mismatch problem.
question: Which repair fits the sun?
options: Nucleotide excision repair removes ultraviolet dimers; mismatch repair fixes replication errors and is Lynch syndrome, not the sun disease
Mismatch repair is the xeroderma pigmentosum pathway
BRCA1 repairs thymine dimers
Ultraviolet light causes double-strand breaks as its main lesion
Lynch syndrome is extreme sun sensitivity
correctAnswer: Nucleotide excision repair removes ultraviolet dimers; mismatch repair fixes replication errors and is Lynch syndrome, not the sun disease
explanation: Ultraviolet light fuses adjacent pyrimidines. Nucleotide excision repair cuts out the dimer; that pathway is xeroderma pigmentosum, with skin cancers. Mismatch repair fixes base-base errors after replication; germline loss is Lynch syndrome and microsatellite cancers, not photosensitivity. BRCA proteins help repair double-strand breaks. Dimers are bulky adducts, not the classic double-strand break. Lynch patients are not the children who burn in minutes.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has unsteady gait, dilated vessels on the eyes, low immunoglobulins, and a high AFP. Radiation for a different indication would be dangerous. A student calls it Friedreich ataxia because of the gait, and says DNA repair is intact.
question: What is not repaired, and why the vessels and the AFP?
options: ATM kinase, which answers double-strand breaks, is missing; telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, and a high AFP come with the cerebellar ataxia
Frataxin is missing, so AFP is high and telangiectasias are required
The disease is pure motor and DNA repair is normal
Immunoglobulins are high
Radiation is the safest imaging because the cells repair breaks well
correctAnswer: ATM kinase, which answers double-strand breaks, is missing; telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, and a high AFP come with the cerebellar ataxia
explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is ATM. Double-strand breaks are not signaled, so radiation and radiomimetic drugs are dangerous, IgA is often low, sinopulmonary infections occur, AFP is high, and the cerebellum fails. Friedreich ataxia is frataxin, dorsal columns, and cardiomyopathy, without telangiectasias or a high AFP. Repair is not intact. Immunoglobulins are low, not high. Radiation is exactly what these cells handle badly.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: Patient A has a long-bone fracture and a petechial rash and confusion a day later. Patient B has calf swelling and then sudden chest pain and a clear chest film. Patient C, after delivery, has sudden dyspnea and seizures. A student says all three are thrombotic pulmonary emboli and all have wedge infarcts on the film.
question: Which one is fat, and which is amniotic?
options: A is fat embolism with the rash and neurologic change; C is amniotic-fluid embolism with a consumptive picture around delivery; B is the thrombus
All three are thrombus because all cause dyspnea
Fat embolism is a cholesterol crystal from an atherosclerotic plaque
Amniotic embolism is a clot from the calf
The chest film is always abnormal in pulmonary thromboembolism
correctAnswer: A is fat embolism with the rash and neurologic change; C is amniotic-fluid embolism with a consumptive picture around delivery; B is the thrombus
explanation: Fat embolism after a long-bone fracture sends marrow fat to the lung and brain and causes a petechial rash. Amniotic-fluid embolism is a peripartum catastrophe of sudden hypoxia, seizure or collapse, and often DIC. Venous thrombus from the leg is the classic pulmonary embolus, and the film is often normal. Dyspnea does not make them the same. Atherosclerotic cholesterol emboli follow a procedure on an artery and infarct toes and kidneys, with eosinophils. Amniotic fluid is not a calf clot. A normal film does not exclude thromboembolism.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: After prolonged hypotension a pathologist sees a pale renal cortex and a congested medulla, patchy liver necrosis around central veins, and a bowel with hemorrhagic mucosa. The brain shows watershed injury. A student says the liver dies first around the portal tract because that is farthest from blood.
question: Which liver zone, and why the kidney cortex?
options: Zone 3 around the central vein is last in the liver's oxygen gradient; the renal cortex is also relatively under-supplied when pressure falls
Zone 1 around the portal tract is the most ischemic
The renal medulla is the first and only renal injury
The bowel is spared in shock because it has a dual blood supply that never fails
Watershed brain injury means the brainstem only
correctAnswer: Zone 3 around the central vein is last in the liver's oxygen gradient; the renal cortex is also relatively under-supplied when pressure falls
explanation: Hepatic blood runs from portal tract to central vein, so zone 3 is the least oxygenated and necroses in shock. The renal cortex, with its filtration demand, shows pale cortical necrosis or tubular injury when pressure falls; the medulla is congested. Zone 1 is best oxygenated. The medulla is vulnerable to some injuries but the classic shock kidney description is cortical pallor. The gut mucosa is a shock target, not a protected dual-supply organ in this setting. Watershed injury is the cortical border zones, not the brainstem alone.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man with type 1 diabetes has high morning glucose. At 3 a.m. his glucose is 48 mg/dL and he wakes sweaty. A second patient has a 3 a.m. glucose of 160 mg/dL and a higher value at 7 a.m. A student raises the bedtime insulin for both.
question: Who needs less night insulin, and who is showing a dawn rise?
options: The first has rebound hyperglycemia after nocturnal hypoglycemia, so night insulin should fall; the second has a dawn rise in counter-regulatory hormones and may need more basal insulin
Both need a higher bedtime dose
The 3 a.m. low means the dawn phenomenon and more insulin
The 3 a.m. high means rebound from an unmeasured low
Morning highs are always from too little dinner carbohydrate
correctAnswer: The first has rebound hyperglycemia after nocturnal hypoglycemia, so night insulin should fall; the second has a dawn rise in counter-regulatory hormones and may need more basal insulin
explanation: The Somogyi effect is overnight hypoglycemia followed by counter-regulatory hormones that overshoot, so the morning glucose is high because the night dose was too strong. You lower it. The dawn phenomenon is an early-morning growth-hormone and cortisol rise with no preceding low, so basal insulin may need to go up. Raising both doses would worsen the first patient's nights. A 3 a.m. low is not the dawn phenomenon. A 3 a.m. high was never a hidden low. Dinner carbohydrate is not the separator these two clock times provide.

references.label: American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026. Diabetes Care 2026

scenario: A boy has severe sinopulmonary infections and a low IgG and IgA with a high or normal IgM. He cannot make germinal centers. CD40 ligand is the protein under discussion. A student says he has Bruton disease because he is a boy with low immunoglobulin, and expects all isotypes including IgM to be absent.
question: What interaction failed?
options: T-cell CD40 ligand cannot tell B cells to class-switch, so IgM stays and other isotypes do not appear
Bruton tyrosine kinase is gone, so IgM is absent too
The defect is neutrophil oxidase, so immunoglobulins are normal
CD40 ligand excess causes the high IgM
Class switching is a T-cell-independent event that does not need CD40
correctAnswer: T-cell CD40 ligand cannot tell B cells to class-switch, so IgM stays and other isotypes do not appear
explanation: Hyper-IgM syndrome is often X-linked CD40 ligand deficiency. B cells can make IgM but cannot switch to IgG, IgA, or IgE, and germinal centers fail, so opportunistic infections occur as well as pyogenic ones. Bruton disease loses all B cells and all isotypes, including IgM. Chronic granulomatous disease is an oxidase defect with normal immunoglobulin amounts. The ligand is missing, not excessive. Class switch requires T-cell help through CD40; it is not purely T-independent.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A patient has recurrent sinus infections and a history of anaphylaxis during a blood transfusion. IgA is undetectable. IgG and IgM are normal. A student says he needs IVIG as the only replacement, and that the transfusion reaction was ABO incompatibility because he wheezed.
question: Why the transfusion reaction?
options: He has made IgG against the IgA present in donor blood; IVIG also contains some IgA and is not a simple replacement
IgA deficiency removes IgG as well
ABO mismatch is the usual cause of anaphylaxis with a normal IgA
IgM is the antibody that reacts to donor IgA
Selective IgA deficiency presents with no infections
correctAnswer: He has made IgG against the IgA present in donor blood; IVIG also contains some IgA and is not a simple replacement
explanation: The most common primary immunodeficiency is selective IgA deficiency. Mucosal infections and giardia are typical, and some patients form anti-IgA IgG. Donor blood contains IgA and can trigger anaphylaxis. Washed cells are used. Standard IVIG contains traces of IgA and can do the same, and it does not replace IgA at the mucosa anyway. Other isotypes are present, which is why it is selective. ABO hemolysis is fever, back pain, and hemoglobinuria, not isolated anaphylaxis with absent IgA. The pathogenic antibody is IgG against IgA, not IgM. Infections do occur.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A boy is well for the first months of life and then has recurrent pneumonias and otitis after maternal antibody fades. B cells are absent. Tonsils are tiny. T cells are present. A sister is healthy. A student expects viral and fungal infections as the dominant problem and a low T-cell count.
question: Which kinase, and which infections?
options: Bruton tyrosine kinase blocks B-cell maturation; pyogenic bacteria dominate after maternal IgG wanes, and T-cell infections are not the lead
Adenosine deaminase, so T and B cells are both absent from birth
Fungal disease is the classic Bruton infection
Tonsils are enlarged
The disease is autosomal and his sister should be equally affected
correctAnswer: Bruton tyrosine kinase blocks B-cell maturation; pyogenic bacteria dominate after maternal IgG wanes, and T-cell infections are not the lead
explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is a block from pro-B to pre-B cell because Bruton tyrosine kinase is gone. There are no B cells, no tonsils, and no immunoglobulin of his own. Maternal IgG protects early, then bacteria with capsules take over. T cells work, so viruses and fungi are not the signature the way they are in SCID. ADA deficiency empties T and B cells. Fungal disease points away from a pure B-cell defect. Tonsils are absent, not big. A healthy sister fits X-linked inheritance.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has recurrent pyogenic infections, partial albinism, and giant granules in neutrophils. Platelets do not function well and he bruises. A student calls it chronic granulomatous disease because of the infections, and expects a normal burst test to be the only abnormality, with no pigment finding.
question: What trafficking step failed?
options: Microtubule polymerization and lysosomal trafficking fail, so granules are giant and melanosomes and neutrophil granules do not deliver; the oxidative burst itself can be present
NADPH oxidase is absent, so albinism is required
CD18 is absent, so there is no pus and the granules are normal size
Giant granules mean the cells kill bacteria better
Albinism here is oculocutaneous albinism type 1 with a normal immune system
correctAnswer: Microtubule polymerization and lysosomal trafficking fail, so granules are giant and melanosomes and neutrophil granules do not deliver; the oxidative burst itself can be present
explanation: Chediak-Higashi is LYST dysfunction. Secretory lysosomes, melanosomes, and neutrophil granules do not traffic, so partial albinism, giant granules, infections, and a bleeding platelet defect travel together. A later accelerated phase looks like hemophagocytosis. CGD is the oxidase, without this pigment and granule picture. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency has no pus and normal-sized granules. The granules do not improve killing; they fail to deliver. Ordinary albinism does not fill neutrophils with giant granules.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A child has coarse facies, retained baby teeth, recurrent staphylococcal abscesses that are oddly cold, eczema, and a very high IgE. Eosinophils are up. A student says the abscesses are cold because the bacteria are dead, and that IgE this high means acute allergy only.
question: Which cytokine signal failed, and why are the abscesses cold?
options: STAT3 and Th17 signaling fail, so neutrophil recruitment is poor and staphylococcal abscesses lack the usual heat; IgE is markedly high
NADPH oxidase has failed
The cold abscess means good neutrophil recruitment
IgE is low in this syndrome
Retained teeth are unrelated to the immune defect
correctAnswer: STAT3 and Th17 signaling fail, so neutrophil recruitment is poor and staphylococcal abscesses lack the usual heat; IgE is markedly high
explanation: Hyper-IgE syndrome is STAT3. Th17 cells do not form, IL-17 does not call neutrophils properly, and staphylococcal abscesses are 'cold.' IgE and eosinophils are high, eczema is present, and nonimmune connective-tissue findings include retained primary teeth, coarse face, and fractures. This is not the oxidase defect of CGD. Cold means poor inflammation, not better recruitment. IgE is high, which is the name of the syndrome. The dental finding is part of the STAT3 phenotype, not a coincidence.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A boy has eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections. IgM is low and IgA and IgE are high. A maternal uncle died of bleeding and infection. A student says the platelets are large, as in Bernard-Soulier, and that the inheritance is autosomal.
question: What cytoskeletal link failed, and what do the platelets look like?
options: WASP, which links receptors to the actin cytoskeleton, is gone; platelets are small, and the triad is eczema, microthrombocytopenia, and infections
Platelets are giant and the gene is autosomal
IgM is high and IgE is low
The disease is pure B-cell failure without a bleeding problem
A healthy maternal uncle would be the expected family pattern
correctAnswer: WASP, which links receptors to the actin cytoskeleton, is gone; platelets are small, and the triad is eczema, microthrombocytopenia, and infections
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich is X-linked WASP. Actin remodeling fails in immune synapses and platelets. The classic triad is eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and infections, with low IgM and high IgA and IgE, and a risk of lymphoma. Bernard-Soulier platelets are giant. IgM is low, not high. Bleeding is part of the disease, not absent. Diseased uncles on the mother's side fit X-linkage; a healthy one would not be the teaching family.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A woman who was transfused years ago during a pregnancy gets a unit of blood. She is fine that day. A week later her hemoglobin has fallen, the bilirubin is up, and the direct antiglobulin test is positive. She did not have fever and back pain during the transfusion. A student calls it acute ABO hemolysis because any post-transfusion anemia is immediate complement lysis.
question: What kind of antibody returned?
options: An anamnestic IgG against a minor red-cell antigen, too low to detect on the crossmatch, rose over days and caused extravascular hemolysis
ABO IgM, which always waits a week
TRALI, because the hemoglobin fell
The crossmatch would have been incompatible if any antibody memory existed
A positive direct antiglobulin test a week later means the unit was never given
correctAnswer: An anamnestic IgG against a minor red-cell antigen, too low to detect on the crossmatch, rose over days and caused extravascular hemolysis
explanation: Delayed hemolytic reactions are memory IgG against antigens such as Kidd or Duffy. The titer was below detection at the crossmatch, exposure boosts it, and days later coated cells are removed outside the vessels. It is not the immediate intravascular ABO disaster. ABO IgM acts in minutes. TRALI is pulmonary edema, not a falling hemoglobin with a positive Coombs test. A negative crossmatch does not prove there was never any memory; the antibody can be below the threshold. The positive direct antiglobulin test is the coated donor cells still circulating.

references.label: Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC. Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease. 10th ed. Elsevier 2021

scenario: A man two weeks after an allogeneic marrow transplant has a rash on the palms and soles, diarrhea, and a rising bilirubin. The donor cells are attacking. A student says this is host-versus-graft rejection of the marrow, and that the skin, gut, and liver are spared in graft-versus-host disease.
question: Which direction is the attack?
options: Donor T cells recognize host tissues; skin, gut, and liver are the targets of acute graft-versus-host disease
The host immune system is rejecting the graft, which is why the rash is host-versus-graft
Graft-versus-host disease spares the liver
The reaction is antibody against neutrophils only
Palms and soles are spared, so this rash is not graft-versus-host
correctAnswer: Donor T cells recognize host tissues; skin, gut, and liver are the targets of acute graft-versus-host disease
explanation: In graft-versus-host disease the transplanted immune system attacks the immunosuppressed host. Acute disease hits skin (often palms and soles), the gut (diarrhea), and the liver (bilirubin). Host-versus-graft is rejection of the organ, the opposite arrow, and would look like loss of the graft rather than this triad. The liver is a classic target. This is T-cell mediated tissue injury, not isolated antineutrophil antibody. Palm and sole involvement is typical, not a reason to exclude the diagnosis.
